This demo takes a few seconds to load (up to a minute on a slow connection, because the first fit runs in your browser) and runs entirely in your browser (NumPy and matplotlib via Pyodide; no tgmm or PyTorch is involved). It mirrors how tutorial 01 builds its synthetic data with tgmm.generate_gmm_data, and the EM fit it then runs with GaussianMixture (covariance_type='full').

Each blob is a Gaussian with a centre \(\mu_k\), a covariance \(\Sigma_k=R(\theta_k)\,\operatorname{diag}(s_{k1}^2,s_{k2}^2)\,R(\theta_k)^{\top}\) (standard deviations \(s_{k1},s_{k2}\) along two axes rotated by \(\theta_k\)), and a number of points \(n_k\), so the mixing weights are \(\pi_k=n_k/n\). Points are drawn as \(x=\mu_k+L_kz\) with \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) and \(L_kL_k^{\top}=\Sigma_k\) (a Cholesky factor), which is what generate_gmm_data does, so the covariance you see in the table is the covariance you get. Pick a preset, or move the sliders (they update when released); Reset blobs returns to the chosen preset. Preset values are rounded to the slider grid, so the tutorial blobs are reproduced to within about 1% for the covariance entries.

The preset Tutorial 01 before the covariance fix uses the squares \(\Sigma^{\top}\Sigma\) of the requested matrices: before the fix, generate_gmm_data sampled Z @ cov, so a requested cov really produced \(\operatorname{cov}^{\top}\operatorname{cov}\).

docs.title: Fit a mixture to your data
docs.text: What to look for: with the well separated preset the BIC minimum sits at the true \(K=3\), and fitting fewer components merges blobs while fitting more splits one of them. With the overlapping preset BIC typically prefers fewer components than you designed, because heavily overlapping blobs look like a single broader one: the same effect that makes the choice of \(K\) hard in practice (see the model selection tutorial). Make one blob tiny (a small \(n_k\)) and watch it disappear from the BIC preference first. The code budget for this page is about 150 lines of Python.

docs.title: EM Step by Step
docs.text:
This demo takes a few seconds to load and runs entirely in your browser (NumPy and matplotlib via Pyodide; no tgmm or PyTorch is involved). It mirrors the E- and M-steps of GaussianMixture in one dimension, together with its algorithm='em' | 'cem' | 'sem' options (see Fitting algorithms).

Two Gaussian components are fitted to 200 fixed points, starting from deliberately bad means. E-step computes the responsibilities

\[r_{ik}=\frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\sigma_k^2)}{\sum_j\pi_j\,\mathcal N(x_i\mid\mu_j,\sigma_j^2)},\]

and M-step re-estimates the parameters from them, with \(n_k=\sum_i r_{ik}\):

\[\pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n},\qquad \mu_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}x_i,\qquad \sigma_k^2=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k)^2.\]

The algorithms differ only in the E-step's output: EM keeps the soft \(r_{ik}\), CEM replaces them by the hard \(\arg\max\) assignment, SEM samples each assignment from \(r_{i\cdot}\) (seeded, so the page is reproducible). The M-step is applied to whatever the E-step produced.

Changing the algorithm resets the fit. M-step first runs an E-step if the responsibilities are stale, so E then M is one EM iteration, and Run 10 does ten.

What to look for: with EM the log-likelihood never decreases, and from this symmetric-ish start it first crawls along a plateau before climbing; CEM jumps to a (crisp, hard-partition) fixed point within a step or two and then stops changing; SEM keeps jittering around a stationary level because each assignment is resampled (that is why tgmm never declares SEM converged and offers 'saem' for a convergent variant).

docs.title: GPCM Covariance Shapes
docs.text:
This demo takes a few seconds to load and runs entirely in your browser (NumPy and matplotlib via Pyodide; no tgmm or PyTorch is involved). It mirrors the covariance parameterisation of GaussianMixture(covariance_type=...) (API: tgmm.covariance.gpcm).

Each component's covariance is split into three factors,

\[\Sigma_k=\lambda_k\,D_k\,A_k\,D_k^{\top},\qquad \det A_k=1,\quad D_k^{\top}D_k=I,\]

a volume \(\lambda_k\) (size), a shape \(A_k=\operatorname{diag}(a_{k1},a_{k2})\) (elongation, \(a_{k1}/a_{k2}\) is the axis ratio) and an orientation \(D_k\) (rotation by \(\theta_k\)). For two components, choose for each factor whether the components share it (E, equal: component 2 copies component 1), let it V**ary (each has its own sliders) or, for shape and orientation, fix it to the **I**dentity (**I: a circle, or no rotation). The three letters give the model's mclust code.

Component 2's slider is ignored whenever its factor is E (it copies component 1), and both shape sliders are ignored for shape I (both orientation sliders for orientation I).

Things to try: with EII / VII both shapes are circles (identity), EEE shares everything (the same ellipse twice), and VVV frees all three factors. The parameter count is what bic/aic charge for the covariances, which is why constrained models win on small data (see the Covariance Structures tutorial).

docs.title: Clustering Metrics and Model Selection
docs.text:
This demo takes a few seconds to load and runs entirely in your browser (NumPy, SciPy and matplotlib via Pyodide; no tgmm or PyTorch involved).

Three Gaussian blobs, a k-means clustering with the \(K\) you choose, and every index of ClusteringMetrics recomputed live with the same formulas. Move the separation slider to watch the indices degrade as the blobs overlap, change \(K\) to see which indices are fooled, and switch on noise (uniform background points). tgmm treats noise by dropping the points labelled as noise and scaling the index by \(f=(n-n_{\text{noise}})/n\) (multiplied for higher-is-better, divided for lower-is-better indexes); the second column below does that, the first lets k-means swallow the noise into clusters.

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Separation: as the blobs overlap, silhouette and Calinski–Harabasz fall and Davies–Bouldin and WB rise. Dunn is the most erratic (it rests on one closest pair and one widest cluster), which is why tgmm's documentation ranks it behind the others; at low separation its best \(K\) jumps around while silhouette and CH keep pointing at \(K=3\).
  • K: at high separation almost every index peaks at the true \(K=3\); when the blobs overlap, WB-index and Davies–Bouldin (and Dunn) are the ones that wander.
  • Noise: the noise points are known here, so the second column drops them (label \(-1\)) and scales by \((n-n_{\text{noise}})/n\). Calinski–Harabasz, WB and Dunn improve a lot; silhouette and Davies–Bouldin barely move. The GMM panel cannot drop noise: it tends to spend an extra component on the background, so BIC and ICL often pick \(K=4\) or \(5\) when noise is switched on.
  • BIC vs. ICL: both are \(-2\log L+p\log n\); ICL adds \(-2\sum_i\log\max_k\tau_{ik}\), which is near 0 for well-separated components and large when they overlap. Around separation \(\approx3\) ICL already prefers fewer components than BIC, because it penalises solutions whose clusters are not clearly distinguishable (see the Model Selection tutorial).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python: 3.9 or higher (the minimum supported by PyTorch 2.5)
  • PyTorch: 2.5 or higher (torch>=2.5.1 in requirements.txt)
  • NumPy: for numerical operations
  • SciPy: special functions and distributions (the von Mises-Fisher Bessel functions, chi-squared quantiles, Hungarian label matching)
  • Matplotlib and seaborn: tgmm.plotting, which import tgmm loads
  • tqdm: progress bars in HDBSCAN

import tgmm imports all of the above at start-up, so all must be installed. If a plain pip install tgmm does not pull them in automatically, install them explicitly:

pip install scipy matplotlib seaborn tqdm

docs.title: From PyPI (Recommended)
docs.text:
The easiest way to install tgmm is using pip:

pip install tgmm

This will install the latest stable release along with all required dependencies.

docs.title: From Source (Development)
docs.text:
For the latest features or if you want to contribute:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/adriansousapoza/tgmm.git
cd tgmm

# Install in editable mode
pip install -e .

The -e flag installs in editable mode, so changes to the source code are immediately available.

docs.title: With GPU Support
docs.text:
tgmm automatically uses CUDA if available. To enable GPU acceleration:

  1. Install CUDA-enabled PyTorch following the official PyTorch installation guide

  2. Verify CUDA availability: 

    import torch
print(f"CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}")
print(f"CUDA device: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")

  3. Use GPU in tgmm: 

    from tgmm import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, device='cuda')
gmm.fit(X)  # X will be automatically moved to GPU

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
For running the tutorial notebooks (scikit-learn is used by some notebooks for datasets and PCA, pandas for the select_model(...).to_dataframe() tables):

pip install jupyter scikit-learn pandas tqdm
# from a source checkout, the "examples" extra installs tqdm and pandas:
pip install -e ".[examples]"

For running the test suite (mpmath supplies reference Bessel values for the von Mises-Fisher tests):

pip install -e ".[test]"

For building this documentation:

pip install -e ".[docs]"   # mkdocs, mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings, mkdocs-jupyter, pymdown-extensions
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Verify your installation:

import tgmm
print(f"tgmm version: {tgmm.__version__}")

# Test basic functionality
from tgmm import GaussianMixture
import torch

X = torch.randn(100, 2)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X)
labels = gmm.predict(X)
print(f"Fitted GMM with {gmm.n_components} components")
print(f"Converged: {gmm.converged_}")

docs.title: Import Errors
docs.text:
If you encounter import errors:

# Ensure all dependencies are installed
pip install torch numpy scipy matplotlib seaborn tqdm

# Reinstall tgmm
pip uninstall tgmm
pip install tgmm

docs.title: CUDA Errors
docs.text:
If you have CUDA-related issues:

  1. Check PyTorch CUDA installation: 

    import torch
print(torch.version.cuda)  # Should show CUDA version

  2. Fall back to CPU: 

    gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, device='cpu')

docs.title: Version Conflicts
docs.text:
If you have version conflicts with dependencies:

# Create a fresh virtual environment
python -m venv tgmm_env
source tgmm_env/bin/activate  # On Windows: tgmm_env\Scripts\activate

# Install tgmm
pip install tgmm

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: This guide will get you up and running with tgmm in minutes.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
The typical workflow with tgmm consists of four steps:

  1. Create a GaussianMixture instance
  2. Fit the model to your data
  3. Predict cluster assignments
  4. Evaluate or visualize results

docs.title: Your First GMM
docs.text:
Let's fit a simple Gaussian Mixture Model:

import torch
import numpy as np
from tgmm import GaussianMixture

# Generate some synthetic data
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.vstack([
    np.random.randn(100, 2) + [0, 0],     # Cluster 1
    np.random.randn(100, 2) + [5, 5],     # Cluster 2
    np.random.randn(100, 2) + [0, 5]      # Cluster 3
])
X = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)

# Create and fit GMM
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X)

# Get cluster assignments
labels = gmm.predict(X)
probabilities = gmm.predict_proba(X)

print(f"Model converged: {gmm.converged_}")
print(f"Final log-likelihood: {gmm.lower_bound_:.2f}")
print(f"Cluster assignments: {labels[:10]}")

docs.title: Choosing Covariance Type
docs.text:
The covariance_type parameter controls the shape of clusters:

# Full covariance - arbitrary ellipses (most flexible)
gmm_full = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='full')

# Diagonal covariance - axis-aligned ellipses
gmm_diag = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='diag')

# Spherical covariance - circles (least flexible, fastest)
gmm_sph = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='spherical')

# Tied full - all clusters share the same full covariance
gmm_tied = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='tied_full')

# Any of the 14 mclust/GPCM codes, e.g. shared orientation, per-cluster volume and shape
gmm_eve = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='VVE')

docs.title: When to Use Each Type
docs.text:
Type Use When Advantages Disadvantages full Clusters can have any shape/orientation Most flexible Most parameters, slowest diag Features are independent Faster than full Cannot capture correlations spherical Clusters are roughly circular Fastest, fewest parameters Very restrictive tied_* All clusters have similar shapes Fewer parameters Less flexible GPCM codes ('EVE', 'VEV', ...) Something in between: e.g. same orientation but different sizes Systematic family between tied_full and full MLE only (no priors, no Gibbs mode) for the 8 codes without a classic name

The number of free covariance parameters grows from 1 (tied_spherical) to \(K\,d(d+1)/2\) (full); see the Gaussian Mixture Model guide and GPCM Covariance Models for the exact update equations and parameter counts, and the Covariance Structures tutorial for a visual comparison.

docs.title: Initialization Methods
docs.text:
Good initialization is crucial for EM convergence:

# K-means initialization (recommended, default)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means='kmeans')

# K-means++ initialization (better for difficult cases)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means='kpp')

# Random initialization
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means='random')

# Custom initialization with provided means
initial_means = torch.tensor([[0, 0], [5, 5], [0, 5]], dtype=torch.float32)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means=initial_means)

docs.title: Multiple Random Restarts
docs.text:
To avoid local minima, use multiple initializations:

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    n_init=10,  # Try 10 different initializations
    random_state=42  # For reproducibility
)
gmm.fit(X)

# The model will automatically select the best result
print(f"Best log-likelihood: {gmm.lower_bound_:.2f}")

docs.title: GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
Enable GPU acceleration for large datasets:

# Check if CUDA is available
device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'

# Create GMM on GPU
gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    device=device
)

# Fit on GPU
gmm.fit(X)  # X will be automatically moved to GPU

# Predictions on GPU
labels = gmm.predict(X)

docs.title: Monitoring Convergence
docs.text:
Track the training process:

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    verbose=True,          # Enable progress output
    verbose_interval=5,    # Print every 5 iterations
    max_iter=200,          # Maximum iterations
    tol=1e-4              # Convergence tolerance
)
gmm.fit(X)

# Check convergence
if gmm.converged_:
    print(f"Converged in {gmm.n_iter_} iterations")
else:
    print(f"Did not converge after {gmm.max_iter} iterations")

docs.title: Generating Samples
docs.text:
Generate new samples from the fitted model:

# Generate 100 new samples
new_samples, component_ids = gmm.sample(100)

print(f"Generated {new_samples.shape[0]} samples")
print(f"Sample from component: {component_ids[:10]}")

# Sample from a specific component
samples_from_comp_0, _ = gmm.sample(50, component=0)

# Sample within confidence region
samples_95, _ = gmm.sample(100, confidence=0.95)

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text:
Compare models with the information criteria. BIC \(=-2\ell+p\ln n\) and AIC \(=-2\ell+2p\) trade the log-likelihood \(\ell\) against the number of free parameters \(p\) (lower is better); ICL additionally penalizes overlapping clusters:

for k in range(2, 10):
    gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=k, n_features=2, random_state=42)
    gmm.fit(X)
    print(f"k={k}: BIC={gmm.bic(X):.1f}  AIC={gmm.aic(X):.1f}  ICL={gmm.icl(X):.1f}")

select_model does the whole sweep over n_components and covariance structures (all 14 GPCM codes by default) and returns the best fit:

from tgmm import select_model

result = select_model(X, n_components=range(1, 8), criterion='bic', random_state=42)
print(result.best_.covariance_type_, result.best_.n_components)
result.to_dataframe().sort_values('bic').head()

Label-free validity indices such as the silhouette score are also available:

from tgmm import ClusteringMetrics

labels = gmm.predict(X)
score = ClusteringMetrics.silhouette_score(X, labels, n_components=gmm.n_components)

If you do not want to choose \(K\) at all, GaussianMixture(n_components=None, ...) infers it with a Dirichlet-process Gibbs sampler (see the user guide).

docs.title: Other Fitting Options
docs.text:
# Stochastic EM / SAEM / classification EM: other variants of the fitting loop
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, algorithm='saem')

# Deterministic annealing: smooth the likelihood early on to avoid poor local optima
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, temperature=(0.1, 30))

# Mini-batch / online EM for large or streaming data
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, batch_size=256, step_size='auto', max_iter=10)

# Partially labeled data: -1 marks unknown labels (semi-supervised EM)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2).fit(X, labels=y_partial)

docs.title: Other Mixture Families
docs.text:
from tgmm import StudentTMixture, VonMisesFisherMixture

# Robust to outliers: heavy-tailed components
stm = StudentTMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2).fit(X)

# Directions on the unit sphere (rows of X_unit must have unit L2 norm)
vmf = VonMisesFisherMixture(n_components=5).fit(X_unit)

Both share GaussianMixture's fit / predict / bic / algorithm options; see Other Mixture Families. For positive-unlabeled data see PositiveUnlabeledMixture in Semi-Supervised and PU Fitting.

docs.title: Saving and Loading Models
docs.text:
Persist trained models:

# Save model
gmm.save('my_gmm_model.pth')

# Load model later
from tgmm import GaussianMixture

loaded_gmm = GaussianMixture.load('my_gmm_model.pth')

# Use loaded model
predictions = loaded_gmm.predict(X_new)

docs.title: Pattern 1: Fit and Predict
docs.text:
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X_train)
labels = gmm.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Pattern 2: Soft Clustering
docs.text:
# Get probability of belonging to each cluster
probabilities = gmm.predict_proba(X)

# Find samples uncertain about their cluster
uncertainty = 1 - probabilities.max(dim=1)[0]
uncertain_samples = X[uncertainty > 0.4]

docs.title: Pattern 3: Anomaly Detection
docs.text:
# Fit GMM on normal data
gmm.fit(X_normal)

# Compute likelihood of new samples
log_likelihood = gmm.score_samples(X_new)

# Low likelihood → potential anomaly
threshold = -10  # Tune based on your data
anomalies = X_new[log_likelihood < threshold]

docs.title: Gaussian Mixture Models: Fitting, Inspecting and Initializing¶
docs.text:
This is the starting point for tgmm. It fits a GaussianMixture to a small synthetic 2-D dataset and walks through everything you do with a fitted model: predicting cluster labels and soft assignments, scoring and sampling, inspecting the learned parameters, and plotting them with plot_gmm.

It then covers how EM is started (initial means, weights and covariances), the controls on the optimization itself, and short tours of Classification EM, MAP estimation with priors, constrained sampling and model persistence -- each of which has a dedicated tutorial later on.

What you'll learn

  • Fit a GaussianMixture and use predict, predict_proba, score_samples and sample
  • Inspect weights_, means_ and covariances_ and visualize them with plot_gmm
  • Compare initialization strategies for the means, weights and covariances
  • Use training controls: n_init, warm_start, max_iter/tol and per-call overrides in fit
  • Get a first look at CEM, MAP priors, constrained sampling, and save/load

Prerequisites: none.

See also: the Gaussian Mixture Model user guide for the underlying equations.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: Synthetic Data Generation¶
docs.text: The synthetic dataset is generated by combining four Gaussian components

docs.title: Fitting the GMM¶
docs.text: Here we fit a GMM to the data. We choose the number of clusters n_components to be the same as the number of Gaussians we defined in the previous section. We choose a random initialisation, i.e. init_means='random' and fit the GMM several times (n_init=2 * N_INIT, ten restarts by default and one in the fast docs build) in order to make it less likely to land in local minima. We set verbose=True and verbose_interval=10 to see what is happening during the fitting process.

docs.title: Methods of the GMM¶
docs.text:
The GaussianMixture provides the following methods:

  • Predicted Cluster Labels: Using the predict method.
  • Per-Sample Log-Likelihoods: Using the score_samples method.
  • Posterior Probabilities: For each data sample across all components.
  • New Samples: Generated from the fitted GMM, along with the corresponding component indices.

Diagnostic information such as mean log-likelihood, convergence status, and number of iterations is printed to verify the model's performance.

docs.title: Inspecting the Learned GMM Parameters¶
docs.text:
After fitting the model, we inspect the parameters learned by the GMM. For each component, the following are printed:

  • Weight: The mixing proportion for the component.
  • Mean: The estimated mean of the component.
  • Covariance: The covariance matrix (or vector/scalar for other types) representing the spread of the component.

docs.title: Visualization of Clustering and Generated Samples¶
docs.text:
In this section, we visualize several key results using our custom plot_gmm function:

  1. Per-Sample Log-Likelihood: A continuous scatter plot where each point is colored by its log-likelihood value. A colorbar is included to indicate the log-likelihood scale.

  2. GMM Clustering Results: A cluster plot where points are colored by their predicted labels. The plot also overlays the final GMM component means and ellipses representing covariance contours.

  3. Generated Samples: The new samples generated by the GMM are plotted along with the model's estimated parameters to evaluate how well the model reproduces the data distribution.

docs.title: Visualizing Component Probability Distributions¶
docs.text:
Finally, we analyze the distribution of component responsibilities (i.e., the probability that each sample belongs to a particular component):

  • Observed Data: A grid of subplots is generated where each subplot shows the probability distribution for a single GMM component across the observed data. Each plot uses a continuous color scale (e.g., 'RdBu') with an associated colorbar.

  • Generated Samples: Similarly, we plot the component probability distributions for the generated samples, using a different colormap (e.g., 'PRGn').

These plots provide insight into how the GMM assigns probabilities to each data point and how well each component is represented in both the original and generated data.

docs.title: Covariance Types¶
docs.text: covariance_type controls the shape constraints placed on each component's covariance matrix: 'full' (the default), 'diag', 'spherical', the three 'tied_*' variants that share one covariance across components, plus 8 additional parsimonious GPCM models. See Covariance Structures for the math and a visual comparison of all of them, and the user guide for a reference of the options.

docs.title: Comparing Different Initialization Methods¶
docs.text:
In this section, we investigate how different initialization methods affect the GMM clustering results when using a fixed covariance type (here, full). The initialization methods compared are:

  • random
  • points
  • kpp (k-means++)
  • kmeans
  • maxdist

Below, we provide a brief mathematical description of each method:

  1. Random Initialization: This method computes the empirical mean $\bar{x} $ and covariance $\Sigma$ of the dataset and then draws each initial center from a Gaussian distribution: $$ \mu_i = \bar{x} + L z, \quad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d), $$ where $ L $ is the Cholesky factor of $\Sigma$ (i.e. $\Sigma = LL^\top$). This yields centers that roughly follow the global data distribution.

  2. Points Initialization: This method simply selects $ k $ points uniformly at random from the dataset. Mathematically, if $ S \subset \{1,2,\dots,N\} $ is a random subset of $ k $ indices, then: $$ \mu_i = x_{s_i}, \quad i = 1, \dots, k. $$

  3. k-means++ Initialization (kpp): The first center is chosen uniformly at random. For each subsequent center, the probability of selecting data point $ x_j $ is proportional to the square of its distance to the nearest already-chosen center: $$ P(x_j) = \frac{D(x_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} D(x_j)}, \quad \text{with } D(x_j) = \min_{l=1,\dots,i-1} \|x_j - \mu_l\|^2. $$ This procedure tends to choose centers that are spread out.

  4. k-means Initialization: Starting from the k-means++ initialization, the standard k-means algorithm is run iteratively:

    • Assignment step: Assign each point $ x_j $ to the nearest center: $$ c_j = \arg\min_{i} \|x_j - \mu_i\|^2. $$
    • Update step: Recompute each center as the mean of its assigned points: $$ \mu_i = \frac{1}{|C_i|} \sum_{x_j \in C_i} x_j. $$ These steps repeat until convergence (i.e. the centers do not change significantly).

  5. Max-Distance Initialization (maxdist): This is a modified k-means++ method:

    • The first center is chosen randomly.
    • For $ i = 2,\dots,k $, choose the next center as: $$ \mu_i = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{D}} \min_{l=1,\dots,i-1} \|x - \mu_l\|, $$ ensuring that the new center is the point with the largest minimum distance to the existing centers.
    • Finally, the first center is reselected as the point with the largest distance from the centers $ \mu_2,\dots,\mu_k $: $$ \mu_1 = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{D}} \min_{l=2,\dots,k} \|x - \mu_l\|. $$

For each initialization method, we obtain a set of initial means which are then passed (via the init_means parameter) to the GMM. This bypasses the model’s internal initialization logic, allowing us to compare the impact of different starting points on the final clustering.

  1. Use a helper function (get_init_means) to obtain the initial means from the corresponding method.
  2. Initialize a GMM with these precomputed initial means by providing them via the init_means parameter (thus bypassing the internal initialization logic).
  3. Fit the GMM to the dataset (X_tensor).
  4. Predict cluster labels and visualize the clustering results with our plot_gmm function, which also overlays the initial means (marked in red).

docs.title: Comparing Different Weight Initialization Methods¶
docs.text:
In this section, we investigate how different weight initialization methods affect the starting mixture weights (before EM optimization). The weight initialization methods compared are:

  • uniform: Equal weight for every component
  • random: Sampled from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution
  • kmeans: Proportional to cluster sizes from a nearest-mean assignment

The initial weights assigned to each component are shown in each panel's title; marker sizes are scaled by weight (scale_size_by_weight=True).

docs.title: Comparing Different Covariance Initialization Methods¶
docs.text:
In this section, we investigate how different covariance initialization methods affect the GMM's starting ellipses (before EM optimization) and the resulting fit. The covariance initialization methods compared are:

  • empirical: Estimated from data assigned to each component by nearest mean (default)
  • eye: Identity-like matrices, scaled by 1 + reg_covar
  • random: Random positive semi-definite matrices
  • global: The single global covariance of the whole dataset, repeated across components

docs.title: Training Controls¶
docs.text:
Beyond covariance type and initialization strategy, a few parameters control the EM optimization itself:

  • max_iter, tol: stop after this many iterations, or once the relative log-likelihood improvement drops below tol.
  • reg_covar: regularization added to the covariance diagonal, needed to avoid singular/degenerate covariances.
  • n_init: run EM from this many independent random initializations and keep the best (highest log-likelihood) one; the winning seed is stored in best_random_state_.
  • warm_start: reuse the previous fit's parameters as the starting point for the next call to fit, instead of re-initializing.
  • random_state: seed for reproducibility. With n_init > 1, initialization i uses random_state + i.

max_iter, tol, random_state, and warm_start can also be overridden on a single call to fit(...), without changing the model's own defaults.

docs.title: Custom (Tensor) Initialization¶
docs.text: init_means, init_weights, and init_covariances each also accept an explicit torch.Tensor instead of a method name, letting you seed the model with domain knowledge -- for example the output of GMMInitializer's static methods (see the GMM Initializer guide), a previous run's fitted parameters, or prior expertise about the data.

docs.title: Classification EM (CEM)¶
docs.text: Setting algorithm='cem' swaps the soft E-step for a hard classification step between the E-step and M-step: each point is assigned entirely to its most likely component instead of a probability distribution over components. This can converge faster, at the cost of being more sensitive to initialization. See the CEM tutorial for a deeper comparison against standard EM.

docs.title: MAP Estimation with Priors¶
docs.text: Each of weight_concentration_prior (Dirichlet), mean_prior + mean_precision_prior (Gaussian), and covariance_prior + degrees_of_freedom_prior (Inverse-Wishart) turns the corresponding M-step update from a maximum-likelihood estimate into a maximum a posteriori one, regularizing it toward the prior. When both the mean and covariance priors are supplied, tgmm uses their Normal-Inverse-Wishart (NIW) conjugate joint update instead of independent ones. See the Priors tutorial and NIW Priors Comparison for a deeper dive.

docs.title: Constrained Sampling¶
docs.text: sample() supports rejection-sampling constraints beyond plain unconstrained sampling: sampling only from a specific component, within a std_radius (Mahalanobis distance) or std_range, within a confidence/confidence_range region (converted internally via the $\chi^2$ distribution), or within center_radius of a center_point. See the Sampling tutorial for the full set of options.

docs.title: Model Saving and Loading¶
docs.text:
This section demonstrates the save/load functionality for GMM models. The GaussianMixture class provides four methods for model persistence:

  1. save(filepath): Save the complete model (parameters + configuration) to a file
  2. load(filepath, device=None): Class method to load a complete model from a file
  3. save_state_dict(): Return a dictionary containing all model state (similar to PyTorch)
  4. load_state_dict(state_dict): Load model state from a dictionary

These methods preserve all model parameters, configuration settings, training state, and prior settings, allowing for complete model reproducibility.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• GaussianMixture(n_components=K).fit(X) is all that is needed for a first fit; predict, predict_proba, score_samples and sample give hard labels, soft assignments, per-point log-likelihoods and new data.
  • plotgmm overlays the fitted means and covariance ellipses on the data and can color points by cluster, responsibility or log-likelihood.
  • Initialization matters: init_means, init_weights and init_covariances each accept a named strategy or an explicit tensor, and n_init restarts guard against poor local optima.
  • max_iter, tol, reg_covar, warm_start and random_state control the optimization and can be overridden per fit call.
  • algorithm='cem', MAP priors, constrained sampling and save/load are each covered in more depth in later tutorials.

Next: 02 -- EM Algorithm Walkthrough for what happens inside fit, then 03 -- Visualization and 15 -- Covariance Structures.

docs.title: Expectation-Maximization Algorithm¶
docs.text:
A hands-on walkthrough of how EM fits a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), from the underlying theory to a step-by-step 1-D example and a fuller 2-D example, using tgmm's internal _e_step / _m_step methods directly so each iteration is visible.

This notebook deliberately uses hand-rolled plotting rather than plot_gmm, so you can see exactly what is being drawn; 03 -- Visualization introduces the plotting toolkit used from there on.

What you'll learn

  • The latent-variable view of a mixture and why maximum likelihood has no closed form
  • The E-step (responsibilities) and M-step (weighted maximum-likelihood updates) and why each iteration never lowers the log-likelihood
  • How a poor initialization is repaired iteration by iteration in 1-D
  • How responsibilities, hard assignments and covariance ellipses evolve in a 2-D example

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models.

See also: the Gaussian Mixture Model user guide and the GMM Initializer guide.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: The Model: A Mixture of Gaussians¶
docs.text:
A Gaussian Mixture Model assumes each data point was generated by first picking one of $K$ components at random, then sampling from that component's Gaussian. Formally, introduce a hidden (latent) label $z_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ for each point $x_i$, with

$$ p(z_i = k) = \pi_k, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = 1, $$

and, given the label,

$$ p(x_i \mid z_i = k) = \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k). $$

Marginalizing out the unobserved label gives the density we actually fit to data:

$$ p(x_i \mid \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k), \qquad \theta = \{\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K . $$

Maximum likelihood estimation asks for the $\theta$ that makes the observed data most probable:

$$ \theta^\star = \arg\max_\theta \; \sum_{i=1}^N \log \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k). $$

The sum inside the logarithm is the obstacle: unlike a single Gaussian, there is no closed-form solution for $\theta^\star$. Expectation-Maximization (EM) sidesteps this by treating the labels $z_i$ as auxiliary variables and optimizing iteratively instead of directly.

docs.title: The EM Algorithm¶
docs.text: Each EM iteration alternates two steps.

docs.title: E-step: soft-assign points to components¶
docs.text:
Using Bayes' rule, compute the posterior probability ("responsibility") that component $k$ generated point $x_i$, under the current parameters:

$$ \gamma_{ik} \;=\; p(z_i = k \mid x_i, \theta) \;=\; \frac{\pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)} {\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}. $$

Each row of $\gamma$ sums to 1: this is a soft, probabilistic cluster assignment, not a hard one. This is exactly what GaussianMixture._e_step computes.

docs.title: M-step: re-estimate parameters from the soft assignments¶
docs.text:
Treat $\gamma_{ik}$ as weights and re-fit each component to the (weighted) points assigned to it:

$$ N_k = \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \qquad \text{(effective number of points in component $k$)} $$

$$ \pi_k = \frac{N_k}{N}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}\, x_i, \qquad \Sigma_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} (x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^\top . $$

This is GaussianMixture._m_step (tgmm additionally adds a small reg_covar to the diagonal of each $\Sigma_k$ to keep it positive definite). Notice these are just the ordinary Gaussian MLE formulas (sample mean, sample covariance, class proportion) with each point weighted by $\gamma_{ik}$ instead of being hard-assigned to one component.

docs.title: Repeat until convergence¶
docs.text:
Alternate E-step and M-step until the log-likelihood

$$ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k) $$

stops improving by more than tol -- tracked in tgmm as gmm.lower_bound_.

docs.title: Why Does It Work?¶
docs.text:
Each EM iteration is guaranteed to never decrease the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta)$. Intuitively:

  • The E-step computes the exact posterior $p(z \mid x, \theta)$. This makes a certain lower bound on $\log p(X \mid \theta)$ (the evidence lower bound, or ELBO) touch the true log-likelihood exactly, at the current $\theta$.
  • The M-step then maximizes that same lower bound over $\theta$. Since the bound was tight at the old parameters, the log-likelihood at the new parameters is at least as high as before.

This guarantees monotonic improvement, but only to a local optimum -- the point EM converges to depends on where it starts (see the GMM Initializer guide for the initialization strategies tgmm provides). To make that dependence -- and the iterative improvement itself -- easy to see, this notebook deliberately starts EM from a poor initial guess and watches it recover.

The rest of the notebook works through this concretely: first a simple 1D example where we can plot the fitted Gaussians directly against the data, then a fuller 2D example with four differently-shaped clusters.

docs.title: 1. A 1D Example¶
docs.text: We start with the simplest possible case: one feature ($d=1$), generated from three true Gaussian components so we have ground truth to compare the fit against.

docs.title: Step 0: A (deliberately) bad initialization¶
docs.text:
We initialize all three components close together around $9$–$10$, even though the true components are centered at $-2$, $2$, and $6$ -- and give them a shared, overly wide initial variance. Calling _allocate_parameters sets these initial parameters directly, without running any EM iterations, and _e_step computes the responsibilities $\gamma_{ik}$ from the formula above using only this initial guess.

Because the initial means are clustered together and far from where two of the three true clusters actually are, the resulting responsibilities are not yet very informative -- this is the starting point EM has to improve on.

docs.title: One EM Iteration¶
docs.text: Running fit(..., max_iter=1) performs exactly one E-step followed by one M-step. Compare the responsibilities and fitted Gaussians below to the previous cell: even a single iteration pulls the estimated components substantially closer to the data.

docs.title: Full EM Run: Watching Convergence¶
docs.text: Now we run EM to (near) convergence, fitting one iteration at a time so we can record $(\mu_k, \sigma_k, \pi_k)$ after every step. The left three panels overlay this trajectory on the log-likelihood surface as a function of one component's $(\text{mean}, \text{std})$ at a time (holding the other two components fixed at their converged values) -- exactly the surface EM is climbing, illustrating the monotonic-improvement guarantee from the theory section above. The final plot compares the converged fit to the true generating distributions.

docs.title: 2. A 2D Example¶
docs.text:
The same algorithm generalizes directly to $d > 1$ dimensions -- only the Gaussian density changes, to the standard multivariate normal

$$ \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)\right), $$

with $\Sigma_k$ now a full $d \times d$ covariance matrix per component rather than a scalar variance. The E-step and M-step formulas above are otherwise unchanged.

Here we fit a 4-component GMM to a 2D dataset made of four differently-shaped blobs (two spherical, one axis-aligned, one with correlated features), again starting from means placed away from the data, and visualize how the responsibilities (soft assignments), the resulting hard assignments, and the fitted covariance ellipses evolve over iterations.

docs.title: Visualizing Responsibilities and Fitted Components Across Iterations¶
docs.text: The helper below plots, for a given iteration count: (left) each point's responsibility per cluster, (middle) the resulting hard assignment (arg-max responsibility, used only for coloring) plotted in data space, and (right) the trajectory of each component's mean and its current covariance ellipse, with the initial means marked x and the current means marked o.

docs.title: Running EM and Plotting Snapshots¶
docs.text: We refit from scratch for an increasing number of iterations (max_iter=i), snapshot at iterations 1, 5, and at convergence, and plot each snapshot as a row. Watch how the soft responsibilities sharpen into confident hard assignments as the ellipses converge onto the four true blobs.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• EM treats the component labels as hidden variables: the E-step computes responsibilities $\gamma_{ik}$ from the current parameters, and the M-step re-fits each component to the $\gamma$-weighted data.
  • Each iteration is guaranteed not to decrease the log-likelihood, but only a local optimum is reached, so the result depends on the initialization.
  • Even from a deliberately poor starting point the 1-D example recovers the three true components, and the log-likelihood surfaces show the climb EM follows.
  • In 2-D the same two steps sharpen soft responsibilities into confident assignments while the covariance ellipses settle onto the clusters.

Next: 03 -- Visualization for plot_gmm, or 04 -- Classification EM for the hard-assignment variant of this algorithm.

docs.title: plot_gmm: Visualizing Gaussian Mixtures¶
docs.text:
plot_gmm is the plotting workhorse of tgmm and is used by nearly every tutorial that follows. This notebook goes through its parameters one group at a time -- point styling, cluster coloring, confidence ellipses, mean markers, weight-based scaling and continuous log-likelihood coloring -- showing how each changes the figure.

What you'll learn

  • Plot raw data, fitted models, and true generating components with plot_gmm
  • Color points by true labels, predicted clusters, or per-sample log-likelihood
  • Control confidence ellipses, mean markers and initial-mean markers
  • Scale markers or transparency by component weight and highlight misclassified points

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models.

See also: the Plotting & Visualization user guide and 08 -- PCA Plotting for data with more than two features.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: Overview of Parameters¶
docs.text:
The plot_gmm function provides extensive control over GMM visualization through several parameter categories:

Core Data Parameters

  • X: Input data points to plot (array-like, shape (n_samples, 2))
  • gmm: Fitted GMM object with predict(), means_, covariances_, etc. (optional)

Data Point Styling

  • show_points (bool, default=True): Whether to display the data points
  • point_size (float, default=5): Size of individual data points
  • point_alpha (float, default=0.5): Transparency of points (0=invisible, 1=opaque)
  • point_color (str/array, default='auto'): Point coloring strategy:
    • 'auto': Smart coloring based on available cluster info
    • 'black': All points in black
    • Colormap name: Use matplotlib colormap (e.g., 'viridis', 'plasma')
    • Single color: Use one color for all points (e.g., 'red', '#FF0000')
    • Array-like: Custom colors/values for each point

Cluster Visualization

  • color_by_cluster (bool, default=False): Enable cluster-based point coloring
  • true_labels (array-like, optional): Ground truth cluster labels for comparison
  • match_labels_to_true (bool, default=False): Remap predicted labels to match true labels using Hungarian algorithm
  • cluster_colors (str/list, default='turbo'): Cluster color specification:
    • Matplotlib colormap name (e.g., 'turbo', 'viridis')
    • Single color for all clusters
    • List of specific colors (e.g., ['red', 'blue', 'green'])
  • show_incorrect_predictions (bool, default=False): Highlight correct (green) vs incorrect (red) predictions

Continuous Coloring

  • log_probs (array-like, optional): Continuous values for color mapping (e.g., log-probabilities)
  • colormap (str, default='viridis'): Matplotlib colormap for continuous values
  • colorbar_label (str, default='Log Probability'): Label for the colorbar

Component Ellipses

  • show_ellipses (bool, default=True): Display confidence ellipses for GMM components
  • ellipse_std_devs (list, default=[1, 2, 3]): Standard deviation levels for ellipse boundaries
  • ellipse_alpha (float, default=0.5): Fill transparency of ellipses
  • ellipse_colors (str/list, default='auto'): Ellipse color specification (same options as cluster_colors)
  • ellipse_fill (bool, default=True): Whether ellipses should be filled or outline-only
  • ellipse_line_style (str, default='dotted'): Line style ('solid', 'dashed', 'dotted')
  • ellipse_line_width (float, default=2): Thickness of ellipse boundaries
  • ellipse_line_color (str, default='black'): Color of ellipse boundary lines
  • ellipse_line_alpha (float, default=0.5): Transparency of ellipse boundaries

Component Centers/Means

  • show_means (bool, default=True): Display component center points
  • mean_marker (str, default='h'): Marker style for means ('x', 'o', '*', 'h', etc.)
  • mean_size (float, default=25): Size of mean markers
  • mean_color (str, default='black'): Color of mean markers

Initial Means (if available)

  • show_initial_means (bool, default=False): Show starting positions from initialization
  • initial_mean_marker (str, default='H'): Marker style for initial means
  • initial_mean_size (float, default=25): Size of initial mean markers
  • initial_mean_color (str, default='red'): Color of initial mean markers

Weight-Based Scaling

  • scale_alpha_by_weight (bool, default=False): Scale ellipse transparency by component weight
  • scale_size_by_weight (bool, default=False): Scale marker size by component weight

Plot Styling & Layout

  • ax (matplotlib.Axes, optional): Axes object to plot on (creates new if None)
  • title (str, default='GMM Visualization'): Plot title
  • xlabel (str, default='Feature 1'): X-axis label
  • ylabel (str, default='Feature 2'): Y-axis label
  • legend (bool, default=True): Whether to show legend
  • legend_labels (list, optional): Custom labels for legend entries

docs.title: Data and a Fitted Model¶
docs.text: A four-component synthetic dataset and a GaussianMixture fitted to it. The fitted model, its per-sample log-likelihoods and its predictions feed every plot in the rest of the notebook.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• plot_gmm(X, gmm=...) draws the data, the fitted component means and nested covariance ellipses in one call; gmm=None plots data only.
  • Points can be colored by true labels, predicted clusters, correctness (show_incorrect_predictions) or a continuous value such as log_probs.
  • Ellipse levels (ellipse_std_devs), fill, line style, mean markers and initial-mean markers are all configurable.
  • scale_alpha_by_weight / scale_size_by_weight make component weights visible, and every call accepts ax= so panels compose into grids.

Next: 04 -- Classification EM, or 08 -- PCA Plotting for plotting high-dimensional models.

docs.title: Classification EM (CEM)¶
docs.text:
This notebook compares the Classification EM (CEM) algorithm with standard Expectation-Maximization (EM) for Gaussian Mixture Models. CEM inserts a hard classification step between the E-step and the M-step, so each point updates only the component it is most likely to belong to. In tgmm it is selected with GaussianMixture(algorithm='cem').

What you'll learn

  • How the C-step changes the EM iteration and what objective CEM maximizes
  • How EM and CEM behave on heavily overlapping clusters (accuracy vs. speed)
  • How they behave on well-separated clusters, where CEM's hard assignments lose little
  • When CEM is a sensible choice

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models and 02 -- EM Algorithm Walkthrough.

See also: the Gaussian Mixture Model user guide for the other EM variants ('sem', 'saem') and 14 -- Stochastic EM.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: Overview¶
docs.text: The CEM algorithm (Celeux and Govaert, 1992) is a variant of the EM algorithm that incorporates a classification step (C-step) between the E-step and M-step. This modification aims to maximize the classification likelihood rather than the traditional likelihood.

docs.title: CEM Algorithm Steps:¶
docs.text:
1. E-step: Calculate conditional probabilities $\tau_{ig}^{(r)}$ that observation $y_i$ belongs to cluster $g$
  2. C-step: Assign each observation to one cluster using the MAP (Maximum A Posteriori) operator: $$z_{ig}^{(r+1)} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } g = \arg\max_g \tau_{ig}^{(r)} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
  3. M-step: Update parameters by maximizing the complete-data log-likelihood $L_C(\theta; y, z^{r+1})$

docs.title: Key Properties:¶
docs.text:
• K-means-like: Produces hard assignments rather than soft probabilistic assignments
  • Biased estimates: Maximizes complete-data likelihood $L_C(\theta)$ rather than actual likelihood $L(\theta)$
  • Fast convergence: CEM generally converges faster and is therefore computationally more efficient

docs.title: When to Use CEM:¶
docs.text:
• Well-separated clusters: When mixture components are well separated with similar proportions
  • Fast clustering: When computational speed is more important than maximum likelihood estimates
  • Initialisation: Can be used as an alternative initialisation if kmeans does not perform well

docs.title: Experiment 1: Overlapping Clusters¶
docs.text:
In this first experiment, we create overlapping clusters with varying sample sizes and covariance structures:

  • Component 1: 1000 samples, spherical covariance (σ² = 1.0)
  • Component 2: 1000 samples, spherical covariance (σ² = 0.5)
  • Component 3: 1000 samples, diagonal covariance
  • Component 4: 1000 samples, full covariance with correlation

This scenario tests how EM vs CEM handle ambiguous cluster boundaries where observations could reasonably belong to multiple clusters.

docs.title: Results Analysis: Overlapping Clusters¶
docs.text:
Expected Behavior with Overlapping Clusters:

When clusters overlap significantly, we expect to see:

  • CEM converges faster but achieves a worse log-likelihood on average than EM
  • EM finds better local optima but requires more iterations
  • CEM's hard assignments may be suboptimal when cluster boundaries are ambiguous

This matches the theoretical expectation that CEM trades accuracy for speed when dealing with overlapping components.

docs.title: Experiment 2: Well-Separated Clusters¶
docs.text:
In this second experiment, we create well-separated clusters by increasing the distance between cluster centers:

  • Component 1: (0, 10) - 1000 samples, spherical covariance (σ² = 1.0)
  • Component 2: (10, -20) - 1000 samples, spherical covariance (σ² = 0.5)
  • Component 3: (0, 0) - 1000 samples, diagonal covariance
  • Component 4: (10, 10) - 1000 samples, full covariance with correlation

This scenario tests the ideal case for CEM where cluster boundaries are clear and unambiguous. According to theory:

"When the mixture components are well separated with similar proportions, the CEM algorithm is expected to provide a relevant clustering" (Celeux and Govaert, 1992)

Expected Behavior:

  • Similar final accuracy for both EM and CEM
  • CEM converges much faster due to clear cluster boundaries
  • Hard assignments are optimal when clusters don't overlap

docs.title: Results Analysis: Well-Separated Clusters¶
docs.text:
Key Observations:

The results confirm the theoretical predictions:

  • The best run of each algorithm reaches the same log-likelihood, i.e. the same optimum. Averaged over the random restarts both are pulled down by a few poor local optima (some init_means='points' starts put two means in the same cluster), and neither is consistently better
  • CEM needs noticeably fewer iterations (roughly 2-3x fewer here) and less time
  • The partitions are essentially identical when clusters are well-separated

This demonstrates the practical advantage of CEM in scenarios with clear cluster structure. The hard assignment strategy becomes optimal when cluster boundaries are unambiguous.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• CEM replaces the soft E-step posterior with a hard assignment (the C-step) and maximizes the classification (complete-data) likelihood rather than the observed-data likelihood.
  • With overlapping clusters, EM's soft assignments typically reach a higher log-likelihood, while CEM stops earlier but can settle on a cruder partition.
  • With well-separated clusters the two reach comparable solutions and CEM needs fewer iterations.
  • Use algorithm='cem' when speed or a crisp partition matters more than the exact maximum-likelihood fit.

Next: 05 -- Supervised Fitting, which adds label information, or 14 -- Stochastic EM for the stochastic variants.

docs.title: Supervised Fitting vs. EM vs. CEM¶
docs.text:
This notebook compares three ways of fitting a GaussianMixture on the same synthetic data:

  • EM: standard soft-assignment fitting, no label information.
  • CEM: Classification EM -- hard assignment via argmax(resp) each iteration, no label information.
  • Supervised: fit(X, labels=y) -- the assignment comes from the true label instead of argmax(resp), converging in a single M-step (see the Supervised Fitting section of the user guide; the approach follows Celeux & Govaert 1992, McLachlan & Peel 2000 and Fraley & Raftery 2002).

The data reuses all 4 Gaussian components from 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models (same centers, covariances and sample counts), but two of them share one label -- so there are only 3 classes even though there are 4 physical blobs. That is deliberate: EM and CEM don't see labels, so with n_components=3 they are free to find whichever 3-way split fits the data best (which turns out not to match the label grouping), while the supervised fit is bound by the label and has to force a single Gaussian across two blobs it is told belong together. This is what makes the three methods diverge visibly instead of agreeing trivially.

What you'll learn

  • How fit(X, labels=y) differs from unsupervised EM/CEM, and why it needs no iteration
  • Why unsupervised components need not line up with class labels (and how match_labels_to_true handles arbitrary component indices)
  • How to read misclassifications and 95% confidence regions in plot_gmm panels

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models and 04 -- Classification EM.

See also: 18 -- Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting, where only some labels are known.

docs.title: Data: 4 Gaussians from 01_gmm.ipynb, 2 sharing one label¶
docs.text: Same 4 centers/covariances/sample counts as in 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models. The two spatially farthest-apart components -- (2, -2) and (2, 2), distance 4.0 -- share Class 2; (0, 2) and (0, 0) keep their own labels. The closest pair, (0, 2) and (0, 0) (distance 2.0), is exactly what an unsupervised 3-component fit tends to merge instead -- the opposite of the label grouping.

docs.title: Fitting all three models¶
docs.text: EM and CEM don't see y_tensor at all; only the supervised fit does.

docs.title: Visual comparison¶
docs.text: 2x2 grid: true classes, EM, CEM, supervised. All four panels use the same 3 blue shades for Class 0/1/2, drawn entirely through plot_gmm -- no hand-rolled matplotlib. The "True Classes" panel uses gmm_proxy to feed the 4 true generating Gaussians (not a fitted model) into plot_gmm, with cluster_colors repeating Class 2's blue for the two merged physical components. EM/CEM component indices are arbitrary, so match_labels_to_true Hungarian-matches them to the true labels for both point and ellipse coloring; show_incorrect_predictions then colors correct points by their matched cluster color and incorrect ones red -- so misclassifications are directly visible, concentrated where the forced 3-way split disagrees with the (arbitrary) label grouping. The supervised fit needs no matching, since its component index already is the label (classes_ == [0, 1, 2]). Ellipses are 95% confidence regions via confidence_ellipse_std_devs(0.95) (Mahalanobis radius sqrt(chi2.ppf(0.95, df=2)), not "2 standard deviations" -- that's a 1D interval, not a 2D confidence region), and markers show each component's mean.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Supervised fitting (fit(X, labels=y)) takes the assignment from the labels, so one M-step already gives the per-class mean, covariance and weight; n_iter_ is always 1.
  • EM and CEM never see the labels, so with a label grouping that disagrees with the data's geometry they find a different 3-way split.
  • Unsupervised component indices are arbitrary; match_labels_to_true=True Hungarian-matches them to the labels so errors can be visualized.
  • Supervised fits trade the flexibility of unsupervised fitting for fidelity to the labels -- useful when the labels are trusted.

Next: 18 -- Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting for partially labeled data, or 06 -- Clustering Metrics to quantify agreement with labels.

docs.title: Clustering Metrics: Evaluating Gaussian Mixture Models¶
docs.text:
This notebook evaluates clustering performance with both unsupervised metrics (which need only the data and the assignments) and supervised metrics (which compare against ground-truth labels), using ClusteringMetrics and the information criteria built into GaussianMixture. It covers both the mathematical definitions and their practical use.

What you'll learn

  • Choose the number of components with Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn, BIC and AIC
  • Compare supervised metrics (Rand/ARI, MI/NMI/AMI, FMI, homogeneity/completeness/V-measure, purity) against scikit-learn
  • Build a confusion matrix and classification report after matching cluster labels to true classes
  • Measure the divergence between two fitted mixtures with a Monte Carlo KL estimate

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models.

See also: the Clustering Metrics user guide and 13 -- Model Selection.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: Synthetic Data Generation¶
docs.text:
The synthetic dataset is generated by combining four Gaussian components:

  • Component 1: Centered at [0, 2] with spherical covariance.
  • Component 2: Centered at [2, -2] with spherical covariance (fewer points).
  • Component 3: Centered at [0, 0] with diagonal covariance.
  • Component 4: Centered at [2, 2] with full covariance.

docs.title: Unsupervised Clustering Metrics Definitions¶
docs.text: Below are the definitions of the unsupervised clustering metrics used in this notebook.

docs.title: Silhouette Score¶
docs.text:
The Silhouette Score quantifies how similar each data point is to its own cluster compared to other clusters. For a data point $ \mathbf{x}_i $ belonging to cluster $ C_k $, the silhouette value is defined as

$$ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i), b(i)\}}, $$

where:

  • $ a(i) $ is the average distance between $\mathbf{x}_i$ and all other points in the same cluster $ C_k $ (i.e., the intra-cluster distance),
  • $ b(i) $ is the smallest average distance between $\mathbf{x}_i$ and all points in any other cluster (i.e., the nearest-cluster distance).

A high silhouette score (close to 1) indicates that the data point is well matched to its own cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters.

docs.title: Davies-Bouldin Index¶
docs.text:
The Davies-Bouldin Index (DB) measures the average similarity between each cluster and its most similar one. It is defined as

$$ \text{DB} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \max_{j \neq i} \frac{S_i + S_j}{M_{ij}}, $$

where:

  • $ S_i $ is the average distance between the points in cluster $ i $ and the centroid of $ i $,
  • $ M_{ij} $ is the distance between the centroids of clusters $ i $ and $ j $.

Lower values of the Davies-Bouldin Index indicate better clustering quality, as they reflect smaller within-cluster dispersion relative to the separation between clusters.

docs.title: Calinski-Harabasz Score¶
docs.text:
The Calinski-Harabasz Score (CH) (also known as the Variance Ratio Criterion) is given by

$$ \text{CH} = \frac{n-k}{k-1}\cdot\frac{\sum _{i=1}^{k}n_{i}||\mathbf {c} _{i}-\mathbf {c} ||^{2}}{\sum _{i=1}^{k}\sum _{\mathbf {x} \in C_{i}}||\mathbf {x} -\mathbf {c} _{i}||^{2}}, $$

where:

  • $ k $ is the number of clusters,
  • $ n $ is the total number of samples.

Higher Calinski-Harabasz scores suggest a model in which clusters are dense and well separated.

docs.title: Dunn Index¶
docs.text:
The Dunn Index seeks to identify clusters that are both compact and well separated. It is defined as

$$ D = \frac{\min\limits_{i \neq j} d(C_i, C_j)}{\max\limits_{k} \mathrm{diam}(C_k)}, $$

where:

  • $ d(C_i, C_j) $ is the minimum distance between any two points in clusters $ C_i $ and $ C_j $,
  • $ \mathrm{diam}(C_k) $ is the maximum distance between any two points in cluster $ C_k $.

A higher Dunn Index indicates better clustering, meaning that the clusters are more compact and well separated.

docs.title: Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)¶
docs.text:
The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) is used for model selection by penalizing model complexity while rewarding goodness-of-fit. It is computed as

$$ \text{BIC} = n_{\text{params}} \cdot \ln(N) - 2 \cdot \mathcal{L}, $$

where:

  • $ n_{\text{params}} $ is the number of free parameters in the model,
  • $ N $ is the number of samples,
  • $ \mathcal{L} $ is the total log-likelihood of the data under the fitted model (GaussianMixture.bic / .aic compute exactly this, with $n_{\text{params}}$ counting the mixture weights, means and covariance parameters).

Lower BIC values indicate a model that better balances fit and simplicity.

docs.title: Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)¶
docs.text:
The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is another metric for model selection defined as

$$ \text{AIC} = 2 \cdot n_{\text{params}} - 2 \cdot \mathcal{L}. $$

As with BIC, lower AIC values suggest a model that achieves a good trade-off between complexity and fit quality.

Note: For selection criteria that account for cluster overlap, see ICL in 13 -- Model Selection. In practice, the ideal number of clusters is typically determined by seeking a maximum in the Silhouette Score, Calinski-Harabasz Score, and Dunn Index, while simultaneously looking for minima in the Davies-Bouldin Index, AIC, and BIC.

docs.title: Supervised Clustering Metrics Definitions¶
docs.text: When ground truth labels are available, we can evaluate clustering performance using supervised metrics that measure the agreement between predicted and true cluster assignments.

docs.title: Rand Index (RI)¶
docs.text:
The Rand Index measures the similarity between two clusterings by considering all pairs of samples and counting pairs that are assigned to the same or different clusters in both clusterings.

$$ \text{RI} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} $$

where:

  • $TP$ (True Positives): pairs that are in the same cluster in both clusterings
  • $TN$ (True Negatives): pairs that are in different clusters in both clusterings
  • $FP$ (False Positives): pairs that are in the same cluster in predicted but different clusters in true
  • $FN$ (False Negatives): pairs that are in different clusters in predicted but same cluster in true

The Rand Index ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates perfect agreement.

docs.title: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)¶
docs.text:
The Adjusted Rand Index corrects the Rand Index for chance by subtracting the expected value and normalizing by the maximum possible value:

$$ \text{ARI} = \frac{\text{RI} - \mathbb{E}[\text{RI}]}{\max(\text{RI}) - \mathbb{E}[\text{RI}]} $$

More explicitly, using the contingency table approach:

$$ \text{ARI} = \frac{\sum_{ij} \binom{n_{ij}}{2} - \left[\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2} \sum_j \binom{b_j}{2}\right] / \binom{n}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2} + \sum_j \binom{b_j}{2}\right] - \left[\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2} \sum_j \binom{b_j}{2}\right] / \binom{n}{2}} $$

where $n_{ij}$ is the number of samples in cluster $i$ of the true clustering and cluster $j$ of the predicted clustering. ARI is at most 1 (perfect agreement), is about 0 for random labeling, and can be negative for worse-than-chance agreement.

docs.title: Mutual Information (MI)¶
docs.text:
Mutual Information measures the amount of information obtained about one clustering by observing the other:

$$ \text{MI}(U,V) = \sum_{i=1}^{|U|} \sum_{j=1}^{|V|} P(i,j) \log\frac{P(i,j)}{P(i)P(j)} $$

where:

  • $U$ and $V$ are the true and predicted clusterings
  • $P(i,j) = \frac{|U_i \cap V_j|}{N}$ is the probability that a point belongs to clusters $U_i$ and $V_j$
  • $P(i) = \frac{|U_i|}{N}$ and $P(j) = \frac{|V_j|}{N}$ are marginal probabilities

docs.title: Normalized Mutual Information (NMI)¶
docs.text:
Normalized Mutual Information scales MI to the range [0,1] by normalizing with the entropy of the clusterings:

$$ \text{NMI}(U,V) = \frac{2 \times \text{MI}(U,V)}{H(U) + H(V)} $$

where $H(U) = -\sum_{i=1}^{|U|} P(i) \log P(i)$ is the entropy of clustering $U$.

docs.title: Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI)¶
docs.text:
Adjusted Mutual Information corrects MI for chance, similar to how ARI corrects RI:

$$ \text{AMI}(U,V) = \frac{\text{MI}(U,V) - \mathbb{E}[\text{MI}(U,V)]}{\tfrac{1}{2}\big(H(U) + H(V)\big) - \mathbb{E}[\text{MI}(U,V)]} $$

where the expectation is the exact hypergeometric expectation over random labelings with the same cluster sizes (Vinh, Epps & Bailey, 2010; the arithmetic-mean normalizer is scikit-learn's default, and average_method selects 'min', 'max' or 'geometric'). tgmm computes it exactly, so its AMI agrees with scikit-learn's to numerical precision -- the comparison table below shows it.

docs.title: Fowlkes-Mallows Index (FMI)¶
docs.text:
The Fowlkes-Mallows Index is the geometric mean of pairwise precision and recall:

$$ \text{FMI} = \sqrt{\frac{TP}{TP + FP} \times \frac{TP}{TP + FN}} = \sqrt{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}} $$

where TP, FP, and FN are defined as in the Rand Index but for pairwise comparisons.

docs.title: Homogeneity and Completeness¶
docs.text:
Homogeneity measures whether each cluster contains only members of a single class:

$$ h = 1 - \frac{H(C|K)}{H(C)} $$

Completeness measures whether all members of a given class are assigned to the same cluster:

$$ c = 1 - \frac{H(K|C)}{H(K)} $$

where $H(C|K)$ is the conditional entropy of the true classes given the cluster assignments.

docs.title: V-Measure¶
docs.text:
The V-Measure is the harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness:

$$ \text{V} = \frac{2 \times h \times c}{h + c} $$

docs.title: Purity¶
docs.text:
Purity measures the extent to which clusters contain a single class:

$$ \text{Purity} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \max_j |C_k \cap T_j| $$

where $C_k$ is the set of samples in cluster $k$ and $T_j$ is the set of samples in true class $j$.

Interpretation Guidelines:

  • Higher is better: RI, ARI, MI, NMI, AMI, FMI, Homogeneity, Completeness, V-Measure, Purity
  • Range [0,1]: RI, NMI, FMI, Homogeneity, Completeness, V-Measure and Purity (AMI is nominally in [0,1], and can dip slightly below 0 for near-random labelings)
  • Other ranges: ARI can be negative; MI is non-negative but not capped at 1 (it is bounded by $\min(H(U), H(V))$)
  • Perfect clustering: RI, ARI, NMI, AMI, FMI, Homogeneity, Completeness, V-Measure and Purity all equal 1

docs.title: Model Comparison: tgmm vs scikit-learn¶
docs.text: This section compares the clustering metrics computed by tgmm's implementation with scikit-learn's implementations to validate correctness and highlight any differences in computation methods.

docs.title: Metrics Comparison Table¶
docs.text:
The table below shows side-by-side comparisons of metrics computed using both implementations. Small differences may occur due to:

  • Different numerical precision
  • Slightly different algorithmic implementations
  • Different handling of edge cases (e.g., single-point clusters)
  • BIC/AIC come from two independently fitted models (tgmm's and scikit-learn's), so they agree only approximately

Key observations:

  • Information-theoretic metrics (MI, NMI, AMI) agree with scikit-learn to numerical precision
  • Pairwise metrics (RI, ARI, FMI) should match exactly for identical cluster assignments
  • Geometric metrics (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz) may show small differences due to distance computation methods

docs.title: Understanding the Confusion Matrix¶
docs.text:
The confusion matrix provides a detailed breakdown of correct and incorrect predictions for each class. Before computing the matrix, we use label matching to align predicted cluster labels with true class labels, as clustering algorithms may assign arbitrary label numbers.

Key metrics derived from the confusion matrix:

  • Precision: $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ - What fraction of predicted positives are actually positive?
  • Recall: $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ - What fraction of actual positives are correctly predicted?
  • F1-Score: $\frac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$ - Harmonic mean of precision and recall
  • Support: Number of true instances for each class

The heatmap below shows the confusion matrix as percentages, normalized by the true class sizes.

docs.title: Kullback-Leibler Divergence Between GMMs¶
docs.text:
The KL divergence $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)$ measures how one probability distribution $P$ diverges from a reference distribution $Q$:

$$ D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \int p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} dx $$

For Gaussian Mixture Models, we approximate this using Monte Carlo sampling:

$$ D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ \log p(x_i) - \log q(x_i) \right] $$

where $x_i \sim P$ are samples drawn from the first GMM.

Interpretation:

  • $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0$ when $P = Q$ (identical distributions)
  • $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) > 0$ always (non-negative)
  • Asymmetric: $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) \neq D_{KL}(Q \parallel P)$ in general
  • Lower values indicate more similar distributions

The plot below shows how KL divergence changes as we vary the number of components in the test GMM while keeping the reference GMM fixed at the true number of components.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Unsupervised indices (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn) and information criteria (BIC, AIC) can be swept over n_components, but they need not agree on the best $K$.
  • Supervised indices compare a clustering with ground truth; tgmm's versions can be checked directly against scikit-learn (AMI uses the exact chance correction).
  • Cluster indices are arbitrary, so predictions are matched to true classes before building a confusion matrix or classification report.
  • kl_divergence_gmm estimates $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)$ between two fitted mixtures by Monte Carlo sampling.

Next: 13 -- Model Selection for BIC, AIC and ICL sweeps with select_model, or 07 -- Sampling.
