exponential rate 1.04 (true 1.0);  normal mean 6.04, variance 0.39 (true 6.0 / 0.49)
converged in 4 iterations; BIC = 2835.4; 3 samples drawn from the fitted components

docs.title: Noise, Missing Values and Conditioning¶
docs.text:
A fitted mixture is more than a clustering. This tutorial shows five things you can do around the EM fit once the model is a proper probability density: give stray points somewhere to go (a uniform noise component), fit data with holes in it (missing-value EM), ask questions of the fitted density (marginals and conditionals, hence Gaussian mixture regression), control what EM is allowed to change (frozen components and sample weights), and bring your own component families (the component protocol and GenericMixture).

What you'll learn

  • how noise=True adds a parameter-free uniform component, what it does to the fitted means, and how predict and noise_proba report it;
  • how missing='em' fits incomplete rows by maximising the likelihood of the observed entries, and what impute returns;
  • how marginal and condition turn a fitted GaussianMixture into a regressor whose conditional distributions can be bimodal;
  • how frozen_components pins a known component and how integer sample_weights equal duplicating rows;
  • how to plug a hand-written component (here an exponential) into GenericMixture by implementing three methods.

Prerequisites: 01 -- Gaussian Mixture Models, 02 -- The EM Algorithm.

See also: the Noise, Missing Values and Conditioning user guide for the equations.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: The next cell imports what the notebook needs and fixes the random seeds. It expects tgmm to be importable: pip install tgmm, or pip install -e . from a clone of the repository. Opened with marimo edit --sandbox, the dependencies listed in the header of this file are installed automatically.

docs.title: 1. A uniform noise component¶
docs.text:
Real data often contain points no cluster explains: background clutter, sensor glitches, mislabelled rows. A Gaussian component asked to cover them has to widen and shift. The classical remedy (Banfield & Raftery, 1993) is to add one more mixture component that is uniform over a region of volume $V$ and has no parameters except its weight $\pi_0$:

$$ p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k f_k(x)+\frac{\pi_0}{V},\qquad \sum_k\pi_k+\pi_0=1 . $$

The E-step simply appends a column $\log\pi_0-\log V$ to the component log-densities, so the responsibilities become $(n,K+1)$; the last column is the noise responsibility $\tau_{i0}$. The M-step sets $\pi_0=\sum_i\tau_{i0}/n$ and updates the $K$ components from the first $K$ columns as usual. By default $V$ is the volume of the bounding box of the data (noise_volume='bbox').

Below: three Gaussian blobs plus 60 points sprinkled uniformly over a larger rectangle.

docs.title: Starting from a density-based guess¶
docs.text: noise_init seeds the noise column from a per-point flag. A boolean tensor means "True = noise"; any other dtype is read as cluster labels with -1 = noise, so the output of HDBSCAN can be passed as it is. The initial means and covariances are then computed from the unflagged points only, and noise_prior is replaced by the flagged fraction.

docs.title: 2. Missing values¶
docs.text:
With missing='em', NaN entries are treated as missing at random and the likelihood is maximised over the entries that were observed. For a row with observed block $o$ and missing block $m$, and component $k$:

  • the E-step uses the marginal density $\mathcal N(x_o;\mu_{k,o},\Sigma_{k,oo})$;
  • the M-step fills the hole with the conditional mean $\hat x_m=\mu_{k,m}+\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}(x_o-\mu_{k,o})$ and adds the conditional covariance $C_k=\Sigma_{k,mm}-\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}\Sigma_{k,om}$ to the second moment, so the variance is not underestimated.

Rows are grouped by missingness pattern, so the cost is one batched solve per pattern, not per row. Below, 20% of the entries of a two-cluster dataset are deleted completely at random (keeping at least one observed entry per row: a row with nothing observed carries no information and is rejected).

docs.title: 3. Marginals and conditionals: Gaussian mixture regression¶
docs.text:
A fitted GaussianMixture is a joint density, so it can answer any question about subsets of coordinates.

  • gmm.marginal(dims) returns a new GaussianMixture over the chosen coordinates (diagonal, spherical and tied types keep their type; the parametrised GPCM codes become full).
  • gmm.condition(x_obs, obs_dims) returns a ConditionalGaussianMixture: for every row of x_obs, the distribution of the remaining coordinates,

$$ p(y\mid x_{o,i})=\sum_{k}w_{ik}\,\mathcal N\big(y;\ m_{ik},\ C_k\big),\qquad w_{ik}\propto\pi_k\mathcal N(x_{o,i};\mu_{k,o},\Sigma_{k,oo}), $$

with $m_{ik}=\mu_{k,m}+\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}(x_{o,i}-\mu_{k,o})$ and $C_k=\Sigma_{k,mm}-\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}\Sigma_{k,om}$. The weights depend on the observed values, the conditional covariances do not. mean() is Gaussian mixture regression: $\mathbb E[y\mid x_o]=\sum_kw_{ik}m_{ik}$.

Fit eight components to noisy samples of $y=\sin 2x$ and regress $y$ on $x$.

docs.title: 4. Controlling what EM changes: frozen_components and sample_weight¶
docs.text: Frozen components. frozen_components=[k, ...] keeps those components' means and covariances (or dof_ / kappa_ for the other families) at their initial values for the whole fit; the mixing weights still update (and so does the noise weight). Use it to pin a component you already know -- a calibrated background, a reference population -- and let the others adapt around it. Priors never shrink a frozen component and SEM never re-seeds it. The initial values come from init_means / init_covariances.

docs.title: 5. Bring your own component: the protocol and GenericMixture¶
docs.text:
Every family in tgmm is a BaseMixture, and GenericMixture is the one that takes its components from you. A component is any object that implements three methods (the shape pomegranate popularised):

method job log_probability(X) return $\log f_k(x_i)$, shape (n,) summarize(X, sample_weight) accumulate weighted statistics of one chunk of data (sample_weight = responsibility $\times$ row weight) from_summaries() update the parameters from everything summarised, then reset the accumulators

The M-step calls summarize once per data chunk and from_summaries once, so batch_size works for free. Optional members are sample(n), n_parameters() (needed for bic/aic/icl) and a frozen flag. A plain torch.nn.Module with a log_prob(X) method is also accepted: it is updated by a few L-BFGS steps that are kept only if they improve the expected complete-data log-likelihood.

Here is a tiny mixture of an exponential (waiting times) and a normal (a burst around 6) over positive data -- neither is a GaussianMixture component.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• noise=True adds a uniform component $\pi_0/V$: predict returns -1 for noise, noise_proba(X) gives the probability, weights_ sums to $1-\pi_0$, and the component covariances are no longer inflated by background points. noise_init accepts a boolean mask or HDBSCAN labels.
  • missing='em' maximises the likelihood of the observed entries: marginal densities in the E-step, conditional means and covariances in the M-step, impute for the filled-in data, and every consumer (predict, score, bic, ...) accepts rows with NaN.
  • marginal(dims) and condition(x_obs, obs_dims) turn a fitted GaussianMixture into marginal and conditional distributions; mean() is Gaussian mixture regression and the conditional can be multimodal where a regression mean is misleading.
  • frozen_components pins components at their initial parameters, and sample_weight counts rows (integer weights equal duplication; per-feature weights for factorising models).
  • GenericMixture fits any family that implements log_probability, summarize and from_summaries (or any nn.Module with log_prob), with batch_size, sample_weight, frozen components and information criteria included.

Next: 18 -- Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting for another way of steering the fit, or the user guide for the equations behind this tutorial.

Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) - Basic introduction to fitting GMMs with tgmm: initialization strategies (means, weights, covariances), training controls (n_init, warm_start, ...), MAP priors, constrained sampling and save/load. docs.title: Clustering Metrics
docs.text:
The ClusteringMetrics class provides comprehensive evaluation metrics for clustering results, including both supervised and unsupervised measures.

ClusteringMetrics is a collection of @staticmethods -- there is no instance to construct, call the methods directly on the class.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Metrics are divided into two categories:

Unsupervised (no ground truth labels needed; n_components is optional -- see Shared options below): - Silhouette Score, Davies-Bouldin Index, Calinski-Harabasz Index, Dunn Index - WB-Index, Wemmert-Gancarski Index, DBCV -- three indexes that ranked at the top of the Simpson, Campello & Stojanovski (2025) clustering-validity benchmark; prefer these over Dunn Index (ranked 25th of 26 in that same benchmark, kept only for completeness)

BIC/AIC/ICL aren't here -- they only need a model's own log-likelihood and parameter count, so they're bic/aic/icl methods on every fitted mixture directly (gmm.bic(X), gmm.aic(X), gmm.icl(X)) -- including when GaussianMixture is constructed with n_components=None for Gibbs-sampling mode -- not ClusteringMetrics calls. See Model Selection below.

Supervised (requires ground truth labels): - Rand Index / Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) - Mutual Information / Normalized (NMI) / Adjusted (AMI) Mutual Information - Purity - Fowlkes-Mallows, Homogeneity, Completeness, V-Measure (weighted via beta) - Normalized Information Distance (NID) - Confusion Matrix - Classification Report (precision, recall, F1, Jaccard, ROC-AUC per class)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from tgmm import ClusteringMetrics, GaussianMixture
import torch

# Fit GMM
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X)
predicted_labels = gmm.predict(X)

# Compute unsupervised metrics (call directly on the class)
silhouette = ClusteringMetrics.silhouette_score(X, predicted_labels, n_components=3)
davies_bouldin = ClusteringMetrics.davies_bouldin_index(X, predicted_labels, n_components=3)
calinski_harabasz = ClusteringMetrics.calinski_harabasz_score(X, predicted_labels, n_components=3)

print(f"Silhouette Score: {silhouette:.3f}")
print(f"Davies-Bouldin Index: {davies_bouldin:.3f}")
print(f"Calinski-Harabasz Index: {calinski_harabasz:.3f}")

# If you have ground truth labels
ari = ClusteringMetrics.adjusted_rand_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)
nmi = ClusteringMetrics.normalized_mutual_info_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)
purity = ClusteringMetrics.purity_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)

print(f"ARI: {ari:.3f}")
print(f"NMI: {nmi:.3f}")
print(f"Purity: {purity:.3f}")

docs.title: Shared options for unsupervised indexes
docs.text:
silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_index, calinski_harabasz_score, dunn_index, wb_index, and wemmert_gancarski_index all share the same extra keyword arguments:

  • n_components: optional now -- if omitted, it's inferred from the distinct values in labels, which no longer need to be contiguous or 0-indexed. Passing it explicitly (the historical required argument) keeps working exactly as before.
  • metric: 'euclidean' (default), 'manhattan', 'cosine', 'mahalanobis' (pass the precision matrix as VI), or -- for silhouette_score and dunn_index only -- 'precomputed' (pass an (n, n) distance matrix as X). The other four indexes need to average points into a cluster centroid, which a precomputed distance matrix doesn't support, and raise a clear ValueError if asked to. Passing the pooled precision of a fitted GaussianMixture (torch.linalg.inv of the weighted average of covariances_) as VI with metric='mahalanobis' gives the GMM-matched version of the index.
  • noise_label: a label value (e.g. -1 for HDBSCAN output) marking noise points. Noise rows are dropped before computing the index, and the result is then penalized for having discarded points: with \(f = (n - n_{\text{noise}})/n\), indexes where higher is better (silhouette, CH, Dunn, WG) are multiplied by \(f\), and indexes where lower is better (Davies-Bouldin, WB) are divided by \(f\).
  • chunk_size (silhouette/Dunn only): row-chunk size for the pairwise distance computation, bounding peak memory regardless of n_samples (default 4096). Chunking is exact, not an approximation.

dbcv has its own, simpler signature (metric, noise_label=-1) -- its noise handling is built into the index's own weighting formula rather than the generic rescaling above.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: Throughout, a clustering assigns each of \(n\) points \(x_i\) to one of \(K\) clusters \(C_1,\dots,C_K\) with sizes \(n_k = |C_k|\) and centroids \(c_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{x\in C_k} x\) (the plain coordinate-wise mean -- note this is the hard-assignment centroid, not the GMM's means_), and \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) is the chosen metric (Euclidean by default). When noise_label is set, noise rows are removed first and \(n\) counts only the remaining points.

docs.title: Silhouette Score
docs.text:
For a point \(i\) in cluster \(C_{k(i)}\), let

\[ a(i) = \frac{1}{n_{k(i)} - 1}\sum_{j \in C_{k(i)},\, j\neq i} d(i,j), \qquad b(i) = \min_{l \neq k(i)} \frac{1}{n_l}\sum_{j \in C_l} d(i,j), \]

the mean distance to its own cluster and to the nearest other cluster. Then

\[ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i),\, b(i)\}}, \qquad \text{Silhouette} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i s(i), \]

with \(s(i) = 0\) for singleton clusters. Requires at least two clusters.

Range: [-1, 1] Interpretation: Higher is better - 1: Perfect clustering - 0: Overlapping clusters - -1: Wrong clustering

silhouette = ClusteringMetrics.silhouette_score(X, labels, n_components=3)

docs.title: Davies-Bouldin Index
docs.text:
With the within-cluster scatter \(S_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{x\in C_k} d(x, c_k)\) (mean distance to the centroid) and centroid separation \(M_{kl} = d(c_k, c_l)\),

\[ \mathrm{DB} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\max_{l \neq k}\frac{S_k + S_l}{M_{kl}}, \]

the average, over clusters, of the similarity to the most similar other cluster (large when two clusters are wide and close).

Range: [0, ∞) Interpretation: Lower is better

db_index = ClusteringMetrics.davies_bouldin_index(X, labels, n_components=3)

docs.title: Calinski-Harabasz Index
docs.text:
Let \(\bar x\) be the global mean,

\[ \mathrm{SSW} = \sum_{k}\sum_{x\in C_k} d(x, c_k)^2, \qquad \mathrm{SSB} = \sum_{k} n_k\, d(c_k, \bar x)^2, \]

the within- and between-cluster sums of squared distances. Then

\[ \mathrm{CH} = \frac{\mathrm{SSB}/(K-1)}{\mathrm{SSW}/(n-K)}, \]

a variance-ratio (pseudo-\(F\)) statistic. For the Euclidean metric \(\mathrm{SSW}+\mathrm{SSB}\) is the total sum of squares.

Range: [0, ∞) Interpretation: Higher is better

ch_index = ClusteringMetrics.calinski_harabasz_score(X, labels, n_components=3)

docs.title: Dunn Index
docs.text:
\[ D = \frac{\min_{k \neq l}\; d(C_k, C_l)}{\max_{k}\;\operatorname{diam}(C_k)}, \qquad d(C_k, C_l) = \min_{x\in C_k,\, y\in C_l} d(x,y), \quad \operatorname{diam}(C_k) = \max_{x,y\in C_k} d(x,y), \]

the smallest between-cluster gap over the largest within-cluster diameter. It depends on only two pairs of points, so it is very sensitive to outliers.

Range: [0, ∞) Interpretation: Higher is better

dunn = ClusteringMetrics.dunn_index(X, labels, n_components=3)

Ranked 25th of 26 indexes on partition ranking in the Simpson, Campello & Stojanovski (2025) benchmark -- kept for completeness/familiarity, not as a recommended choice. Prefer WB-Index, Wemmert-Gancarski, or DBCV below.

docs.title: WB-Index
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{WB} = K\,\frac{\mathrm{SSW}}{\mathrm{SSB}} \]

(Zhao & Fränti, 2014) -- same SSW/SSB as Calinski-Harabasz, with the number of clusters as a built-in penalty.

Range: [0, ∞) Interpretation: Lower is better

wb = ClusteringMetrics.wb_index(X, labels, n_components=3)

docs.title: Wemmert-Gancarski Index
docs.text:
Compares each point's distance to its own centroid against its distance to the nearest other centroid:

\[ R(x) = \frac{d(x, c_{k(x)})}{\min_{l \neq k(x)} d(x, c_l)}, \qquad J_k = \max\Big(0,\; 1 - \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{x\in C_k} R(x)\Big), \qquad \mathrm{WG} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k n_k J_k . \]

A cluster contributes \(0\) when, on average, its points are no closer to their own centroid than to another's.

Range: [0, ∞) (in practice [0, 1]) Interpretation: Higher is better

wg = ClusteringMetrics.wemmert_gancarski_index(X, labels, n_components=3)

docs.title: DBCV (Density-Based Clustering Validation)
docs.text:
Moulavi, Jaskowiak, Campello, Zimek & Sander (2014). The natural validity index for density-based partitions (e.g. HDBSCAN output, including noise points), where centroid-based indexes like Davies-Bouldin don't make sense for non-convex clusters. For every cluster \(C\) (computed within the cluster, using the \(d_f\) = n_features-th power of distances):

  1. All-points core distance of \(x\in C\): $\(a_{ ext{core}}(x) = \Big( rac{1}{|C|-1}\sum_{y\in C,\,y eq x} d(x,y)^{-d_f}\Big)^{-1/d_f}.\)$
  2. Mutual reachability: \(d_{ ext{mreach}}(x,y) = \max\{a_{ ext{core}}(x),\, a_{ ext{core}}(y),\, d(x,y)\}\).
  3. A minimum spanning tree (MST) over \(C\)'s mutual-reachability graph. Density sparseness \(\mathrm{DSC}(C)\) = the largest MST edge weight.
  4. Density separation \(\mathrm{DSPC}(C_i, C_j)\) = the smallest mutual-reachability distance between an internal node (MST degree \(\ge 2\)) of \(C_i\) and an internal node of \(C_j\).

The per-cluster validity and the index are

\[ V(C_i) = rac{\min_{j eq i}\mathrm{DSPC}(C_i,C_j) - \mathrm{DSC}(C_i)} {\max\{\min_{j eq i}\mathrm{DSPC}(C_i,C_j),\; \mathrm{DSC}(C_i)\}}, \qquad \mathrm{DBCV} = \sum_i rac{n_i}{n}\, V(C_i), \]

where \(n\) includes the noise points (they add to the denominator only), which is DBCV's own noise handling -- so it does not use the generic noise_label rescaling of the other indexes. Clusters with fewer than 2 points contribute \(0\). Note this is the all-points core distance of the DBCV paper, not the \(k\)-NN core distance that HDBSCAN itself uses internally.

Range: [-1, 1] Interpretation: Higher is better

score = ClusteringMetrics.dbcv(X, labels, noise_label=-1)  # -1 is HDBSCAN's noise label

docs.title: Supervised Metrics
docs.text:
These compare a predicted partition \(V\) (labels_pred) with a reference partition \(U\) (labels_true). Most are built from the contingency table \(n_{ij} = |\{x : u(x) = i,\ v(x) = j\}|\) with row sums \(a_i = \sum_j n_{ij}\), column sums \(b_j = \sum_i n_{ij}\) and total \(n\). Cluster labels are arbitrary, so every score here is invariant to relabeling the clusters.

Label format

The supervised scores build the contingency table by indexing, so they expect non-negative, 0-indexed integer labels (e.g. from gmm.predict). To score density-based output containing a -1 noise label, drop or remap the noise rows first.

docs.title: Rand Index and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)
docs.text:
Count pairs of points: \(\mathrm{TP}\) = pairs together in both partitions, \(\mathrm{TN}\) = apart in both, \(\mathrm{FP}\)/\(\mathrm{FN}\) the disagreements. Then

\[ \mathrm{RI} = \frac{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{TN}}{\binom{n}{2}}, \qquad \mathrm{ARI} = \frac{\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}{2} - \Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\Big]\Big/\binom{n}{2}} {\tfrac12\Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}+\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\Big] - \Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\Big]\Big/\binom{n}{2}}. \]

ARI subtracts the Rand index's expected value under random labeling with the same cluster sizes (the generalized hypergeometric model), so a random partition scores \(\approx 0\).

Range: ARI in [-1, 1]; RI in [0, 1] Interpretation: Higher is better - 1: Perfect agreement - 0: Random labeling - Negative: Worse than random

ari = ClusteringMetrics.adjusted_rand_score(true_labels, pred_labels)

docs.title: Mutual Information, NMI and AMI
docs.text:
With \(p_{ij} = n_{ij}/n\), \(p_i = a_i/n\), \(p_j = b_j/n\), entropies \(H(U) = -\sum_i p_i\ln p_i\), \(H(V) = -\sum_j p_j \ln p_j\):

\[ \mathrm{MI}(U,V) = \sum_{ij} p_{ij}\ln\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i\,p_j}, \qquad \mathrm{NMI} = \frac{2\,\mathrm{MI}}{H(U) + H(V)} . \]

NMI uses the arithmetic-mean normalization and lies in \([0, 1]\) (all in nats). The AMI (adjusted_mutual_info_score) is meant to correct MI for chance, \(\mathrm{AMI} = \dfrac{\mathrm{MI} - \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MI}]}{\tfrac12(H(U)+H(V)) - \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MI}]}\).

The chance correction uses the exact expected mutual information under the permutation (hypergeometric) model of Vinh, Epps & Bailey (2010), with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MI}] = \sum_{i,j}\ \sum_{n_{ij}=\max(1,\,a_i+b_j-n)}^{\min(a_i,\,b_j)} \frac{n_{ij}}{n}\ln\frac{n\,n_{ij}}{a_ib_j}\; \frac{a_i!\,b_j!\,(n-a_i)!\,(n-b_j)!}{n!\,n_{ij}!\,(a_i-n_{ij})!\,(b_j-n_{ij})!\,(n-a_i-b_j+n_{ij})!}. \]

The summand depends only on \((a_i, b_j)\), so tgmm groups equal cluster sizes and evaluates each distinct pair once, vectorised over \(n_{ij}\) with log-gamma in float64 (adapted from scikit-learn's expected_mutual_information, BSD-3). adjusted_mutual_info_score and normalized_mutual_info_score take average_method ('arithmetic' by default, 'min', 'max', 'geometric') and agree with scikit-learn to about \(10^{-8}\) or better; the exact expectation is exposed as ClusteringMetrics.expected_mutual_information(contingency).

Range: NMI in [0, 1]; AMI \(\lesssim 1\), may be slightly negative Interpretation: Higher is better - 1: Perfect agreement - 0: Independent labelings

nmi = ClusteringMetrics.normalized_mutual_info_score(true_labels, pred_labels)

docs.title: Fowlkes-Mallows
docs.text:
The geometric mean of pairwise precision and recall,

\[ \mathrm{FM} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}}, \qquad \mathrm{TP} = \sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}{2}. \]

Range: [0, 1] -- Higher is better.

docs.title: Homogeneity, Completeness, V-Measure
docs.text:
Homogeneity asks "does each cluster contain only one true class?"; completeness asks "is each true class kept in one cluster?" (Rosenberg & Hirschberg, 2007):

\[ h = 1 - \frac{H(U \mid V)}{H(U)}, \qquad c = 1 - \frac{H(V \mid U)}{H(V)}, \qquad V_\beta = \frac{(1+\beta)\,h\,c}{\beta\,h + c}, \]

with the conventions \(h = 1\) when \(H(U) = 0\) and \(c = 1\) when \(H(V) = 0\). V-measure is their weighted harmonic mean, via beta (beta=1.0, the default, weighs them equally and gives \(2hc/(h+c)\), the same as NMI with arithmetic normalization; beta > 1 favours completeness, beta < 1 favours homogeneity).

Range: [0, 1] each. Interpretation: Higher is better.

h = ClusteringMetrics.homogeneity_score(true_labels, pred_labels)
c = ClusteringMetrics.completeness_score(true_labels, pred_labels)
v = ClusteringMetrics.v_measure_score(true_labels, pred_labels, beta=1.0)

docs.title: Normalized Information Distance (NID)
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{NID} = 1 - \frac{I(U;V)}{\max\{H(U), H(V)\}} \]

(Vinh, Epps & Bailey, 2010) -- an information-theoretic distance between two partitions.

Range: [0, 1] Interpretation: Lower is better; 0 for identical partitions.

nid = ClusteringMetrics.normalized_information_distance(true_labels, pred_labels)

docs.title: Purity
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{purity} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}\max_i n_{ij}, \]

the fraction of points that belong to the majority true class of their predicted cluster. It never decreases as the number of clusters grows (a cluster per point has purity 1), so only compare it at the same \(K\).

Range: [0, 1] Interpretation: Higher is better

purity = ClusteringMetrics.purity_score(true_labels, pred_labels)

docs.title: Confusion Matrix
docs.text:
conf_matrix = ClusteringMetrics.confusion_matrix(true_labels, pred_labels)
print(conf_matrix)

Rows (true labels) and columns (predicted labels) are both indexed by the sorted union of the labels present in true_labels and pred_labels, so a predicted id that never occurs in true_labels gets its own (all-zero) row and a column instead of being silently dropped. Pass labels=[...] to fix the order (and, as in scikit-learn, to ignore samples with other labels). Cluster ids are arbitrary in clustering, so align them to the class ids first (e.g. by the Hungarian algorithm) if you want the diagonal to mean "correct".

docs.title: Classification Report (Precision / Recall / F1)
docs.text:
Treats each true class \(c\) one-vs-rest, with \(\mathrm{TP}_c\), \(\mathrm{FP}_c\), \(\mathrm{FN}_c\):

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}, \quad \text{recall} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}, \quad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P+R}, \quad \text{Jaccard} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}} . \]

Returns a dict keyed by class label, each with precision, recall, f1-score, support, jaccard, and roc_auc. Like the confusion matrix, it matches predicted and true labels by value, so align cluster ids to class ids first. The classes are the sorted union of the true and predicted labels; a label that is only ever predicted is listed with support 0.

report = ClusteringMetrics.classification_report(true_labels, pred_labels)
for label, scores in report.items():
    print(f"Class {label}: F1={scores['f1-score']:.3f}, precision={scores['precision']:.3f}, recall={scores['recall']:.3f}")

roc_auc is the AUC of the hard predictions

ClusteringMetrics.roc_auc_score is the rank-based (Mann-Whitney) AUC with average ranks for ties, \(\mathrm{AUC}=\bigl(\sum_{i:\,y_i=1}\mathrm{rank}(s_i)-n_+(n_++1)/2\bigr)/(n_+n_-)\), so it equals sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score and does not depend on the order of the samples. In classification_report it is applied to the binary one-vs-rest predictions, where it reduces to \((\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2\) (balanced accuracy); for a real AUC pass scores or probabilities to roc_auc_score directly. It is 1.0 by convention when only one class is present.

docs.title: Other helpers
docs.text:
• ClusteringMetrics.kl_divergence_gmm(gmm_p, gmm_q, n_samples=10000): a Monte-Carlo estimate of \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\Vert\,q) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}[\log p(x) - \log q(x)]\) between two fitted mixtures, averaging \(\log p - \log q\) over samples drawn from gmm_p. It is not symmetric and has Monte-Carlo noise \(\propto 1/\sqrt{n_{\text{samples}}}\).
  • ClusteringMetrics.evaluate_clustering(gmm_model, X, true_labels=None, metrics=None): computes a requested subset of the above for a fitted model in one call (supervised scores only when true_labels is given).
  • rand_score, mutual_info_score: the unadjusted building blocks of ARI and NMI.

docs.title: Model Comparison Example
docs.text:
from tgmm import GaussianMixture, ClusteringMetrics

results = []

for cov_type in ['full', 'diag', 'spherical']:
    gmm = GaussianMixture(
        n_components=3,
        n_features=2,
        covariance_type=cov_type,
        random_state=42
    )
    gmm.fit(X)
    labels = gmm.predict(X)

    results.append({
        'type': cov_type,
        'silhouette': ClusteringMetrics.silhouette_score(X, labels, n_components=3),
        'davies_bouldin': ClusteringMetrics.davies_bouldin_index(X, labels, n_components=3),
        'log_likelihood': gmm.lower_bound_,
        'bic': gmm.bic(X),
        'aic': gmm.aic(X),
    })

# Print comparison
for result in results:
    print(f"{result['type']:12s} - "
          f"Silhouette: {result['silhouette']:.3f}, "
          f"DB: {result['davies_bouldin']:.3f}, "
          f"LogLik: {result['log_likelihood']:.2f}, "
          f"BIC: {result['bic']:.2f}, "
          f"AIC: {result['aic']:.2f}")

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text:
Likelihood-based criteria need a model's own log-likelihood and parameter count, so they are bic/aic/icl methods on every fitted mixture (GaussianMixture, StudentTMixture, VonMisesFisherMixture -- including GaussianMixture(n_components=None, ...) in Gibbs mode), not ClusteringMetrics calls. With \(\ell(\hat\theta) = \sum_i \log p(x_i \mid \hat\theta)\) the maximized log-likelihood (gmm.score(X) * n) and \(p\) the number of free parameters:

\[ \mathrm{BIC} = -2\,\ell(\hat\theta) + p\,\ln n, \qquad \mathrm{AIC} = -2\,\ell(\hat\theta) + 2p \]

(both "lower is better"). BIC's \(\ln n\) penalty is heavier than AIC's \(2\) once \(n > 7\), so BIC prefers smaller models and is consistent for the true \(K\) when the model family is correct; AIC targets predictive accuracy and tends to pick more components.

docs.title: Free parameter counts
docs.text:
For GaussianMixture, \(p = (K-1) + Kd + p_\Sigma\): \(K-1\) free weights, \(Kd\) means, and covariance parameters

covariance_type \(p_\Sigma\) covariance_type \(p_\Sigma\) full / VVV \(K\,d(d+1)/2\) VEI \(K + (d-1)\) diag / VVI \(Kd\) EVI \(1 + K(d-1)\) spherical / VII \(K\) VEE \(K + (d-1) + d(d-1)/2\) tied_full / EEE \(d(d+1)/2\) EVE \(1 + K(d-1) + d(d-1)/2\) tied_diag / EEI \(d\) EEV \(d + K\,d(d-1)/2\) tied_spherical / EII \(1\) VVE \(Kd + d(d-1)/2\) VEV \(K + (d-1) + K\,d(d-1)/2\) EVV \(1 + K(d-1) + K\,d(d-1)/2\)

(the GPCM codes are explained in GPCM Covariance Models). Student-t adds \(K\) (or \(1\), or \(0\)) degrees-of-freedom parameters, and vMF has \((K-1) + K(d-1) + K\) (or \(+1\) for a shared \(\kappa\)) -- see Other Mixture Families. In Gibbs mode, \(K\) is the number of active components.

docs.title: ICL (Integrated Completed Likelihood)
docs.text:
icl(X, mode='hard') adds an entropy penalty to bic for ambiguous, overlapping-cluster assignments (Biernacki, Celeux & Govaert, 2000). With responsibilities \(r_{ik}\) and \(\hat z_i = \arg\max_k r_{ik}\),

\[ \mathrm{ICL}_{\text{hard}} = \mathrm{BIC} - 2\sum_i \ln r_{i\hat z_i}, \qquad \mathrm{ICL}_{\text{soft}} = \mathrm{BIC} - 2\sum_{i,k} r_{ik}\ln r_{ik}. \]

Both penalties are \(\ge 0\), so lower is better, same convention as bic; \(\mathrm{ICL} \ge \mathrm{BIC}\) always, and the two are identical when responsibilities are one-hot (perfectly separated clusters). \(-\sum r\ln r\) is the entropy of the soft assignment: ICL is BIC applied to the completed (data + cluster labels) likelihood, so it penalizes solutions whose components overlap.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, random_state=0)
gmm.fit(X)
print(gmm.bic(X), gmm.icl(X))       # icl(X) >= bic(X)
print(gmm.icl(X, mode='soft'))      # entropy-form penalty instead of hard-argmax

ICL tends to prefer fewer, better-separated components than BIC on data with overlapping clusters -- see the Model Selection notebook for a worked BIC-vs-ICL comparison where they pick different K.

docs.title: select_model: sweeping n_components and covariance_type
docs.text:
from tgmm import select_model

result = select_model(
    X,
    n_components=range(1, 11),
    covariance_types=('full', 'diag', 'spherical', 'tied_full'),
    criterion='bic',   # or 'aic', 'icl'
    n_init=3,
    random_state=0,
)

print(result.best_.n_components, result.best_.covariance_type)
df = result.to_dataframe()  # lazy pandas import

covariance_types defaults to all 14 GPCM codes (the mclust-style workflow); pass an explicit subset, as above, to narrow the search. result.table has one row per (n_components, covariance_type) combination (bic, aic, icl, log_likelihood, converged); a combination whose fit raises (e.g. a singular covariance at a large K) gets None scores instead of aborting the whole sweep. result.models_[(K, covariance_type)] gives the fitted model for any successful combination, and best_ is the one minimizing criterion. Any other keyword (max_iter, reg_covar, ...) is forwarded to every GaussianMixture. See the API reference for the full signature.

docs.title: Complete API Reference
docs.text: For full details on all metrics, see the API Reference.

docs.title: Gaussian Mixture Model
docs.text:
The GaussianMixture class is the core component of tgmm. It fits a mixture of Gaussians by Expectation-Maximization (EM) or one of its variants (classification, stochastic, annealed, online), with optional Bayesian priors (MAP estimation), a choice of 6 classic or 14 eigen-decomposed (GPCM) covariance structures, semi-supervised fitting, and a Dirichlet-process (Gibbs-sampling) mode that infers the number of components.

This page explains what is computed: the model, every update equation the code implements, and how each option changes them. For runnable examples see the Tutorials.

Notation (used throughout the documentation)

\(n\) samples \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \(K\) components. \(r_{ik}\) is the responsibility of component \(k\) for sample \(i\), and

\[ n_k=\sum_i r_{ik},\qquad \bar y_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\,x_i,\qquad W_k=\sum_i r_{ik}\,(x_i-\bar y_k)(x_i-\bar y_k)^\top . \]

\(n_k\) is the "effective sample count", \(\bar y_k\) the responsibility-weighted mean and \(W_k\) the responsibility-weighted scatter matrix. Together with \(n\) these are the sufficient statistics of the M-step (tgmm.SufficientStats stores \(n_k\), \(\sum_i r_{ik}x_i\) and \(W_k\) -- or its diagonal / trace for diag / spherical types).

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
A Gaussian mixture represents the density of the data as a weighted sum of \(K\) Gaussians:

\[ p(x\mid\theta)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k),\qquad \pi_k\ge 0,\ \ \sum_k\pi_k=1, \] \[ \mathcal{N}(x\mid\mu,\Sigma)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{-1/2} \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 (x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Big), \]

with parameters \(\theta=\{\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K\). Equivalently, there is a hidden (latent) label \(z_i\in\{1,\dots,K\}\) per sample with \(p(z_i=k)=\pi_k\) and \(x_i\mid z_i=k\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\); clustering means inferring \(z_i\).

Maximum likelihood maximizes the observed-data log-likelihood

\[ \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k), \]

which has a log of a sum and so no closed-form maximizer. If the labels were observed, the complete-data log-likelihood

\[ \ell_c(\theta)=\sum_{i,k}\mathbb{1}[z_i=k]\,\big(\log\pi_k+\log\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\big) \]

would split into one independent, closed-form problem per component. EM exploits this.

from tgmm import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,         # number of Gaussian components K
    n_features=2,           # data dimensionality d (optional: inferred from X)
    covariance_type='full'  # structure of each Sigma_k
)
gmm.fit(X)

labels = gmm.predict(X)              # hard assignments, argmax_k r_ik
probabilities = gmm.predict_proba(X)  # soft assignments r_ik
log_likelihood = gmm.score(X)         # average log-likelihood (1/n) * ell(theta)

docs.title: How EM works
docs.text:
For any distribution \(q_{ik}\) over the labels, Jensen's inequality gives a lower bound on \(\ell\):

\[ \ell(\theta)\ \ge\ \mathcal{F}(q,\theta)=\sum_{i,k}q_{ik}\log\frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{q_{ik}}, \]

with equality exactly when \(q_{ik}=p(z_i=k\mid x_i,\theta)\). EM alternates

  1. E-step: set \(q\) to that posterior (making the bound tight at the current \(\theta^{(t)}\));
  2. M-step: maximize \(\mathcal{F}(q,\theta)\) over \(\theta\).

Then \(\ell(\theta^{(t+1)})\ge\mathcal{F}(q,\theta^{(t+1)})\ge\mathcal{F}(q,\theta^{(t)})=\ell(\theta^{(t)})\): the log-likelihood never decreases, so EM converges to a stationary point (a local maximum in practice, which is why initialization and n_init matter). With priors the same argument applies to the log-posterior \(\ell(\theta)+\log p(\theta)\) (MAP-EM).

docs.title: E-step: responsibilities
docs.text:
\[ r_{ik}=p(z_i=k\mid x_i,\theta)= \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j}\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)} =\operatorname{softmax}_k\!\big(\log\pi_k+\log\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\big). \]

tgmm works entirely in log space: the per-component log-density \(\log\mathcal{N}(x\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)=-\tfrac12\big[d\log 2\pi+\log|\Sigma_k|+(x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\big]\) is evaluated per covariance type (for full, via a Cholesky factor \(\Sigma_k=L_kL_k^\top\): \(\log|\Sigma_k|=2\sum\log\operatorname{diag}L_k\), and the Mahalanobis term by a triangular solve; for diag / spherical / tied_* the corresponding cheap closed forms), the mixing weight is added, and the normalizer is a logsumexp. The same normalizer gives the per-sample log-likelihood \(\log p(x_i\mid\theta)\), whose mean is lower_bound_ (and what score returns).

docs.title: M-step: maximum-likelihood updates
docs.text:
Maximizing \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\theta\) (using the responsibilities as soft counts) gives

\[ \pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n},\qquad \mu_k=\bar y_k, \]

and a covariance update that depends on covariance_type. For each component the \(\Sigma_k\)-dependent part of \(\mathcal{F}\) is

\[ -\tfrac12\Big[n_k\log|\Sigma_k|+\operatorname{tr}\big(\Sigma_k^{-1}W_k\big)\Big] \qquad(\text{at }\mu_k=\bar y_k), \]

so constraining \(\Sigma_k\) to a family and minimizing \(n_k\log|\Sigma_k|+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_k^{-1}W_k)\) within that family yields the closed forms below. With \(\varepsilon\) = reg_covar (added to keep \(\Sigma\) positive definite):

covariance_type Shape of covariances_ Update Free covariance parameters full \((K,d,d)\) \(\Sigma_k=\dfrac{W_k}{n_k}+\varepsilon I\) \(K\,d(d+1)/2\) diag \((K,d)\) \(\sigma^2_{kj}=\dfrac{(W_k)_{jj}}{n_k}+\varepsilon\) \(Kd\) spherical \((K,)\) \(\sigma_k^2=\dfrac{\operatorname{tr}W_k}{n_k\,d}+\varepsilon\) \(K\) tied_full \((d,d)\) \(\Sigma=\dfrac{\sum_kW_k}{\sum_kn_k}+\varepsilon I\) \(d(d+1)/2\) tied_diag \((d,)\) \(\sigma^2_{j}=\dfrac{\sum_k(W_k)_{jj}}{\sum_kn_k}+\varepsilon\) \(d\) tied_spherical scalar \(\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum_k\operatorname{tr}W_k}{d\sum_kn_k}+\varepsilon\) \(1\)

Why these forms: for full the minimizer of \(n_k\log|\Sigma|+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}W_k)\) is \(W_k/n_k\) (the weighted sample covariance); for a diagonal \(\Sigma\) the objective separates per coordinate; for \(\Sigma=\sigma^2I\) it is \(n_kd\log\sigma^2+\operatorname{tr}(W_k)/\sigma^2\), minimized at \(\operatorname{tr}(W_k)/(n_kd)\); for tied types the same objective is summed over \(k\) with a single shared \(\Sigma\), so the scatter is pooled over components and divided by the total count.

More covariance structures: the 14 GPCM models

covariance_type also accepts all 14 Celeux & Govaert (1995) mclust codes ('EII', 'VEI', 'EVE', 'VVV', ... -- the six names above are aliases for six of them). These decompose \(\Sigma_k=\lambda_kD_kA_kD_k^\top\) into volume, shape and orientation, each shared across or free per component. See GPCM Covariance Models for the decomposition, the M-step derivations and parameter counts; covariance_type_ always reports the canonical code.

Where reg_covar enters

In the plain MLE updates above, \(\varepsilon\) is added to the covariance itself. In the MAP / NIW updates below it is added to the posterior scale matrix \(\Psi_n\) before dividing by \(\nu_n\), so its effective size is \(\varepsilon/\nu_n\).

docs.title: Parameter counts
docs.text: The total number of free parameters used by bic / aic / icl is \(p=(K-1)+Kd+p_\Sigma\), where \(p_\Sigma\) is the last column of the table above (for the 8 extra GPCM codes see the GPCM page). In Gibbs mode \(K\) is the inferred number of active components.

docs.title: Covariance types at a glance
docs.text:
Per-component covariances (full, diag, spherical) let each cluster have its own size, shape and orientation to the degree the type allows; tied_* types force every cluster to share one covariance (different centers only), which saves parameters and stabilizes fits with few points per cluster.

GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='full')            # arbitrary ellipsoids
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='diag')            # axis-aligned ellipsoids
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='spherical')       # one variance per cluster
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='tied_full')       # one shared full covariance
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='tied_diag')       # one shared diagonal
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='tied_spherical')  # one shared variance
GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='EVE')             # any of the 14 mclust GPCM codes

Aliases: 'tied' is 'tied_full' and 'isotropic' is 'spherical'. The covariance tutorial compares all of them visually.

docs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
docs.text:
The default: the updates above.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X)

docs.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) with priors
docs.text:
Priors regularize each M-step. All priors are conjugate:

Parameter Prior Constructor arguments weights \(\pi\) \(\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K)\) weight_concentration_prior \(=\alpha\) mean \(\mu_k\) \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_{0,k},\ \Sigma_k/\kappa_0)\) mean_prior \(=\mu_0\), mean_precision_prior \(=\kappa_0\) covariance \(\Sigma_k\) \(\operatorname{Inverse\text{-}Wishart}(\Psi_0,\nu_0)\) covariance_prior \(=\Psi_0\), degrees_of_freedom_prior \(=\nu_0\) 
gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    weight_concentration_prior=torch.ones(3) * 2.0,                  # Dirichlet on weights
    mean_prior=torch.zeros(3, 2),                                     # Gaussian on means
    mean_precision_prior=0.01,
    covariance_prior=torch.eye(2).unsqueeze(0).repeat(3, 1, 1),      # Inverse-Wishart on covariances
    degrees_of_freedom_prior=3.0,
)
gmm.fit(X)

Weights (independent of everything else; works with all covariance types, including all 14 GPCM codes): the MAP estimate of a Dirichlet-multinomial,

\[ \pi_k=\frac{n_k+\alpha_k-1}{\,n+\sum_j\alpha_j-K\,} . \]

Means only (mean_prior without covariance_prior):

\[ \mu_k=\frac{\sum_ir_{ik}x_i+\kappa_0\mu_{0,k}}{n_k+\kappa_0} =\frac{n_k\bar y_k+\kappa_0\mu_{0,k}}{n_k+\kappa_0}, \]

a precision-weighted average of the data mean and the prior mean (shrinkage toward \(\mu_0\) that is strong when \(n_k\ll\kappa_0\)). The covariance is then the ordinary MLE form, but with the scatter taken about the shrunk mean \(\mu_k\) rather than \(\bar y_k\) (by the parallel-axis identity \(\sum_ir_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k)(x_i-\mu_k)^\top=W_k+n_k(\bar y_k-\mu_k)(\bar y_k-\mu_k)^\top\)).

Covariance only (covariance_prior without mean_prior), with scatter \(S_k\) about \(\mu_k=\bar y_k\):

\[ \Sigma_k=\frac{\Psi_0+W_k+\varepsilon I}{\nu_0+n_k}\quad(\texttt{full}), \]

with the analogous diagonal / trace forms for the other types (diag: per coordinate, divide by \(\nu_0+n_k\); spherical: \(\sigma_k^2=(\psi_0+\operatorname{tr}W_k+\varepsilon)/\big((\nu_0+n_k)d\big)\); tied_*: pool \(W_k\) over \(k\) and use \(\nu_0+\sum_kn_k\)).

docs.title: Normal-Inverse-Wishart (NIW) conjugate prior
docs.text:
When both mean_prior and covariance_prior are given, tgmm uses the joint NIW prior \(\mu_k,\Sigma_k\sim\operatorname{NIW}(\mu_0,\kappa_0,\Psi_0, u_0)\), i.e. \(\Sigma_k\sim\operatorname{IW}(\Psi_0, u_0)\) and \(\mu_k\mid\Sigma_k\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\Sigma_k/\kappa_0)\). The posterior is again NIW with

\[ \kappa_n=\kappa_0+n_k,\quad u_n= u_0+n_k,\quad \mu_n= rac{\kappa_0\mu_0+n_k ar y_k}{\kappa_n}, \] \[ \Psi_n=\Psi_0+W_k+ rac{\kappa_0\,n_k}{\kappa_0+n_k}\,( ar y_k-\mu_0)( ar y_k-\mu_0)^ op+\varepsilon I, \]

and the M-step sets

\[ \mu_k=\mu_n,\qquad \Sigma_k= rac{\Psi_n}{ u_n}. \]

The third term of \(\Psi_n\) penalizes a data mean that disagrees with the prior mean: it is the price of the prior's uncertainty about \(\mu_k\) and vanishes as \(n_k o\infty\) or \(\kappa_0 o0\).

\(\Psi_n/ u_n\) is a deliberate choice, not the textbook posterior mean or mode

For an Inverse-Wishart posterior the textbook point estimates are the mean \(\Psi_n/( u_n-d-1)\) and the mode \(\Psi_n/( u_n+d+1)\). tgmm uses \(\Psi_n/ u_n\) for every covariance type, in both MAP and NIW updates and in Gibbs mode. The mean is undefined whenever \( u_n\le d+1\), which a nearly empty component can reach, while \(\Psi_n/ u_n\) stays finite and positive for every \( u_n>0\); and the three agree closely when \( u_n\gg d\). In particular, with \(\kappa_0 o0\) and \(\Psi_0 o0\) it reduces to the MLE \(W_k/n_k\).

The other covariance types use the same \(\Psi_n\) in structured form:

Type \(\Psi_n\) \(\Sigma\) diag per coordinate: \(\psi_{0,j}+(W_k)_{jj}+ rac{\kappa_0n_k}{\kappa_n}( ar y_{kj}-\mu_{0,kj})^2+\varepsilon\) \(\Psi_n/ u_n\) per coordinate spherical \(\psi_0+\operatorname{tr}W_k+ rac{\kappa_0n_k}{\kappa_n}\lVert ar y_k-\mu_{0,k} Vert^2+d\,\varepsilon\) \(\sigma_k^2=\Psi_n/( u_n\,d)\) tied_full \(\Psi_0+\sum_kW_k+\sum_k rac{\kappa_0n_k}{\kappa_n}( ar y_k-\mu_{0,k})( ar y_k-\mu_{0,k})^ op+\varepsilon I\) \(\Psi_n/( u_0+\sum_kn_k)\) tied_diag, tied_spherical the tied analogues (sums over \(k\)) \(\Psi_n/( u_0+\sum_kn_k)\), divided by \(d\) for spherical

(For tied_spherical the code adds \(\varepsilon\cdot n\cdot d\) rather than \(\varepsilon\cdot d\) to the numerator, so there \(\varepsilon\) acts at its face value on the variance.)

MAP/NIW are for the six classic covariance types

mean_prior / covariance_prior raise NotImplementedError for the 8 GPCM codes without a tgmm name; a conjugate prior would have to be derived per parameterization. weight_concentration_prior is independent of the covariance parameterization and works with all 14.

See the Priors tutorial and the NIW comparison for worked examples.

docs.title: Initialization strategies
docs.text:
EM converges to a local optimum, so where it starts matters. init_means chooses the initial means (the E-step then yields the first responsibilities from them), init_weights and init_covariances the rest; all three also accept an explicit tensor.

init_means How the \(K\) initial centers are chosen 'kmeans' (default) Lloyd's algorithm (pure PyTorch), started from k-means++ 'kpp' k-means++: pick each new center with probability \(\propto D(x)^2\) (squared distance to the nearest chosen center) 'random' \(\mu=\bar x+Lz\), \(z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\), \(LL^\top\) = the data covariance 'points' \(K\) data points chosen uniformly at random 'maxdist' greedy farthest-point selection

init_weights: 'uniform' (default), 'random' (Dirichlet draw), 'kmeans' (cluster proportions). init_covariances: 'empirical' (default; covariance of the points nearest each mean), 'eye', 'random', 'global' (the data covariance for every component). See the GMM Initializer guide.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means='kpp')

initial_means = torch.tensor([[0, 0], [5, 5], [0, 5]], dtype=torch.float32)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means=initial_means)   # custom

docs.title: Multiple restarts
docs.text:
n_init=m runs the whole fit \(m\) times from different initializations and keeps the run with the highest final log-likelihood. With random_state=s, run \(i\) is seeded with \(s+i\) and the winner's seed is stored in best_random_state_:

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, n_init=10, random_state=42)
gmm.fit(X)
print(gmm.best_random_state_)

docs.title: Fitting algorithms
docs.text:
algorithm selects the EM variant that drives fit(). Every variant feeds some matrix of (soft or hard) assignments into the same M-step, which computes \(n_k,\bar y_k,W_k\) from it exactly as above.

algorithm What goes into the M-step When to use it 'em' (default) soft responsibilities \(r_{ik}\) the right default 'cem' hard one-hot \(\mathbb{1}[k=\arg\max_jr_{ij}]\) faster, crisper partition; more local-minimum prone 'sem' a hard label sampled from \(r_{i\cdot}\) escape poor optima; diagnose an overspecified \(K\) 'saem' statistics averaged over sampled sweeps with step \(\gamma_t\) SEM's exploration with a convergent stopping point

temperature (deterministic annealing) and step_size (online / mini-batch EM) are independent knobs layered on top.

docs.title: Classification EM (CEM)
docs.text:
CEM inserts a classification step between E and M: \(\hat r_{ik}=\mathbb{1}\big[k=\arg\max_jr_{ij}\big]\). It maximizes the classification likelihood \(\sum_i\log\big(\pi_{z_i}\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_{z_i},\Sigma_{z_i})\big)\) over parameters and labels, rather than the mixture likelihood. It is a hard-assignment generalization of k-means (k-means is CEM with equal weights and a shared spherical covariance, tied_spherical) and converges in few iterations, but it estimates the parameters from truncated data, so it is biased when clusters overlap.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, algorithm='cem')
gmm.fit(X)

cem=True is deprecated

The older cem=True keyword still works (treated as algorithm='cem') but emits a DeprecationWarning; passing it together with algorithm='sem'/'saem' raises. Use algorithm='cem'.

docs.title: Stochastic EM (SEM)
docs.text:
SEM (Celeux & Diebolt, 1985) replaces the soft assignment by one draw per sample, \(z_i\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(r_{i1},\dots,r_{iK})\), and runs the M-step on the resulting one-hot matrix. The iterates form a Markov chain that keeps exploring instead of settling, so SEM can leave poor local optima.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, algorithm='sem', max_iter=200)
gmm.fit(X)

print(gmm.log_likelihood_history_)   # per-sweep log-likelihood trace
print(gmm.n_empty_components_)       # > 0 re-seeds suggest n_components is too large

SEM has no pointwise convergence, so it always runs exactly max_iter sweeps (and sets converged_=True). A component that receives fewer than one sampled point in a sweep has its mean re-seeded at one of the worst-fit data points (and, for full/diag/spherical, its covariance reset to the data covariance); each re-seed is counted in n_empty_components_. The returned parameters are computed from the sweeps at or after sem_burn_in (default max(1, max_iter // 5)): sem_estimate='best' (default) keeps the snapshot with the highest log-likelihood; 'mean' averages the parameters across all of them, which presumes no label switching between sweeps -- prefer 'best' whenever \(K\) may be overspecified.

docs.title: Stochastic Approximation EM (SAEM)
docs.text:
SAEM (Delyon, Lavielle & Moulines, 1999) averages the sufficient statistics of the sampled sweeps with a decreasing step size \(\gamma_t\) (Robbins-Monro):

\[ \tilde S_t=(1-\gamma_t)\,\tilde S_{t-1}+\gamma_t\,S\big(z^{(t)}\big),\qquad \tilde S_0=S\big(z^{(0)}\big), \]

where \(S=(n_k,\ \sum_ir_{ik}x_i,\ W_k)\), and the M-step then maps \(\tilde S_t\) to parameters. The default step_size='auto' is \(\gamma_t=(t+2)^{-0.7}\) (so \(\sum\gamma_t=\infty\) while \(\sum\gamma_t^2<\infty\)); a positive float gives a constant step and a callable \(t\mapsto\gamma_t\) a custom schedule. Because the averaged statistics converge, the usual tol test applies -- SAEM is "the SEM that converges".

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, algorithm='saem', max_iter=200)
gmm.fit(X)
print(gmm.converged_)

docs.title: Deterministic Annealing (DAEM)
docs.text:
DAEM (Ueda & Nakano, 1998) tempers the posterior with an inverse temperature \(\beta\in(0,1]\):

\[ r_{ik}(\beta)=\frac{\big(\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\big)^{\beta}} {\sum_j\big(\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\big)^{\beta}} . \]

At \(\beta\to0\) every sample is assigned almost uniformly to all components (a smooth, nearly unimodal objective); at \(\beta=1\) this is the ordinary E-step. temperature=(beta_0, n_anneal) starts at \(\beta_0\in(0,1)\) and raises \(\beta\) geometrically to 1 over n_anneal iterations:

\[ \beta_t=\begin{cases}\beta_0^{\,1-t/n_{\text{anneal}}}, & t<n_{\text{anneal}}\\[2pt] 1, & t\ge n_{\text{anneal}}\end{cases} \] 
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, temperature=(0.1, 30))
gmm.fit(X)
print(gmm.annealing_schedule_)  # beta actually used at each E-step

Works with algorithm in {'em', 'cem', 'sem'}. While \(\beta<1\) convergence checks are suspended, and the entries of log_likelihood_history_ recorded then are the tempered normalizers, not true log-likelihoods -- compare only the entries from \(\beta=1\) on. Annealing is a heuristic, not a guarantee: a perfectly symmetric start (e.g. identical means) stays symmetric under any \(\beta\), so some asymmetry in the initialization is needed for annealing to amplify.

docs.title: Mini-batch and online EM
docs.text:
With batch_size alone, the E-step and statistics accumulation run in row chunks. This is exact (a per-row softmax and additive statistics) and only bounds peak memory at \(O(\text{batch\_size}\cdot K\cdot d)\). Adding step_size switches to online EM (Cappe & Moulines, 2009): for each shuffled mini-batch \(B\) of the epoch, compute \(S_B\) from the current parameters, rescale it to the full data size, blend it into a running estimate with step \(\gamma_t\) (where \(t\) counts mini-batches globally), and run the M-step from it:

\[ \tilde S\leftarrow(1-\gamma_t)\,\tilde S+\gamma_t\,\frac{n}{|B|}\,S_B ,\qquad \theta\leftarrow\text{M-step}(\tilde S). \]

max_iter counts epochs; there is no tol test (converged_ is set to True), and log_likelihood_history_ has one entry per epoch. step_size requires batch_size.

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3, n_features=2,
    batch_size=256, step_size='auto',  # or a float, or a callable t -> gamma_t
    max_iter=10,                        # epochs
)
gmm.fit(X)

For streaming data, partial_fit performs one such update per call on an already-initialized model:

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, batch_size=256, step_size='auto')
gmm.fit(first_batch)
for batch in stream_of_batches:
    gmm.partial_fit(batch)

partial_fit assumes a roughly constant batch size across calls: unlike fit()'s epoch loop it does not rescale to a known total size (there is none in a true stream).

A caveat on blended scatter

\(W_k\) is centered on each accumulation's own mean \(\bar y_k\). SAEM and online EM blend \(W_k\) (and \(n_k\), \(\sum_ir_{ik}x_i\)) linearly, which is exact for the first two but only approximate for \(W_k\) when the means shift between accumulations: the true scatter about the blended mean also contains a between-accumulation term. The approximation vanishes as the iterates stabilize.

docs.title: Convergence control
docs.text:
gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3, n_features=2,
    max_iter=200,        # maximum EM iterations
    tol=1e-4,            # convergence tolerance
    verbose=True, verbose_interval=10,
)
gmm.fit(X)
print(gmm.converged_, gmm.n_iter_, gmm.lower_bound_)

Let \(L_t=\frac1n\ell(\theta^{(t)})\) be the average log-likelihood (lower_bound_). convergence='relative' (default) stops when

\[ \frac{|L_t-L_{t-1}|}{|L_{t-1}|}<\texttt{tol}. \]

convergence='aitken' uses Aitken's acceleration: EM's log-likelihood sequence is asymptotically geometric, so with \(a_t=\dfrac{L_t-L_{t-1}}{L_{t-1}-L_{t-2}}\) (when \(a_t<1\)) the limit is estimated as

\[ L_\infty=L_{t-1}+\frac{L_t-L_{t-1}}{1-a_t}, \]

and the fit stops when \(L_\infty-L_t<\texttt{tol}\) (an absolute gap to the extrapolated limit). It can stop earlier on fits that improve slowly but steadily, and falls back to the relative test until three values exist (or when \(a_t\ge1\)).

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, convergence='aitken')

fit() also accepts per-call overrides of max_iter, tol, random_state and warm_start (continue from the previous fit's parameters) without changing the model's defaults.

docs.title: Model selection
docs.text:
Choosing \(K\) (and the covariance structure) is a trade-off between fit and complexity. With \(p\) the parameter count above and \(\bar L=\frac1n\ell(\hat\theta)\):

\[ \operatorname{AIC}=-2n\bar L+2p,\qquad \operatorname{BIC}=-2n\bar L+p\ln n,\qquad \operatorname{ICL}=\operatorname{BIC}+2\,\mathrm{EN}. \]

All are "lower is better" (gmm.aic(X), gmm.bic(X), gmm.icl(X)). \(\mathrm{EN}\ge0\) is the classification-entropy penalty of Biernacki, Celeux & Govaert (2000): with mode='hard' (default) \(\mathrm{EN}=-\sum_i\log\hat\tau_{i}\), where \(\hat\tau_i=\max_kr_{ik}\) is the posterior of the assigned cluster; with mode='soft' it is the entropy \(-\sum_{i,k}r_{ik}\log r_{ik}\). ICL therefore penalizes overlapping clusters on top of BIC and favors well-separated partitions.

select_model sweeps a grid and returns the best fit (by criterion='bic', 'aic' or 'icl'); by default it tries all 14 GPCM covariance codes:

from tgmm import select_model

result = select_model(X, n_components=range(1, 8), criterion='bic')
print(result.best_.covariance_type_, result.best_.n_components)
df = result.to_dataframe()   # every (K, covariance_type) with bic, aic, icl, log_likelihood, converged

See the Model Selection tutorial and Clustering Metrics for label-free validity indices.

docs.title: Supervised and semi-supervised fitting
docs.text:
Passing labels to fit uses known class information; -1 marks an unknown label.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type='full')
gmm.fit(X, labels=y)             # fully labeled
gmm.fit(X, labels=y_partial)     # some entries -1: semi-supervised EM
gmm.predict_class(X)             # class labels (via classes_), not component indices

Fully labeled. Each point's responsibility is the one-hot vector of its true class, so there is nothing to iterate: a single M-step recovers the per-class \(\pi_k=n_k/n\), \(\mu_k\), \(\Sigma_k\) -- exactly what CEM would converge to with the correct partition. n_components must equal the number of distinct labels (times components_per_class for a components_per_class > 1; then each class's block of components is fit by ordinary EM on that class's rows, weights scaled by the class fraction, and n_init applies within each block); label values need not be contiguous (classes_[k] recovers the original value). n_init and warm_start are ignored, converged_ is True and n_iter_ is 1. Priors still apply (a regularized fit for classes with few samples).

Partially labeled. Semi-supervised EM maximizes

\[ \sum_{i\in\text{labeled}}\log\sum_{k\in\text{block}(c_i)}\pi_k\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k) +\sum_{i\in\text{unlabeled}}\log\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k), \]

by clamping each labeled row's responsibility to its class's block of components (zero outside, renormalized inside) and leaving unlabeled rows with the full posterior. unlabeled_weight \(u\) multiplies the unlabeled rows' responsibilities before the M-step (\(u=0\) uses the labeled rows only), label_confidence \(c<1\) keeps mass \(c\) on the class block and gives \(1-c\) to the unclamped posterior outside it (for noisy labels), and components_per_class (an int or a dict) gives a class several components. Partial labels support algorithm='em'/'cem' only. See Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting for the full treatment, including PositiveUnlabeledMixture, and the Supervised Fitting notebook and Semi-supervised notebook for worked examples.

docs.title: Gibbs sampling: inferring the number of components
docs.text: If \(K\) is unknown, GaussianMixture(n_components=None, ...) replaces EM by a collapsed Gibbs sampler for a Dirichlet-process mixture, which infers the number of components from the data.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
A Dirichlet process \(G\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,G_0)\) with a NIW base measure \(G_0\) gives mixture weights by stick-breaking:

\[ v_k\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,\alpha),\qquad \pi_k=v_k\prod_{j<k}(1-v_j), \]

an infinite sequence of weights summing to 1 -- larger \(\alpha\) spreads mass over more components. Marginalizing the weights gives the equivalent Chinese Restaurant Process: sample \(i\) joins an existing cluster \(k\) with probability \(\propto n_k^{-i}\) (the other points already there) or opens a new one with probability \(\propto\alpha\).

docs.title: The sampler
docs.text:
Component parameters are integrated out too (collapsed sampling, Neal's Algorithm 3). With the NIW prior \((\mu_0,\kappa_0,\Psi_0,\nu_0)\), the posterior given the other points of cluster \(k\) has the same form as the NIW update above (\(\kappa_n,\nu_n,\mu_n,\Psi_n\)), and the posterior predictive of a point is a multivariate Student-\(t\):

\[ x\mid X_k^{-i}\ \sim\ t_{\nu_n-d+1}\!\Big(\mu_n,\ \frac{\kappa_n+1}{\kappa_n(\nu_n-d+1)}\,\Psi_n\Big). \]

Each sweep resamples every assignment from

\[ p(z_i=k\mid z_{-i},X)\ \propto\ n_k^{-i}\;t_{\nu_n-d+1}\big(x_i;\ \mu_n,\ \cdots\big) \quad(\text{existing } k),\qquad p(z_i=\text{new}\mid z_{-i},X)\ \propto\ \alpha\;t_{\nu_0-d+1}\big(x_i;\ \mu_0,\ \cdots\big). \]

For diag the predictive is a product of per-coordinate Student-\(t\) with \(\nu_n\) degrees of freedom; for spherical a single isotropic \(t\) with \(\nu_0+n_kd\) degrees of freedom. tied_* types and the 8 extra GPCM codes are not supported (a coupling across components breaks the per-cluster factorization).

from tgmm import GaussianMixture

# Gibbs mode has no default prior; suggest_priors gives a sensible start from a k-means pass.
mean_prior, mean_precision_prior, covariance_prior, degrees_of_freedom_prior = \
    GaussianMixture.suggest_priors(X, n_components=10)

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=None,       # switches to Gibbs sampling
    covariance_type='full',  # 'full', 'diag' or 'spherical'
    max_components=20,       # upper bound on tracked components (None = unbounded)
    alpha=1.0,               # DP concentration
    mean_prior=mean_prior,
    mean_precision_prior=mean_precision_prior,
    covariance_prior=covariance_prior,
    degrees_of_freedom_prior=degrees_of_freedom_prior,
    max_iter=50,             # an exact sweep count in Gibbs mode
)
gmm.fit(X)

print(gmm.n_components_)  # the inferred component count
print(gmm.active_)        # which of the tracked slots are in use
  • Truncated (max_components=K, default 20): \(K\) fixed slots. The CRP rule is replaced by its finite Dirichlet-multinomial approximation, \(p(z_i=k)\propto(n_k^{-i}+\alpha/K)\times\text{predictive}_k\), which converges to the CRP as \(K\) grows past the number of clusters actually used.
  • Unbounded (max_components=None): components are created and destroyed on the fly (Neal's Algorithm 3 exactly). init_k sets the number of components the sampler is seeded with, and burn_in (default max_iter // 5) the number of sweeps excluded from n_components_history_, the per-sweep trace of the number of active components.
  • The fitted parameters come from the final sweep's partition (one posterior draw, not an average -- averaging over sweeps is not meaningful because labels permute): \(\mu_k=\mu_n\), \(\Sigma_k=\Psi_n/\nu_n\), \(\pi_k=n_k/n\). A component is active (counted in n_components_ / active_) when its expected point count \(\pi_kn\) exceeds weight_threshold (default 1.0).
  • suggest_priors(X, n_components) sets \(\mu_0=\bar x\), \(\kappa_0=0.1\), \(\nu_0=d+2\) and \(\Psi_0\) to the pooled within-cluster scatter of a \(k\)-means partition (not the marginal data covariance, which for well-separated clusters conflates between- and within-cluster spread and inflates every fitted covariance).
  • There is no EM-style convergence test: max_iter is an exact sweep count and converged_ is always True there. Each sweep is an \(O(n)\) Python-level loop, so the EM default of 1000 can be very slow -- pass an explicit, usually much smaller, max_iter. Supervised fitting (labels=) is not available.

See the Dirichlet Process Mixture notebook for the stick-breaking and Gibbs-sampling math, a step-by-step walkthrough and a comparison against classical EM, and the design document for the full derivation.

docs.title: Frozen components and sample weights
docs.text:
frozen_components=(1, 3) holds those components' parameters at their initial values for the whole fit (give them with tensor init_means / init_covariances, or with warm_start); their mixing weights still update, and MAP / NIW priors never shrink them. It is useful for anchoring known classes (a "reference" population) while the rest of the mixture is learned, and it is what PositiveUnlabeledMixture(anchor='fixed') uses. It is not available for the tied covariance types or the 8 GPCM codes without a classic name (one factor is shared across components).

fit(X, sample_weight=w) fits a weighted sample. With w of shape (n,) row \(i\) counts \(w_i\) times: every responsibility is multiplied by \(w_i\) before the statistics of the M-step, the mixing weights use \(n_\mathrm{eff}=\sum_iw_i\) as the sample count, and the convergence criterion is the weighted mean log-likelihood. Integer weights are therefore equivalent to duplicating rows and weight \(0\) to dropping the row. For covariance_type='diag' or 'spherical' (maximum likelihood only) w may also have shape (n, d): entry \(w_{ij}\) then weights feature \(j\) of row \(i\) in both steps,

\[ \mu_{kj}=\frac{\sum_i r_{ik}w_{ij}x_{ij}}{\sum_i r_{ik}w_{ij}},\qquad \sigma^2_{kj}=\frac{\sum_i r_{ik}w_{ij}(x_{ij}-\mu_{kj})^2}{\sum_i r_{ik}w_{ij}}, \]

and \(w_{ij}=0\) makes that entry invisible, which is exact marginalisation of an independent feature. inertia (as in pomegranate) is not provided: step_size (online EM / SAEM) is the same control on the sufficient statistics.

docs.title: Sampling from the model
docs.text:
Generate new samples from the fitted mixture: pick \(z\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\pi)\), then draw \(x=\mu_z+L_zg\) with \(g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) and \(L_zL_z^\top=\Sigma_z\).

samples, component_ids = gmm.sample(100)                          # basic sampling
samples, _ = gmm.sample(50, component=0)                          # one component only
samples, _ = gmm.sample(100, confidence=0.95)                     # within the 95% region
samples, _ = gmm.sample(100, std_range=(1.0, 2.0))                # Mahalanobis radius in [1, 2]
outliers, _ = gmm.sample(20, std_range=(3.0, float('inf')))       # beyond 3 standard deviations

Constraints are applied by rejection sampling on the Mahalanobis distance \(\sqrt{(x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)}\); confidence \(q\) is converted to a radius through the \(\chi^2_d\) quantile, \(\sqrt{\chi^2_{d,q}}\) (so in \(d=2\), 95% is a radius of about 2.45, not 2). See the Sampling tutorial.

docs.title: Large datasets: batch_size
docs.text:
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=10, n_features=64, batch_size=4096)
gmm.fit(X)  # same result as batch_size=None, bounded peak memory

As explained under online EM, batch_size alone changes nothing about the result (up to floating-point summation order) -- it is purely a memory/speed knob.

docs.title: Model persistence
docs.text:
gmm.save('my_model.pth')
loaded_gmm = GaussianMixture.load('my_model.pth', device='cuda')

state_dict = gmm.save_state_dict()          # PyTorch-style
torch.save(state_dict, 'model_state.pth')
new_gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
new_gmm.load_state_dict(torch.load('model_state.pth'))

classes_ / class_of_component_ are not persisted.

docs.title: GPU acceleration
docs.text:
device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, device=device)
gmm.fit(X)  # X can be on CPU or GPU; it is moved to `device`

docs.title: Fitted attributes
docs.text:
After fitting, the model exposes:

Attribute Meaning weights_ mixing weights \(\pi\), shape \((K,)\) means_ component means, shape \((K,d)\) covariances_ covariances; shape depends on covariance_type (table above); always the assembled \((K,d,d)\) matrices for the 8 extra GPCM codes covariance_type_ canonical mclust code of covariance_type (e.g. 'VVV' for 'full') volume_, shape_, orientation_ the GPCM decomposition \(\Sigma_k=\lambda_kD_kA_kD_k^\top\) for the 8 extra codes; None otherwise converged_, n_iter_ whether EM converged and in how many iterations (True / sweeps count for SEM, online EM, Gibbs) lower_bound_ final average log-likelihood of the best run log_likelihood_history_ per-iteration / sweep / epoch average log-likelihood (EM modes; None in Gibbs mode) best_random_state_ seed of the winning run when n_init > 1 initial_weights_, initial_means_, initial_covariances_ parameters before the first EM iteration annealing_schedule_ the \(\beta\) used at each E-step when temperature is set n_empty_components_ algorithm='sem': number of component re-seeds classes_, class_of_component_ label values seen by a fit(X, labels=...) call and each component's class; None otherwise n_components_, active_ inferred component count and active-slot mask (Gibbs mode; n_components_ equals n_components in EM mode) n_components_history_ Gibbs mode, unbounded variant: active-component trace after burn_in fitted_ whether the model has been fitted

docs.title: Related models
docs.text: StudentTMixture (robust to outliers) and VonMisesFisherMixture (directional data) share this page's fit / predict / bic / algorithm / semi-supervised machinery through BaseMixture; see Other Mixture Families. A uniform noise component (noise=True), missing-value EM (missing='em'), marginal / condition, frozen_components, sample_weight and GenericMixture are described in Noise, Missing Values and Conditioning.

docs.title: GMM Initializer
docs.text:
The GMMInitializer class provides various strategies for initializing Gaussian Mixture Models. Good initialization is crucial for the EM algorithm to converge to a good solution.

GMMInitializer is a collection of @staticmethods -- there is no instance to construct. Each method takes the data (and sometimes the current means) directly and returns a tensor.

docs.title: Why initialization matters
docs.text: The mixture log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \log \sum_k \pi_k \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\) is non-convex with many local maxima (and singular maxima, where a component collapses onto one point and \(\ell \to \infty\) -- the reason for reg_covar). EM only climbs monotonically from wherever it starts (\(\ell\) never decreases from one iteration to the next), so it ends at a local optimum determined by the starting \((\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\). The initial means matter most; the initial weights and covariances matter mainly because the first E-step computes responsibilities \(r_{ik} \propto \pi_k \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\) from them. Running n_init > 1 independent initializations and keeping the best \(\ell\) is the standard guard.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Available initialization methods:

Means (init_means):

  • kmeans: Lloyd's algorithm, started from a k-means++ initialization (recommended)
  • kpp: K-means++ initialization only (no Lloyd iterations)
  • random: Sample from a Gaussian fit to the data's mean/covariance
  • points: Randomly selected data points
  • maxdist: Greedily maximize the minimum distance between centers

Weights (init_weights):

  • uniform / equal: All components start with equal weight (default)
  • random: Sample from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution
  • kmeans: Proportional to cluster sizes from a nearest-mean assignment

Covariances (init_covariances):

  • empirical: Estimated from data assigned to each component by nearest mean (default)
  • eye: Identity-like matrices/vectors, scaled by 1 + reg_covar
  • random: Random positive semi-definite matrices/vectors
  • global: The single global covariance of the whole dataset, shared or repeated across components

All three also accept a torch.Tensor of explicit values instead of a method name.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
GMMInitializer is used internally by GaussianMixture (and by StudentTMixture for the same method names), but its static methods can also be called directly to build custom initial parameters:

from tgmm import GMMInitializer
import torch

# Initialize means using K-means (or .kpp, .random, .points, .maxdist)
means = GMMInitializer.kmeans(X, k=3)

# Initialize weights proportional to cluster sizes
weights = GMMInitializer.init_weights_from_clusters(X, means)

# Initialize covariances from the data assigned to each component
covariances = GMMInitializer.init_covariances_empirical(
    X, means, covariance_type='full', reg_covar=1e-6
)

docs.title: K-means Initialization
docs.text:
A pure PyTorch implementation of Lloyd's algorithm, started from a k-means++ initialization (no scikit-learn dependency). Alternate

\[ c_j = \arg\min_{i} \lVert x_j - \mu_i \rVert^2 \qquad\text{(assignment)}, \qquad \mu_i = \frac{1}{|C_i|}\sum_{x_j \in C_i} x_j \qquad\text{(update)} \]

until the centers stop moving (torch.allclose with atol=1e-4) or max_iter=1000 is reached. Each Lloyd step does not increase the k-means objective \(\sum_j \lVert x_j - \mu_{c_j}\rVert^2\), so it converges to a local minimum of it.

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    init_means='kmeans',
    random_state=42
)

Advantages: Usually provides good starting points Disadvantages: Slower than a single k-means++ pass, no convergence guarantee within max_iter

docs.title: K-means++ Initialization
docs.text:
Smart initialization that spreads centers apart. The first center is a uniformly random data point; each next center \(x_j\) is drawn with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest center already chosen:

\[ P(x_j) = \frac{D(x_j)}{\sum_{j'=1}^{N} D(x_{j'})}, \qquad D(x_j) = \min_{l < i} \lVert x_j - \mu_l \rVert^2 . \]

(This is \(D^2\)-sampling; Arthur & Vassilvitskii (2007) show the resulting k-means objective is within \(O(\log K)\) of optimal in expectation.)

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    init_means='kpp',
    random_state=42
)

Advantages: Better than random, avoids clustering centers too close Disadvantages: Slightly slower than random

docs.title: Random Initialization
docs.text:
Draws centers from a Gaussian fit to the data's empirical mean and covariance:

\[ \mu_i = \bar x + L z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d), \qquad \hat\Sigma = L L^\top, \]

with \(L\) the Cholesky factor of the sample covariance \(\hat\Sigma\) (so the data covariance must be positive definite -- constant or duplicated features fail here). Centers follow the global data distribution but are not data points.

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    init_means='random',
    random_state=42
)

Advantages: Fast, simple Disadvantages: May lead to poor convergence

docs.title: Random Data Points
docs.text:
init_means='points' picks \(K\) distinct data points uniformly at random (sampling without replacement):

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_means='points')

docs.title: Custom Points
docs.text:
Provide specific initial centers:

initial_means = torch.tensor([
    [0.0, 0.0],
    [5.0, 5.0],
    [0.0, 5.0]
], dtype=torch.float32)

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    init_means=initial_means
)

docs.title: Maximum Distance Initialization
docs.text:
Greedily select centers to maximize the minimum distance to those already chosen (a deterministic, farthest-first traversal after a random first pick):

\[ \mu_i = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{D}} \min_{l = 1,\dots,i-1} \lVert x - \mu_l \rVert, \qquad \mu_1 \leftarrow \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{D}} \min_{l = 2,\dots,K} \lVert x - \mu_l \rVert, \]

where the second formula re-selects the first center once the others are known (so the arbitrary first pick doesn't bias the result). It spreads centers maximally, but is sensitive to outliers, which are the farthest points.

gmm = GaussianMixture(
    n_components=3,
    n_features=2,
    init_means='maxdist'
)

docs.title: Weight Initialization
docs.text:
init_weights Initial \(\pi_k\) 'uniform' / 'equal' \(1/K\) for every component 'random' one draw from \(\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1, \dots, 1)\) (uniform over the simplex) 'kmeans' \(n_k/n\), where \(n_k\) counts points whose nearest initial mean is \(\mu_k\) (empty components get a tiny floor) tensor the given values, renormalized to sum to 1 
# Equal weight for every component (default)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_weights='uniform')

# Random weights sampled from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_weights='random')

# Proportional to cluster sizes (nearest-mean assignment)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_weights='kmeans')

# Explicit weights (normalized to sum to 1)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_weights=torch.tensor([0.5, 0.3, 0.2]))

docs.title: Covariance Initialization
docs.text:
Written for the full type (the diagonal, spherical and tied types use the corresponding diagonal / mean-of-diagonal / pooled forms):

init_covariances Initial \(\Sigma_k\) 'empirical' (default) assign every point to its nearest initial mean to get clusters \(C_k\); \(\Sigma_k = \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(C_k) + \texttt{reg\_covar}\,I\), with the unbiased (\(n_k - 1\)) sample covariance; an empty cluster gets \((1 + \texttt{reg\_covar})\,I\) 'global' the whole dataset's sample covariance \(+\ \texttt{reg\_covar}\,I\), the same for every component 'eye' \((1 + \texttt{reg\_covar})\,I\) 'random' \(A A^\top + \texttt{reg\_covar}\,I\) with \(A_{ab} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) (diagonal types: uniform\((0,1)\) entries; spherical: uniform\((0,1) + 1\)) tensor the given values (shape per covariance_type)

For the tied types, 'empirical' pools the within-cluster scatter around each cluster's own mean and divides by \(n\) (the biased/maximum- likelihood normalization): \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k \sum_{x\in C_k}(x - \bar x_{C_k})(x - \bar x_{C_k})^\top + \texttt{reg\_covar}\,I\). For diag the diagonal of the corresponding matrix is kept; for spherical the mean of that diagonal. With the 8 non-classical GPCM codes (see GPCM Covariance Models), 'empirical' and 'global' are projected onto the requested parameterization, and 'eye'/ 'random' just start from plain identity/random full matrices.

# Estimated from data assigned to each component (default)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_covariances='empirical')

# Identity-like matrices, scaled by (1 + reg_covar)
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_covariances='eye')

# Random positive semi-definite matrices
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_covariances='random')

# Shared global covariance of the whole dataset
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, init_covariances='global')

# Explicit covariances
init_covs = torch.eye(2).unsqueeze(0).repeat(3, 1, 1) * 0.5
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type='full', init_covariances=init_covs)

docs.title: Other families
docs.text: StudentTMixture uses the same init_means / init_weights / init_covariances options (its init_covariances has no 'random' option; the covariance starts as the scale matrix, and dof_init sets the initial degrees of freedom). VonMisesFisherMixture instead initializes mean directions by spherical k-means and sets every \(\kappa_k\) to kappa_init; see Other Mixture Families.

docs.text:
