docs.title: GPCM Covariance Models
docs.text: GaussianMixture supports all 14 Celeux & Govaert (1995) Gaussian Parsimonious Clustering Models (GPCM) -- the same family mclust implements -- not just the six classic covariance types in the main Gaussian Mixture Model guide. This page defines the models, states the M-step each one uses and why it is correct, and lists what is and isn't supported. The Covariance Structures tutorial walks through the same material with runnable code, figures, and a numerical check of every formula below.

docs.title: Where the covariance enters EM
docs.text:
Given responsibilities \(r_{ik}\) from the E-step, write

\[ n_k=\sum_{i} r_{ik},\qquad \bar y_k=\frac1{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}x_i,\qquad W_k=\sum_{i} r_{ik}\,(x_i-\bar y_k)(x_i-\bar y_k)^{\top}. \]

After maximising the expected complete-data log-likelihood over \(\pi_k\) and \(\mu_k\), the only terms left that depend on the covariances are, up to a factor \(-\tfrac12\),

\[ J(\Sigma_1,\dots,\Sigma_K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big[\,n_k\log|\Sigma_k|+\operatorname{tr}\big(\Sigma_k^{-1}W_k\big)\Big]. \]

Every covariance type is the same objective \(J\) minimised over a different feasible set, and the M-step needs the data only through \((n_k, W_k)\) (the SufficientStats.nk and .s2 fields). For full the minimiser is \(\Sigma_k=W_k/n_k\); the other classic types are the restrictions listed in the Gaussian Mixture Model guide. reg_covar is added to the diagonal of the assembled matrices afterwards.

docs.title: The idea: a decomposed covariance
docs.text:
Each component's covariance is written through its eigendecomposition as

\[ \Sigma_k=\lambda_k\,D_k\,A_k\,D_k^{\top},\qquad \det A_k=1,\quad D_k^{\top}D_k=I,\quad A_k=\operatorname{diag}(a_{k1}\ge\dots\ge a_{kd}>0). \]
  • \(\lambda_k=|\Sigma_k|^{1/d}\) (volume): a scalar controlling the component's overall size (its ellipsoid's volume scales as \(\lambda_k^{d/2}\)).
  • \(A_k\) (shape): a diagonal matrix with determinant 1 and decreasing entries -- how stretched the component is along its own axes.
  • \(D_k\) (orientation): an orthogonal matrix -- which way those axes point.

The semi-axes of the one-standard-deviation ellipsoid are \(\sqrt{\lambda_k a_{kj}}\) along the \(j\)-th column of \(D_k\).

Each factor can be **E**qual across components, **V**ary per component, or (for shape and orientation only) be the **I**dentity: \(A_k=I\) makes the component spherical, and \(D_k=I\) makes it axis-aligned (no rotation). Volume has no identity option -- it is always a free scalar, shared or not. The 14 valid combinations are named by their three-letter mclust code (Volume-Shape-Orientation); the last column is the number of free covariance parameters, which is what bic/aic charge for the covariances:

Code tgmm name Meaning Free covariance parameters EII 'tied_spherical' one shared variance, spherical \(1\) VII 'spherical' per-component variance, spherical \(K\) EEI 'tied_diag' one shared diagonal covariance \(d\) VEI (new) per-component volume, shared diagonal shape \(K+(d-1)\) EVI (new) shared volume, per-component diagonal shape \(1+K(d-1)\) VVI 'diag' per-component diagonal covariance \(Kd\) EEE 'tied_full' one shared full covariance \(d(d+1)/2\) VEE (new) per-component volume, shared shape & orientation \(K+(d-1)+d(d-1)/2\) EVE (new) shared volume & orientation, per-component shape \(1+K(d-1)+d(d-1)/2\) EEV (new) shared volume & shape, per-component orientation \(d+K\,d(d-1)/2\) VVE (new) shared orientation, per-component volume & shape \(Kd+d(d-1)/2\) VEV (new) shared shape, per-component volume & orientation \(K+(d-1)+K\,d(d-1)/2\) EVV (new) shared volume, per-component shape & orientation \(1+K(d-1)+K\,d(d-1)/2\) VVV 'full' fully unconstrained per-component covariance \(K\,d(d+1)/2\)

The counts are sums of three independent contributions:

factor E V I volume \(\lambda\) \(1\) \(K\) -- shape \(A\) (\(d-1\) free ratios) \(d-1\) \(K(d-1)\) \(0\) orientation \(D\) (\(d(d-1)/2\) free angles) \(d(d-1)/2\) \(K\,d(d-1)/2\) \(0\)

The total number of parameters adds \(K-1\) free mixture weights and \(Kd\) mean coordinates. The 14 models are nested: a model is a special case of another if it is at least as constrained in all three factors (V before E before I), so \(\min J\) can only grow as constraints are added.

Pass either name to covariance_type (mclust codes are case-insensitive):

from tgmm import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=4, covariance_type='EVE')
gmm.fit(X)

print(gmm.covariance_type_)   # always the canonical mclust code, 'EVE' here
print(gmm.volume_, gmm.shape_, gmm.orientation_)  # the decomposition

covariances_ is always the assembled (n_components, n_features, n_features) matrices regardless of which of the 14 codes you use -- predict/sample/score/plot_gmm/save/load all work unchanged. volume_/shape_/orientation_ expose the decomposition itself (None for the six classic types, which don't compute one). reg_covar is added to the assembled matrices, not to the decomposition, so the three factors describe the unregularised fit.

docs.title: Why bother with 8 more models?
docs.text:
More constrained models (fewer free parameters) are less prone to overfitting on small or high-dimensional data, at the cost of flexibility. The 14-model family lets you search this trade-off systematically instead of jumping straight from "fully tied" to "fully free" -- which is exactly what select_model does by default:

from tgmm import select_model

result = select_model(X, n_components=range(1, 8), criterion='bic')
print(result.best_.covariance_type_, result.best_.n_components)

select_model's default covariance_types is all 14 GPCM codes (the mclust workflow); pass an explicit subset to narrow the search.

docs.title: How each model is estimated
docs.text:
With the decomposition, \(|\Sigma_k|=\lambda_k^d\) and \(\Sigma_k^{-1}=\lambda_k^{-1}D_kA_k^{-1}D_k^{\top}\), so

\[ J=\sum_{k}\Big[\,n_k\,d\log\lambda_k+\frac1{\lambda_k}\operatorname{tr}\big(A_k^{-1}D_k^{\top}W_kD_k\big)\Big]. \]

Two lemmas do most of the work.

Lemma 1 (shape)

For symmetric positive-definite \(B\) and positive-definite \(C\) with \(\det C=1\): \(\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}B)\ge d(\det B)^{1/d}\), with equality iff \(C=B/(\det B)^{1/d}\).

Proof. The eigenvalues \(\mu_j\) of \(C^{-1/2}BC^{-1/2}\) multiply to \(\det B\). By AM-GM, \(\sum_j\mu_j\ge d(\prod_j\mu_j)^{1/d}\), with equality iff all \(\mu_j\) are equal, i.e. \(B\propto C\).

Lemma 2 (orientation)

For symmetric \(W\) with eigenvalues \(\omega_1\ge\dots\ge\omega_d\) and \(a_1\ge\dots\ge a_d>0\), over orthogonal \(D\): \(\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}D^{\top}WD)\ge\sum_j\omega_j/a_j\), attained when the columns of \(D\) are the eigenvectors of \(W\) in decreasing eigenvalue order. (The diagonal of \(D^{\top}WD\) is majorised by \(\omega\) -- Schur-Horn -- and increasing weights \(1/a_j\) are minimised by pairing the largest \(\omega\) with the largest \(a\).) This is why tgmm keeps shapes sorted in decreasing order.

docs.title: Closed-form models
docs.text:
The six classic codes (EII, VII, EEI, VVI, EEE, VVV) have the closed forms of the Gaussian Mixture Model guide. Three of the new ones do too:

Code Estimate EVI \(A_k=B_k/\lvert B_k\rvert^{1/d}\) with \(B_k=\operatorname{diag}(W_k)\); \(\lambda=\frac1n\sum_k\lvert B_k\rvert^{1/d}\) EEV \(D_k\) = eigenvectors of \(W_k\) (eigenvalues \(\Omega_k\)); with \(\Omega=\sum_k\Omega_k\): \(A=\Omega/\lvert\Omega\rvert^{1/d}\), \(\lambda=\lvert\Omega\rvert^{1/d}/n\) EVV \(C_k=D_kA_kD_k^{\top}=W_k/\lvert W_k\rvert^{1/d}\); \(\lambda=\frac1n\sum_k\lvert W_k\rvert^{1/d}\)

(For EVI, only \(\operatorname{diag}(W_k)\) enters \(\operatorname{tr}(A_k^{-1}W_k)\); Lemma 1 gives \(A_k\) and \(J=nd\log\lambda+\frac d\lambda\sum_k|B_k|^{1/d}\), minimised at the stated \(\lambda\). EEV and EVV follow the same pattern, using Lemma 2 for EEV's orientations.)

docs.title: The iterative models: VEI, VEE, VEV
docs.text:
With per-component volumes and a shared shape, the factors are coupled but each has a closed form given the other, so tgmm alternates:

  • given the shape: \(\lambda_k=\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}D_k^{\top}W_kD_k)/(n_k d)\);
  • given the volumes: \(A=B/|B|^{1/d}\) (Lemma 1) with \(B=\sum_kD_k^{\top}W_kD_k/\lambda_k\) -- namely \(\operatorname{diag}(\sum_kW_k/\lambda_k)\) for VEI; \(\sum_kW_k/\lambda_k\) for VEE, where the shared matrix \(C=DAD^{\top}\) is updated as a whole; and \(\sum_k\Omega_k/\lambda_k\) for VEV, where each \(D_k\) is fixed once and for all to the eigenvectors of \(W_k\) (Lemma 2).

Each sub-step is an exact minimiser, so \(J\) is non-increasing (coordinate descent).

docs.title: The two numerically-optimised models: EVE, VVE
docs.text:
Given a shared orientation \(D\) everything else is closed-form: with \(B_k=\operatorname{diag}(D^{\top}W_kD)\),

\[ A_k=\frac{B_k}{|B_k|^{1/d}},\qquad \lambda=\frac1n\sum_k|B_k|^{1/d}\ \ (\texttt{EVE}),\qquad \lambda_k=\frac{|B_k|^{1/d}}{n_k}\ \ (\texttt{VVE}). \]

Given the shapes and volumes, the best \(D\) minimises \(\sum_k\lambda_k^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(A_k^{-1}D^{\top}W_kD)\) over orthogonal matrices -- the common principal components problem (Flury, 1984), which has no closed form for \(K>1\). (Profiling out \(\lambda_k\) and \(A_k\) from VVE gives Flury's criterion \(\sum_kn_k\log|\operatorname{diag}(D^{\top}S_kD)|\), \(S_k=W_k/n_k\), which by Hadamard's inequality is bounded below by the VVV optimum, with equality iff one \(D\) diagonalises every \(S_k\).) tgmm solves it with a few L-BFGS steps on the orthogonal manifold (PyTorch's orthogonal parametrisation), warm-started at the previous \(D\), and accepts the result only if the objective decreases -- a generalised EM step (Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977): \(Q\) is improved rather than exactly maximised, which keeps the log-likelihood monotone across EM iterations as for every other covariance type.

docs.title: Stopping and warm starts
docs.text:
VEI, VEE, VEV, EVE and VVE repeat their inner alternation until the relative change in \(J\) falls below gpcm_tol (default 1e-6) or gpcm_max_iter (default 20) sweeps are done:

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=4, covariance_type='VEE',
                       gpcm_tol=1e-8, gpcm_max_iter=50)

Each EM iteration's alternation is warm-started from the previous EM iteration's decomposition, so in practice it usually takes only 1-2 sweeps to re-settle.

docs.title: Numerical verification
docs.text: The tutorial compares every code's mstep_gpcm objective value with an independent brute-force L-BFGS minimisation of \(J\) over each model's feasible set (log-volumes, mean-centred log-shapes for \(\det A=1\), orthogonal matrices from the matrix exponential of a skew-symmetric one): all 14 agree to optimiser tolerance, including the alternating and orthogonal-manifold models.

docs.title: What's and isn't supported for the 8 new codes
docs.text:
• MLE only. mean_prior/covariance_prior (MAP/NIW estimation) raise NotImplementedError for the 8 new codes -- a conjugate-prior derivation specific to each parameterization is out of scope. full/diag/ spherical/tied_* still support MAP/NIW as before. weight_concentration_prior (the Dirichlet weight prior) is independent of the covariance parameterization and works with all 14.
  • No Gibbs mode. GaussianMixture(n_components=None, covariance_type=...) raises NotImplementedError for the 8 new codes, the same way it already does for tied_* -- a covariance that couples components (shared shape or orientation) doesn't factor per component the way Neal's Algorithm 3 needs.
  • init_covariances='empirical'/'global' project the usual empirical starting point onto the requested GPCM parameterization (the constrained MLE of that starting point); 'eye'/'random' just start from plain identity/random full matrices, since there's nothing to project yet.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Celeux, G. & Govaert, G. (1995). Gaussian parsimonious clustering models. Pattern Recognition, 28(5), 781-793. Banfield, J. D. & Raftery, A. E. (1993). Model-based Gaussian and non-Gaussian clustering. Biometrics, 49(3), 803-821. Flury, B. N. (1984). Common principal components in \(k\) groups. JASA, 79(388), 892-898. mclust's own naming and model definitions (Scrucca, Fop, Murphy & Raftery, 2016, The R Journal 8(1)) are followed here for compatibility, but every M-step in tgmm is derived independently from the papers' equations -- see docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-14-phase3-gpcm-covariance-models-design.md for the original derivation (tgmm is MIT-licensed; mclust is GPL, and its source was not read or ported).

docs.title: Noise, Missing Values and Conditioning
docs.text:
Five features that every mixture family inherits from BaseMixture (or, for the Gaussian-specific ones, from GaussianMixture) and that change what the fit is allowed to do rather than which density it fits:

Feature What it gives you Section noise=True a parameter-free uniform component that absorbs stray points Uniform noise component missing='em' maximum likelihood from rows with NaN entries, and impute Missing values marginal / condition marginal and conditional distributions, Gaussian mixture regression Marginals and conditionals frozen_components, sample_weight pin known components; weighted observations Frozen components and sample weights Component protocol, GenericMixture bring your own component family Custom components

Notation as elsewhere: \(n\) samples, \(d\) features, \(K\) components, responsibilities \(r_{ik}\), \(n_k=\sum_i r_{ik}\). The tutorial runs every example below.

docs.title: Uniform noise component
docs.text:
Real data often contain points that no cluster explains. A Gaussian component forced to cover them widens and drifts. Banfield & Raftery (1993) add one more component that is uniform over a region of volume \(V\):

\[ p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k f_k(x)+\frac{\pi_0}{V},\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k+\pi_0=1 . \] 
from tgmm import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, noise=True).fit(X)
labels = gmm.predict(X)        # -1 where the noise component is the most probable
p_noise = gmm.noise_proba(X)   # posterior probability of the noise component
gmm.noise_weight_              # pi_0

E-step. A column \(\log\pi_0-\log V\) is appended to the \((n,K)\) component log-densities, so the responsibilities have shape \((n,K+1)\) and the last column is \(\tau_{i0}\). \(\log V\) is a constant, so the noise log-density is the same at every \(x\) (also outside the data's bounding box: new points beyond the box are not given zero noise density).

M-step. \(\pi_0=\sum_i\tau_{i0}/n\). The \(K\) components are updated from the first \(K\) columns by the family's usual M-step, so weights_ \(=n_k/n\) sums to \(1-\pi_0\) rather than to 1.

weights_ and noise_weight_

With noise=True, weights_ keeps shape \((K,)\) and holds the component weights, which sum to 1 - noise_weight_. This keeps sample, plot_gmm, plot_vmf and save/load working unchanged.

Argument Default Meaning noise False switch the component on; with False every fit is bit-identical to before noise_volume 'bbox' 'bbox': volume of the axis-aligned bounding box of the fit data, \(\prod_j(\max_j-\min_j)\) (each extent floored at \(10^{-12}\)); or a positive float, a user-supplied hypervolume noise_prior 0.05 initial \(\pi_0\in(0,1)\) noise_init None per-sample initial flag of length \(n\). A bool tensor is a mask (True = noise); any other dtype is read as cluster labels with -1 = noise, so HDBSCAN(...).labels_ can be passed as is. It overrides noise_prior, and the initial means and covariances come from the unflagged rows only

Family hook. The noise log-density is -log V for GaussianMixture (all covariance types and GPCM codes) and StudentTMixture. For VonMisesFisherMixture it is \(-\log A_d\) with \(A_d=2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2)\) the surface area of the unit sphere \(S^{d-1}\) (the uniform density on the sphere), independent of noise_volume. Families without bounded continuous support raise ValueError.

Behaviour. predict_proba(X) is \((n,K+1)\); score_samples, bic, aic, icl and select_model include the noise term (one extra parameter). sample draws a noise point with probability \(\pi_0\), uniform in the stored bounding box noise_bounds_ (uniform on the sphere for vMF), with component index -1. Works with em, cem, sem, saem, temperature, batch_size, n_init, warm_start and persistence.

Unsupported combinations (they raise)

Gibbs mode (n_components=None); fit(X, labels=...) (a point cannot be labelled "known noise": -1 still means unlabelled); online EM (step_size) and partial_fit; weight_concentration_prior; constrained GaussianMixture.sample variants (component=, confidence=, ...); missing='em'.

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text:
With missing='em', NaN entries of X are missing at random and EM maximises the likelihood of the observed entries (Ghahramani & Jordan, 1994; Hunt & Jorgensen, 2003). It is available for GaussianMixture (all six classic covariance types and all 14 GPCM codes) and StudentTMixture. fit, predict, predict_proba, score_samples, score and bic/aic/icl then accept incomplete rows.

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=2, missing='em').fit(X_with_nans)
X_filled = gmm.impute(X_with_nans)

For a row with observed index set \(o\) and missing index set \(m\), and component \(k\):

  • E-step (marginal likelihood): \(\log p(x_i\mid k)=- frac12 ig[p\log2\pi+\log|\Sigma_{k,oo}|+\delta_o ig]\) with \(\delta_o=(x_o-\mu_{k,o})^ op\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}(x_o-\mu_{k,o})\) and \(p=|o|\).
  • Conditional mean and covariance of the hole, with \(A_k=\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}\): $$ \hat x_{m}=\mu_{k,m}+A_k(x_o-\mu_{k,o}),\qquad C_k=\Sigma_{k,mm}-A_k\Sigma_{k,om}. $$
  • Completed statistics. With \( ilde x_{ik}\) the row with the hole replaced by \(\hat x_m\): \(n_k=\sum_ir_{ik}\), \(s_{1,k}=\sum_ir_{ik} ilde x_{ik}\), \( ar y_k=s_{1,k}/n_k\) and $$ s_{2,k}=\sum_i r_{ik}( ilde x_{ik}- ar y_k)( ilde x_{ik}- ar y_k)^ op+\sum_i r_{ik}\,C_{k, ext{pattern}(i)}\quad(C ext{ in the }m imes m ext{ block}), $$ which is exactly \(\mathbb E[\sum_ir_{ik}(x_i- ar y_k)(x_i- ar y_k)^ op\mid x_o, heta^{ ext{old}}]\). Every M-step formula of the Gaussian guide (MLE, MAP, NIW, GPCM) reads only \((n_k,s_1,s_2)\), so it applies unchanged.

Rows are grouped by missingness pattern (torch.unique(torch.isnan(X), dim=0)), so the cost is one batched solve per pattern per component, not per row (UserWarning when more than 1000 distinct patterns). For diag/spherical types \(\Sigma_{mo}=0\), so \(\hat x_m=\mu_m\) and \(C=\operatorname{diag}\Sigma_{mm}\): no solves at all. impute(X) replaces each NaN by \(\sum_k au_{ik}\hat x_{ik}\) and leaves observed entries untouched.

Student-t. With the scale-mixture form (\(w\sim\mathrm{Gamma}( u/2, u/2)\), \(x\mid w\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma/w)\)) the observed block is a \(t_p\) and \(u_{ik}=( u_k+p)/( u_k+\delta_o)\) uses the number \(p\) of observed entries. The conditional mean does not depend on \(w\), so \(\mathbb E[w\,x_m\mid x_o]=u\,\hat x_m\) and \(\mathbb E[w(x_m-c)(x_m-c)^ op\mid x_o]=u(\hat x_m-c)(\hat x_m-c)^ op+C_k\) (the conditional covariance carries no factor \(u\)). Degrees of freedom use the textbook form per row with that row's own \(p\). scale_update='ecme' is not available with missing='em'.

Initialisation runs on the column-mean-imputed data. Defaults: with missing='error' a NaN raises a ValueError pointing at missing='em' (earlier versions silently propagated NaN into the parameters); missing='em' on data without NaN gives results identical to 'error'.

What raises

Rows with no observed entry and entirely-NaN columns (ValueError: they carry no information); noise=True, Gibbs mode, labels=, online EM / partial_fit (NotImplementedError); VonMisesFisherMixture (ValueError).

docs.title: Marginals and conditionals
docs.text:
A fitted GaussianMixture is a joint density, so it can be restricted and conditioned.

gmm.marginal(dims) returns a new fitted GaussianMixture over the chosen coordinates: component \(k\) becomes \(\mathcal N(\mu_k[\text{dims}],\Sigma_k[\text{dims},\text{dims}])\) with the same weights. diag, spherical and tied_* keep their type; full and the GPCM codes without a classic name return full (the volume/shape/orientation decomposition does not survive restriction). StudentTMixture.marginal is exact too (same \(\nu\), restricted scale matrix).

gmm.condition(x_obs, obs_dims) returns a ConditionalGaussianMixture: for every row \(x_{o,i}\) the distribution of the remaining coordinates,

\[ p(y\mid x_{o,i})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{ik}\,\mathcal N\!\big(y;\,m_{ik},\,C_k\big),\qquad w_{ik}\propto\pi_k\,\mathcal N(x_{o,i};\mu_{k,o},\Sigma_{k,oo}), \] \[ m_{ik}=\mu_{k,m}+\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}(x_{o,i}-\mu_{k,o}),\qquad C_k=\Sigma_{k,mm}-\Sigma_{k,mo}\Sigma_{k,oo}^{-1}\Sigma_{k,om}. \]

The weights depend on the observed values; the conditional covariances do not. All steps are batched Cholesky solves, with no loop over samples.

cond = gmm.condition(x_obs, obs_dims=[0])
cond.mean()        # (n, d_m): Gaussian mixture regression, E[y | x] = sum_k w_ik m_ik
cond.log_prob(Y)   # (n,) conditional log-density (a single-row conditional broadcasts against many Y)
cond.sample(50)    # (n, 50, d_m)
cond.as_gmm(i)     # conditional of row i as an ordinary GaussianMixture over the missing coordinates

obs_dims keeps the order you give (column \(j\) of x_obs is coordinate obs_dims[j]); the conditional is over the sorted complement. Attributes: weights_ (n, K), means_ (n, K, d_m), covariances_ (K, d_m, d_m), obs_dims, missing_dims. The mean is a regression curve; the distribution can be multimodal, which a single regression mean would hide.

Not supported

Gibbs-mode and noise=True models (a noise component has no Gaussian-mixture form after conditioning); StudentTMixture.condition (the conditional t has degrees of freedom \(\nu+d_o\) and a sample-dependent scale, so it is not a member of this class); VonMisesFisherMixture.

docs.title: Frozen components and sample weights
docs.text:
frozen_components=[k, ...] keeps component \(k\)'s means and covariances (or dof_, kappa_) at their initial values for the whole fit. Mixing weights, and the noise weight, still update, and \(\sum_k\pi_k+\pi_0=1\) is preserved. Initial values come from init_means/init_covariances or warm_start. Priors never shrink a frozen component and SEM never re-seeds it. Not supported (ValueError): tied covariance types and GPCM codes without a classic name, dof='shared', concentration='shared', Gibbs mode. PositiveUnlabeledMixture(anchor='fixed') is built on it.

fit(X, sample_weight=w)

  • Row weights, shape \((n,)\): responsibilities are scaled by \(w_i\) before the sufficient statistics, so \(n_k\), \(s_1\), \(s_2\) (and the Student-t and vMF analogues) are weighted. The effective sample count is \(n_{\text{eff}}=\sum_iw_i\) (mixing weights \(\pi_k=n_k/n_{\text{eff}}\); MAP priors use \(n_{\text{eff}}\)), and lower_bound_ is \(\sum_iw_i\log p(x_i)/\sum_iw_i\). Hence integer weights equal duplicating rows, a weight of 0 drops the row, a constant rescaling changes nothing, and all-ones is bit-identical to no weights. Initialisation ignores weights (except to exclude zero-weight rows), and bic/aic/icl/score take only X.
  • Per-feature weights, shape \((n,d)\): for models that factorise over features (GaussianMixture 'diag'/'spherical', StudentTMixture 'diag'), maximum likelihood only. A weight \(w_{ij}=0\) hides feature \(j\) of row \(i\) (exact marginalisation). For 'diag': $$ \log p(x_i\mid k)=-\tfrac12\sum_jw_{ij}\Big[\log2\pi+\log s_{kj}+\frac{(x_{ij}-m_{kj})^2}{s_{kj}}\Big],\quad m_{kj}=\frac{\sum_ir_{ik}w_{ij}x_{ij}}{N_{kj}}, s_{kj}=\frac{\sum_ir_{ik}w_{ij}(x_{ij}-m_{kj})^2}{N_{kj}}, $$ with \(N_{kj}=\sum_ir_{ik}w_{ij}\). Other models raise ValueError.

Row weights work with em/cem/sem/saem, batch_size, n_init, warm_start, noise=True and missing='em' (each on its own: the two cannot be combined); they raise NotImplementedError in Gibbs mode, with labels= and with online EM.

No inertia

pomegranate's inertia is deliberately not added: step_size (online EM / SAEM) is the same control on the statistics.

docs.title: Custom components: the Component protocol and GenericMixture
docs.text:
tgmm.mixtures.protocol.Component is a runtime-checkable typing.Protocol that describes a mixture component as EM sees it (the API shape is borrowed from pomegranate 1.x, MIT; tgmm does not import it):

Method Role log_probability(X) \(\log f_k(x_i)\), shape (n,) summarize(X, sample_weight) accumulate weighted statistics of one chunk (sample_weight = responsibility \(\times\) row weight) from_summaries() update the parameters from everything summarised and reset the accumulators

Optional members: sample(n), n_parameters() (fallback: the number of scalar entries in the object's public tensors), frozen, reseed(x).

from tgmm import GenericMixture

gm = GenericMixture(components=[Exponential(0.5), Normal1D(5.0, 1.0)]).fit(X)

M-step. For every data chunk and every non-frozen component, summarize(X_chunk, resp_chunk[:, k]); then from_summaries() once. Because summarize accumulates, batch_size works and chunked equals unchunked. Mixing weights are \(\pi_k=n_k/n\) as in every family.

Autograd components. A torch.nn.Module with learnable parameters and a log_prob(X) method (and no summarize) is wrapped automatically. Its M-step maximises \(Q_k(\theta_k)=\sum_iw_{ik}\log f_k(x_i\mid\theta_k)/\sum_iw_{ik}\) with a few L-BFGS steps (BaseMixture._gem_step) and keeps the update only if \(Q_k\) increases, so the log-likelihood stays monotone (a generalised EM step).

Decisions. The components you pass are the starting point (no k-means); n_init must be 1; frozen parameters still count in BIC; em, cem, sem (with sem_estimate='best') and temperature work, while saem, online EM and partial_fit raise NotImplementedError (opaque summarize state cannot be blended); noise=True needs a float noise_volume; per-feature weights and missing='em' raise ValueError; save/load pickle the components, so their classes must be importable.

docs.title: Other Mixture Families
docs.text:
GaussianMixture assumes every component is normally distributed. That's the right assumption for a lot of data, but not all of it: outliers can drag a Gaussian component's covariance around, and directional data (unit vectors -- normalized embeddings, in practice) isn't naturally described by a density defined over all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) in the first place. tgmm has two more mixture families for exactly those two cases, StudentTMixture and VonMisesFisherMixture, built on the same shared BaseMixture machinery as GaussianMixture -- the same fit/predict/ score/bic/aic/icl API, the same algorithm/temperature/ step_size options for the EM loop itself.

Both families also support partial and full label information through fit(X, labels=...) (see Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting). Neither supports Gibbs-sampling mode (n_components=None), the 14 GPCM covariance codes, or MAP/NIW priors -- those stay GaussianMixture-only.

Notation used on this page and throughout the user guide: \(n\) samples \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\), \(K\) components, mixing weights \(\pi_k\), responsibilities \(r_{ik} = P(z_i = k \mid x_i)\), effective component counts \(n_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\).

docs.title: The shared machinery: one EM loop for every family
docs.text:
Every mixture family in tgmm is a finite mixture

\[ p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, f_k(x \mid \theta_k), \qquad \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, f_k(x_i \mid \theta_k), \]

and BaseMixture implements the generic loop once. A family only supplies the component log-density \(\log f_k\) (_component_log_prob), the accumulation of its sufficient statistics (_compute_stats), and its M-step (_m_step_from_stats).

E-step. The responsibilities are computed in log space (a softmax over components, so nothing under/overflows):

\[ r_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k f_k(x_i)}{\sum_{j} \pi_j f_j(x_i)} = \exp\!\Big(\log \pi_k + \log f_k(x_i) - \operatorname{logsumexp}_j\big(\log \pi_j + \log f_j(x_i)\big)\Big). \]

The per-sample normalizer \(\log \sum_j \pi_j f_j(x_i)\) is also what score_samples returns, and its mean is lower_bound_ (the average log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta)/n\) that tol is checked against).

M-step. Each family maximizes (or, for Student-t, conditionally maximizes) the expected complete-data log-likelihood \(\sum_{i,k} r_{ik} \big[\log \pi_k + \log f_k(x_i)\big]\). The mixing weights are always

\[ \pi_k = \frac{n_k}{n}. \]

Variants of the loop, all shared by every family:

algorithm What replaces the soft \(r_{ik}\) fed to the M-step 'em' \(r_{ik}\) itself. 'cem' One-hot \(\mathbb{1}[k = \arg\max_j r_{ij}]\) (Classification EM). 'sem' One-hot of a sample \(z_i \sim \mathrm{Categorical}(r_{i\cdot})\) (Stochastic EM). 'saem' A running average of sampled-assignment statistics with a decaying step size.

temperature=(beta_0, n_anneal) (deterministic annealing) tempers the E-step: \(r_{ik} \propto \big(\pi_k f_k(x_i)\big)^{\beta}\) with \(\beta\) rising geometrically from beta_0 to \(1\) over the first n_anneal iterations, \(\beta_t = \beta_0^{\,1 - t/n_{\text{anneal}}}\). step_size switches to online/mini-batch EM, blending each batch's sufficient statistics into a running accumulator. See the Gaussian Mixture Model guide for when to use each.

Model selection. All families share

\[ \mathrm{BIC} = -2\,\ell(\hat\theta) + p \ln n, \qquad \mathrm{AIC} = -2\,\ell(\hat\theta) + 2p, \] \[ \mathrm{ICL} = \mathrm{BIC} + 2\,\mathrm{EN}(r), \qquad \mathrm{EN}(r) = -\sum_{i} \ln r_{i\hat z_i} \;\;(\texttt{mode='hard'}), \quad \text{or} \quad -\sum_{i,k} r_{ik}\ln r_{ik} \;\;(\texttt{mode='soft'}), \]

(all "lower is better"), where \(p\) is the number of free parameters (_n_parameters(), family-specific; given in each section below) and \(\hat z_i = \arg\max_k r_{ik}\). The entropy term is \(\ge 0\) and vanishes when every responsibility is one-hot, so \(\mathrm{ICL} \ge \mathrm{BIC}\) with equality only for perfectly separated clusters. Criteria are directly comparable within a family at different \(K\) (or covariance structure), and between families whose densities share a base measure -- Gaussian and Student-t, both on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). They are not comparable between a vMF mixture (density on the sphere) and the other two.

docs.title: Why heavy tails help
docs.text: A multivariate Student-t distribution looks like a Gaussian near its center but has polynomially decaying tails, controlled by its degrees of freedom \( u\): small \( u\) means heavy tails (very forgiving of far-away points), and as \( u o \infty\) it converges to a Gaussian exactly. A Gaussian component's covariance estimate is a plain average of squared deviations, so a single far-away point can inflate it arbitrarily; the t-component instead downweights such points automatically (derived below).

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Component \(k\) has mean \(\mu_k\), scale matrix \(\Sigma_k\) and degrees of freedom \( u_k\):

\[ t(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k, u_k) = rac{\Gamma\! ig( frac{ u_k + d}{2} ig)}{\Gamma\! ig( frac{ u_k}{2} ig)\,( u_k \pi)^{d/2}\,|\Sigma_k|^{1/2}} \Big(1 + rac{\delta_{ik}}{ u_k}\Big)^{- rac{ u_k + d}{2}}, \qquad \delta_{ik} = (x_i - \mu_k)^ op \Sigma_k^{-1} (x_i - \mu_k). \]

This is exactly what _component_log_prob evaluates (and it matches scipy.stats.multivariate_t to machine precision). The key to fitting it is its scale-mixture representation: draw a latent precision multiplier \(w \sim \mathrm{Gamma}( u_k/2, u_k/2)\) (shape/rate, mean \(1\)), then \(x \mid w \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k / w)\). Marginalizing \(w\) gives the t density above. (sample uses this representation directly: \(x = \mu_k + z/\sqrt{w}\) with \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_k)\).)

Scale matrix vs. covariance

covariances_ holds the scale matrix \(\Sigma_k\), not the covariance of the distribution. For \( u_k > 2\) the actual covariance is \( rac{ u_k}{ u_k - 2}\,\Sigma_k\); for \( u_k \le 2\) it is infinite.

docs.title: E-step: responsibilities and robustness weights
docs.text:
Besides the usual \(r_{ik}\), the latent multiplier has a closed-form posterior given \(x_i\) and \(z_i = k\): \(w_{ik} \mid x_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\! ig( frac{ u_k + d}{2}, frac{ u_k + \delta_{ik}}{2} ig)\), whose mean is

\[ u_{ik} = \mathbb{E}[w_{ik} \mid x_i, z_i = k] = rac{ u_k + d}{ u_k + \delta_{ik}}. \]

Points near the center (\(\delta_{ik} \ll u_k\)) get \(u_{ik} \approx ( u_k + d)/ u_k > 1\); points far away (\(\delta_{ik} \gg u_k\)) get \(u_{ik} o 0\). That is the robustness mechanism: \(u_{ik}\) is a per-sample, per-component weight that shrinks with Mahalanobis distance. sample_weights(X) returns \(u_{i\hat z_i}\) at each point's predicted component, so small values flag likely outliers.

docs.title: M-step (ECM)
docs.text:
With \(m_k = \sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik}\), the updates are

\[ \pi_k = rac{n_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = rac{\sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik}\, x_i}{m_k}, \qquad \Sigma_k = rac{\sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik}\,(x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^ op}{n_k} \;\;(+\, exttt{reg\_covar}\cdot I). \]

Compare with the Gaussian M-step: the only change is the extra weight \(u_{ik}\) inside the sums (and the mean's denominator being \(m_k\), not \(n_k\)). With \( u o \infty\), \(u_{ik} o 1\) and these reduce to the Gaussian updates (dof=1e4 is an easy sanity check against GaussianMixture). The statistics \(\mu_k\) and \(\Sigma_k\) are computed with \(u_{ik}\) evaluated at the previous parameters within the same iteration, which is what makes this an ECM (expectation conditional maximization) algorithm rather than plain EM: each parameter block is maximized conditionally on the others.

For covariance_type='diag' the scatter and the denominator are the per-feature (diagonal) versions; 'spherical' uses \(\sigma_k^2 = \sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik}\,\lVert x_i - \mu_k Vert^2 / (d\, n_k)\); 'tied_full' pools the scatter and the denominator across components, \(\Sigma = \sum_k \sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik} (x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^ op ig/ \sum_k n_k\).

scale_update='ecme' divides by \(m_k\) instead of \(n_k\). At the maximum-likelihood fixed point the two coincide: the stationarity condition for \(\Sigma_k\) gives \(\sum_i r_{ik} u_{ik} \delta_{ik} = d\, n_k\), and since \(u\,\delta = ( u + d) - u\, u\) this forces \(m_k = n_k\). Both variants therefore converge to the same estimate; 'ecme' just takes a different path and often needs a few fewer iterations.

docs.title: Degrees of freedom
docs.text:
For dof='per_component' each \( u_k\) solves a one-dimensional equation every M-step. Writing

\[ c_k = rac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\, ig(\ln u_{ik} - u_{ik} ig), \]

tgmm solves

\[ 1 - \psi\!\Big( rac{ u}{2}\Big) + \ln\!\Big( rac{ u}{2}\Big) + c_k + \psi\!\Big( rac{ u + d}{2}\Big) - \ln\!\Big( rac{ u + d}{2}\Big) = 0 \]

for \( u\) (\(\psi\) the digamma function) by 60 bisection steps inside dof_bounds followed by 4 Newton steps on \(\ln u\), clamping to dof_bounds (default (0.1, 1000)) -- if the root lies outside the bounds the fit lands on the bound. This is the first-order condition of the expected complete-data log-likelihood in \( u\) (the Gamma\(( u/2, u/2)\) part). For dof='shared', \(c\) is the pooled average over all components, \(\sum_k \sum_i r_{ik}(\ln u_{ik} - u_{ik}) / \sum_k n_k\), and one \( u\) is solved for. A numeric dof fixes every \( u_k\) for the whole fit.

Where this deviates from the textbook

The textbook update (Peel & McLachlan, 2000) evaluates the last two terms, \(\psi ig( frac{ u^{(t)} + d}{2} ig) - \ln ig( frac{ u^{(t)} + d}{2} ig)\), at the previous iterate \( u^{(t)}\). tgmm evaluates them at the candidate \( u\) itself. The two share the same fixed point (at convergence \( u^{(t)} = u\); the residual of the textbook equation at a converged tgmm fit is \(\sim 10^{-6}\)), so the final estimate is the same maximum-likelihood solution, but the per-iteration step is not literally the textbook EM step.

docs.title: Parameters, attributes, and counts
docs.text:
Attribute Shape Meaning weights_ \((K,)\) \(\pi_k\) means_ \((K, d)\) \(\mu_k\) covariances_ by covariance_type scale matrix \(\Sigma_k\) (not the covariance) dof_ \((K,)\) fitted \( u_k\) (all entries equal for 'shared' or a fixed float)

The number of free parameters used by bic/aic/icl is \(p = (K-1) + Kd + p_\Sigma + p_ u\), with \(p_\Sigma = K\,d(d+1)/2\) (full), \(Kd\) (diag), \(K\) (spherical) or \(d(d+1)/2\) (tied_full), and \(p_ u = K\) (per_component), \(1\) (shared) or \(0\) (fixed dof).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from tgmm import StudentTMixture

stm = StudentTMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type='full', dof='per_component')
stm.fit(X)

stm.means_        # (n_components, n_features)
stm.covariances_  # the scale matrix, not technically a covariance for finite dof
stm.dof_          # (n_components,) -- fitted nu_k
  • covariance_type: one of 'full', 'diag', 'spherical', 'tied_full' (the GPCM parameterizations and the Gibbs-only axis-aligned tied types aren't supported here).
  • dof: 'per_component' (default, one \(\nu_k\) per component), 'shared' (one \(\nu\) for every component), or a fixed float. dof_init (default 5.0) is the starting value, dof_bounds the clamp.
  • scale_update: 'ecm' (default) or 'ecme', see above.

docs.title: Flagging outliers with sample_weights
docs.text:
After fitting, sample_weights(X) returns each point's \(u_{ik}\) at its predicted component -- small values flag points the model effectively treated as outliers:

weights = stm.sample_weights(X)
likely_outliers = X[weights < 0.3]

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• A fitted \( u_k\) near dof_bounds[1] means that component is indistinguishable from a Gaussian; near dof_bounds[0] means a very heavy tail (infinite mean for \( u \le 1\)).
  • Each iteration needs the full \((n, K)\) matrix of Mahalanobis distances in memory (batch_size only chunks the E-step's reduction, not this).
  • Student-t and Gaussian densities share the same base measure (Lebesgue on \(\mathbb{R}^d\)), so a StudentTMixture's score, bic, aic and icl are directly comparable with those of a GaussianMixture fitted to the same data (the t pays for its extra \( u\) parameters in the count).

docs.title: Why a different density
docs.text: For L2-normalized data -- points on the unit hypersphere \(\mathbb{S}^{d-1} = \{x : \lVert x\rVert = 1\}\), as you get from normalizing text or image embeddings before clustering by cosine similarity -- a Gaussian (or Student-t) mixture is the wrong model: it's defined over all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and has no notion of "direction only." The von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution is the natural analogue restricted to the sphere.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Component \(k\) has a mean direction \(\mu_k\) (unit norm) and a concentration \(\kappa_k \ge 0\):

\[ f(x \mid \mu_k, \kappa_k) = C_d(\kappa_k)\,\exp\!\big(\kappa_k\, \mu_k^\top x\big), \qquad C_d(\kappa) = \frac{\kappa^{d/2 - 1}}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\, I_{d/2 - 1}(\kappa)}, \]

where \(I_\nu\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind. The log-density tgmm evaluates is \(\log C_d(\kappa_k) + \kappa_k\, x^\top \mu_k\) (verified against scipy.stats.vonmises_fisher). The density depends on \(x\) only through the cosine similarity \(\mu_k^\top x\): higher \(\kappa_k\) is a tighter cluster around \(\mu_k\), and \(\kappa_k \to 0\) approaches the uniform distribution on the sphere. \(\log I_\nu(\kappa)\) is computed from scipy.special.ive (exponentially scaled, so it doesn't overflow), with a uniform large-order asymptotic expansion as a fallback when ive underflows -- which happens in high dimension at modest \(\kappa\).

docs.title: E-step and M-step
docs.text:
The E-step is the generic one above with these \(f_k\). For the M-step, form the resultant vector of each component,

\[ \mathbf{R}_k = \sum_{i} r_{ik}\, x_i, \qquad \bar R_k = \frac{\lVert \mathbf{R}_k \rVert}{n_k} \in [0, 1], \]

(the length of the responsibility-weighted mean vector; \(\bar R_k\) near \(1\) means the points are nearly parallel). The maximum-likelihood updates are

\[ \pi_k = \frac{n_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{\mathbf{R}_k}{\lVert \mathbf{R}_k \rVert}, \qquad A_d(\hat\kappa_k) = \bar R_k, \quad A_d(\kappa) = \frac{I_{d/2}(\kappa)}{I_{d/2 - 1}(\kappa)}. \]

\(A_d(\kappa) = \bar R\) has no closed-form solution. tgmm follows Banerjee, Dhillon, Ghosh & Sra (2005): start from the closed-form approximation

\[ \kappa^{(0)} = \frac{\bar R\,(d - \bar R^2)}{1 - \bar R^2}, \]

then refine with two Newton steps on \(A_d(\kappa) - \bar R = 0\) using \(A_d'(\kappa) = 1 - A_d(\kappa)^2 - \frac{d-1}{\kappa} A_d(\kappa)\) (Sra, 2012), clamping \(\kappa\) to \([10^{-3}, 10^{5}]\). (The Banerjee approximation alone leaves a residual \(A_d(\kappa^{(0)}) - \bar R\) of up to \(\sim 10^{-2}\); after the two Newton steps the residual is \(\lesssim 10^{-7}\) in the cases we checked.) With concentration='shared', one \(\kappa\) is solved from the pooled resultant length \(\sum_k \lVert\mathbf{R}_k\rVert / \sum_k n_k\).

Relation to spherical k-means

With algorithm='cem', equal weights and a common \(\kappa\), the E/C-step assigns each point to the component of largest cosine similarity and the M-step sets each mean direction to the normalized sum of its members -- i.e. spherical k-means (Dhillon & Modha, 2001). tgmm's default init_means='kmeans' runs exactly that, seeded with a cosine-distance k-means++ scheme (the next center is drawn with probability proportional to \(1 - \max_{\text{chosen}} \cos\)) to avoid two initial centers landing in one true cluster.

docs.title: Parameters, attributes, and counts
docs.text:
Attribute Shape Meaning weights_ \((K,)\) \(\pi_k\) means_ \((K, d)\) unit-norm mean directions \(\mu_k\) kappa_ \((K,)\) fitted concentrations \(\kappa_k\) (all equal for 'shared')

Each \(\mu_k\) lives on a \((d-1)\)-sphere, so \(p = (K-1) + K(d-1) + p_\kappa\) with \(p_\kappa = K\) (per_component) or \(1\) (shared).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from tgmm import VonMisesFisherMixture

vmf = VonMisesFisherMixture(n_components=5, concentration='per_component')
vmf.fit(X_normalized)  # X_normalized rows must have unit L2 norm

vmf.means_   # (n_components, n_features), each row unit-norm
vmf.kappa_   # (n_components,) -- fitted concentration

If X isn't already unit-norm, fit/predict/score all normalize it automatically and warn once per call -- but fitting on already-normalized data is still the right thing to do, since that's what the ambient dimensionality (n_features) and the density itself assume.

  • concentration: 'per_component' (default) or 'shared' (one \(\kappa\) for every component). kappa_init (default 10.0) is the starting value.
  • init_means: 'kmeans' (default, spherical k-means as above), 'random' (uniform on the sphere), 'points' (random rows of X), or a tensor (normalized and used directly). See the design doc for the seeding failure mode this fixes.
  • sample(n) uses Wood's (1994) rejection sampler. reg_covar is accepted for interface parity but unused (there is no covariance).

docs.title: Visualizing a vMF fit
docs.text: plot_gmm cannot draw data on a sphere, so tgmm.plotting has vMF-specific tools: plot_vmf draws a fitted model on the circle (\(d=2\)) or sphere (\(d=3\)) -- points, mean-direction arrows, and spherical caps holding a chosen probability mass of each component -- and plot_vmf_cosine compares, in any dimension, each component's histogram of angles to its mean direction with the fitted density \(f_{\kappa}(\theta)\propto e^{\kappa\cos\theta}\sin^{d-2}\theta\). See von Mises-Fisher mixtures in the plotting guide and the tutorial.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• \(\kappa\) is clamped to \([10^{-3}, 10^{5}]\); an extremely tight cluster (or duplicate points, \(\bar R \to 1\)) lands on the upper bound.
  • The Bessel normalizer is evaluated per component in Python each E-step, which is cheap (\(K\) scalars) but not GPU-resident.
  • vMF has no notion of cluster shape -- every component is isotropic around its mean direction. For elongated clusters on the sphere, consider PCA-reducing and a GaussianMixture/StudentTMixture instead.

docs.title: Comparing against GaussianMixture on normalized data
docs.text: Nothing stops you from fitting GaussianMixture(covariance_type='diag') on the same L2-normalized data -- it's a reasonable baseline, just not one that respects the data living on a sphere. Do not compare their bic/ aic/icl: a vMF density is taken with respect to the surface measure of the sphere, a Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), so the log-likelihoods are not on the same scale (information criteria are comparable only among vMF fits). Compare across families with a cosine-based clustering metric or agreement with known labels instead; see notebook 17 for a worked example on high-dimensional embeddings.

docs.title: Supervised and semi-supervised fitting
docs.text: Because fit(X, labels=...) lives in BaseMixture, both families accept it: with every row labeled they fit one block of components per class directly, and with -1 marking unknown rows they run semi-supervised EM (components_per_class, unlabeled_weight, label_confidence, predict_class). The math and the options are covered in Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting.

docs.title: Noise, missing values and custom families
docs.text: noise=True works for all three families (the noise density is uniform in the data's bounding box, or on the sphere for vMF); missing='em' for GaussianMixture and StudentTMixture; frozen_components and sample_weight for all of them. To fit a family that tgmm does not ship, implement the three-method Component protocol and use GenericMixture. See Noise, Missing Values and Conditioning.

docs.title: Shared machinery summary
docs.text: bic/aic/icl work the same way on both classes as on GaussianMixture (see the formulas above). sample(n) draws from the fitted mixture for both: a Gaussian scaled by \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Gamma}(\nu_k/2, \nu_k/2)}\) for StudentTMixture, and Wood's (1994) rejection sampler for VonMisesFisherMixture. algorithm='cem'/'sem'/'saem', temperature (deterministic annealing), step_size (mini-batch/online EM, plus partial_fit), and n_init all work exactly as documented for GaussianMixture, since they're implemented once, in BaseMixture, and shared by every family.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Peel, D. & McLachlan, G. J. (2000). Robust mixture modelling using the t distribution. Statistics and Computing, 10, 339-348.
  • Banerjee, A., Dhillon, I. S., Ghosh, J. & Sra, S. (2005). Clustering on the unit hypersphere using von Mises-Fisher distributions. JMLR, 6, 1345-1382.
  • Sra, S. (2012). A short note on parameter approximation for von Mises-Fisher distributions. Computational Statistics, 27, 177-190.
  • Wood, A. T. A. (1994). Simulation of the von Mises Fisher distribution. Communications in Statistics -- Simulation and Computation, 23(1), 157-164.
  • Dhillon, I. S. & Modha, D. S. (2001). Concept decompositions for large sparse text data using clustering. Machine Learning, 42, 143-175.
  • Biernacki, C., Celeux, G. & Govaert, G. (2000). Assessing a mixture model for clustering with the integrated completed likelihood. IEEE TPAMI, 22(7), 719-725.

docs.title: Plotting and Visualization
docs.text: The tgmm.plotting module provides plot_gmm for visualizing 2D mixture-model clustering results, plot_vmf and plot_vmf_cosine for directional (unit-norm) data, plus a few small helpers: dynamic_figsize, match_predicted_to_true_labels, confidence_ellipse_std_devs and gmm_proxy. plot_gmm accepts any fitted tgmm mixture (it only needs means_, covariances_, weights_, covariance_type and predict), including every GPCM covariance code, and the module exports the colour constants CATEGORICAL_PALETTE, SEQUENTIAL_CMAP and STATUS_CRITICAL used as its defaults.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plot_gmm supports:

  • 2D scatter plots colored by predicted cluster, true labels, or a continuous value (e.g. log-likelihood)
  • Confidence ellipses at one or more standard-deviation levels per component
  • Component means, and optionally the pre-EM initial means
  • Weight-scaled marker size/alpha to visualize mixing weights
  • Highlighting incorrect predictions against ground truth

plot_gmm only accepts 2D data (X.shape[1] == 2) -- for higher-dimensional data, project to 2D yourself first (e.g. with PCA) and pass the projected coordinates. See the PCA Plotting tutorial for a worked example.

docs.title: Basic 2D Plotting
docs.text:
from tgmm import GaussianMixture, plot_gmm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Fit GMM
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(X_tensor)

# Plot results (X can be a numpy array or torch tensor)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plot_gmm(X, gmm, title='GMM Clustering Results', show_ellipses=True, show_means=True)
plt.show()

docs.title: Coloring by Cluster and Comparing to Ground Truth
docs.text:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6))

# Color by predicted cluster
plot_gmm(X, gmm, ax=axes[0], color_by_cluster=True, title='Predicted Clusters')

# Compare against ground truth, highlighting misclassifications
plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    ax=axes[1],
    true_labels=true_labels,
    color_by_cluster=True,
    match_labels_to_true=True,
    show_incorrect_predictions=True,
    title='Predictions vs Truth'
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Continuous Coloring (Log-Likelihood)
docs.text:
log_probs = gmm.score_samples(X_tensor)

plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    log_probs=log_probs.cpu().numpy(),
    colormap='viridis',
    colorbar_label='Log Probability',
    show_ellipses=False,
    title='Colored by Log-Likelihood'
)
plt.show()

docs.title: Confidence Ellipses
docs.text:
Show one or more standard-deviation levels per component:

plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    show_ellipses=True,
    ellipse_std_devs=[1, 2, 3],  # 1, 2, and 3 std-dev ellipses
    ellipse_alpha=0.3,
    ellipse_fill=True
)

docs.title: Ellipses that enclose a given probability
docs.text:
ellipse_std_devs is in units of standard deviations (Mahalanobis radius). In \(d=2\) a radius of \(r\) encloses \(1-e^{-r^2/2}\) of a Gaussian's mass -- 39% for \(r=1\), 86.5% for \(r=2\), 98.9% for \(r=3\) -- not the 68/95/99.7% of the 1-D rule. To draw ellipses with a chosen coverage \(q\), convert it through the \(\chi^2_2\) quantile, \(r=\sqrt{\chi^2_{2,q}}\), with confidence_ellipse_std_devs:

from tgmm import confidence_ellipse_std_devs

plot_gmm(X, gmm, ellipse_std_devs=confidence_ellipse_std_devs([0.5, 0.95]))  # 50% and 95% regions

docs.title: Initial vs Final Means
docs.text:
Show where EM started (gmm.initial_means_) alongside the fitted means:

plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    show_initial_means=True,
    show_means=True,
    ellipse_std_devs=[1],
    title='Initial vs Final Means'
)

docs.title: Weight Visualization
docs.text:
Scale marker size and/or ellipse transparency by each component's mixing weight:

plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    scale_alpha_by_weight=True,
    scale_size_by_weight=True,
    title='Scaled by Component Weight'
)

docs.title: Custom Styling
docs.text:
plot_gmm(
    X, gmm,
    # Point styling
    point_size=8,
    point_alpha=0.7,

    # Ellipse styling
    ellipse_std_devs=[1, 2, 3],
    ellipse_alpha=0.3,
    ellipse_fill=True,
    ellipse_line_style='--',

    # Mean markers
    mean_marker='*',
    mean_size=100,
    mean_color='red',

    title='Custom Styled GMM'
)

docs.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text:
from tgmm import dynamic_figsize

cov_types = ['full', 'diag', 'spherical']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(cov_types), figsize=dynamic_figsize(1, len(cov_types)))

for ax, cov_type in zip(axes, cov_types):
    gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_features=2, covariance_type=cov_type, random_state=42)
    gmm.fit(X_tensor)
    plot_gmm(X, gmm, ax=ax, show_ellipses=True, title=f'{cov_type.capitalize()} Covariance')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: High-Dimensional Data
docs.text:
plot_gmm requires exactly 2 features. Project higher-dimensional data down first, for example with PCA:

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_2d = pca.fit_transform(X_hd.numpy())

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=5, n_features=2)
gmm.fit(torch.tensor(X_2d, dtype=torch.float32))

plot_gmm(X_2d, gmm, show_ellipses=True, title='PCA Projection with Clusters')

See the PCA Plotting tutorial for fitting directly in the original high-dimensional space and only projecting for visualization.

docs.title: Matching Predicted Labels to Ground Truth
docs.text:
Cluster indices from predict() are arbitrary -- use match_predicted_to_true_labels to remap them (via the Hungarian algorithm) before computing supervised metrics or coloring plots consistently:

from tgmm import match_predicted_to_true_labels

predicted_labels = gmm.predict(X_tensor)
aligned_labels = match_predicted_to_true_labels(true_labels, predicted_labels)

plot_gmm's match_labels_to_true=True option does this internally when both true_labels and a fitted gmm are supplied.

docs.title: Tips for Effective Visualization
docs.text:
1. Project first: Use PCA (or another method) for data with more than 2 features
  2. Adjust transparency: Use point_alpha / ellipse_alpha to see overlapping clusters
  3. Use multiple std-dev levels: ellipse_std_devs=[1, 2, 3] shows spread at a glance
  4. Compare models side-by-side: Loop over covariance_type or initialization method with one ax per panel
  5. Check initial vs. final means: show_initial_means=True helps debug poor convergence

docs.title: Complete API Reference
docs.text: For full details on plot_gmm and its helpers, see the API Reference.

docs.title: von Mises-Fisher Mixtures
docs.text: plot_gmm draws Euclidean ellipses, so it cannot represent a VonMisesFisherMixture, whose data live on the unit sphere and whose components are described by a mean direction \(\mu_k\) and a concentration \(\kappa_k\). Two functions cover that case.

docs.title: plot_vmf: the circle (\(d=2\)) and the sphere (\(d=3\))
docs.text:
from tgmm import VonMisesFisherMixture, plot_vmf

vmf = VonMisesFisherMixture(n_components=3).fit(X_unit)   # X_unit: (n, 3), rows of unit norm

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection='3d')                      # a 3-D axes for d=3; omit `ax` to create one
plot_vmf(X_unit, vmf, ax=ax, cap_masses=(0.5, 0.9))

Points are coloured by predicted component (or by true_labels=). Each mean direction is an arrow from the origin, and each concentration is drawn as nested spherical caps -- the vMF analogue of confidence ellipses. A cap of angular radius \(\theta_m\) around \(\mu_k\) contains probability \(m\) of the component, where \(\theta_m\) solves \(P(\theta\le\theta_m)=m\) under the angle density

\[ f_\kappa(\theta)\;\propto\;e^{\kappa\cos\theta}\sin^{d-2}\theta,\qquad\theta=\arccos(\mu^{\top}x)\in[0,\pi]. \]

(The \(\sin^{d-2}\theta\) factor is the surface area of the ring at angle \(\theta\); the density is normalised numerically.) On the circle the caps are arcs just outside the unit circle, on the sphere they are rings of constant angular distance from \(\mu_k\). show_means, show_caps, cap_masses, legend_labels, view_elev and view_azim control the rest.

docs.title: plot_vmf_cosine: any dimension
docs.text:
from tgmm import plot_vmf_cosine

plot_vmf_cosine(X_embeddings, vmf)   # works for d = 768 just as for d = 5

For every component it histograms the angle between each assigned point and the component's mean direction and overlays the fitted \(f_{\kappa_k}(\theta)\) (dashed). If the vMF assumption holds, histogram and curve agree. In high dimension the typical angle is far from \(0^\circ\) even for large \(\kappa\): the mode solves \(\kappa\sin^2\theta=(d-2)\cos\theta\).

The helpers vmf_angle_density(kappa, n_features, theta) and vmf_cap_angle(kappa, n_features, mass) expose the angle density and cap radius directly. See the von Mises-Fisher tutorial for a gallery of vMF distributions on the circle and the sphere and worked examples of all three.

docs.title: Semi-Supervised and Positive-Unlabeled Fitting
docs.text:
Every tgmm mixture family (GaussianMixture, StudentTMixture, VonMisesFisherMixture) can be fit with partial label information, from "every row has a known class" down to "I only know some rows are positive, and nothing about the rest." This page covers the model, the algorithm (with the equations tgmm actually implements), the API, and which option to reach for.

Notation: \(n\) samples \(x_i\), \(K\) components with weights \(\pi_k\) and densities \(f_k\) (Gaussian, Student-t or von Mises-Fisher), responsibilities \(r_{ik}\), effective counts \(n_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\), log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta)\).

docs.title: The model: classes own blocks of components
docs.text:
Let the classes be \(c \in \{1, \dots, C\}\) (these are classes_, the sorted distinct label values). The \(K\) components are partitioned into contiguous blocks \(B_c\), one per class: with components_per_class=m every class owns \(m\) components (so \(K = mC\)), and with a dict, class \(c\) owns components_per_class[c] components -- the same idea as mclust's MclustDA. class_of_component_[k] says which class component \(k\) belongs to.

The density of an observation without a label is the ordinary mixture

\[ p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k f_k(x), \]

and the joint density of an observation \(x\) with known class \(c\) is the restriction of that sum to class \(c\)'s block:

\[ p(x, c) = \sum_{k \in B_c} \pi_k f_k(x). \]

So the weights \(\pi_k\) are joint class-and-component probabilities (summing to one over all components), and class proportions in the labeled data influence them. With \(L\) the set of labeled rows (class \(c_i\) for \(i \in L\)) and \(U\) the unlabeled rows, the semi-supervised log-likelihood is

\[ \ell_{\text{SS}}(\theta) = \sum_{i \in L} \log \sum_{k \in B_{c_i}} \pi_k f_k(x_i) \;+\; \sum_{i \in U} \log \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k f_k(x_i). \]

This is exactly what lower_bound_ reports for a semi-supervised fit (averaged over rows).

docs.title: Fitting with labels
docs.text:
import torch
from tgmm import GaussianMixture

labels = torch.full((X.shape[0],), -1)
labels[known_idx] = known_labels  # -1 everywhere else

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3)
gmm.fit(X, labels=labels)
gmm.predict_class(X)  # class labels, not raw component indices

n_components must equal the total number of components the components_per_class layout implies (for the default 1, the number of distinct labels). Label values needn't be contiguous integers.

docs.title: Fully labeled (no -1): no iteration needed
docs.text:
When every row is labeled, the class of each row never depends on the current parameters, so one M-step is exact:

  • With one component per class, each row's responsibility is the one-hot vector of its class, and a single M-step gives the per-class weight \(\pi_c = n_c/n\), mean and covariance (or \(\mu_c\), \(\kappa_c\), ...). This is the fully-labeled limit of Classification EM. n_iter_ is 1, converged_ is True.
  • With \(m_c > 1\) components for a class, that class's block is fit by ordinary unsupervised EM on only that class's rows, and its weights are rescaled by \(n_c / n\) so they sum to the class proportion. (Tied covariance types can't be assembled from independent blocks and raise a ValueError in this case.)

Any configured mean_prior/covariance_prior (Gaussian) still applies, giving a regularized supervised fit for classes with few samples.

docs.title: Partially labeled (some -1): semi-supervised EM
docs.text:
E-step. Compute the ordinary posterior \(r_{ik} \propto \pi_k f_k(x_i)\) for every row, then clamp the labeled rows to their class block: for \(i \in L\),

\[ r_{ik} \;\leftarrow\; \begin{cases} \dfrac{\pi_k f_k(x_i)}{\sum_{j \in B_{c_i}} \pi_j f_j(x_i)} & k \in B_{c_i},\\[2mm] 0 & k \notin B_{c_i}, \end{cases} \]

(one-hot when the block has a single component). A labeled row can then never "vote" for another class, but with \(m_c > 1\) it still softly splits across its own class's components. Unlabeled rows keep the full, ordinary posterior. This is the exact EM E-step for \(\ell_{\text{SS}}\), because the posterior over components given that \(x_i\) is known to belong to class \(c_i\) is the in-block renormalization above.

M-step. The family's usual M-step, run on the (clamped) \(r_{ik}\) -- for the Gaussian, \(n_k\), \(\bar y_k = \sum_i r_{ik}x_i / n_k\) and \(W_k = \sum_i r_{ik}(x_i - \bar y_k)(x_i - \bar y_k)^\top\) feed the same updates as in the Gaussian guide, and the Student-t/vMF M-steps are as in Other Mixture Families.

With unlabeled_weight=1 and label_confidence=1 this is plain EM on \(\ell_{\text{SS}}\), so the log-likelihood never decreases. A few labels per class are often enough to resolve what plain unsupervised EM can't -- which cluster is which class, and where the boundary falls on overlapping data. (The initialization itself is still unsupervised, e.g. k-means; the clamping then pulls each block onto its class. Use n_init > 1 if a poor start matters.)

docs.title: The two weighting knobs
docs.text:
unlabeled_weight \(=w\) (default 1.0). Before the M-step, every unlabeled row's responsibilities are multiplied by \(w\): \(r_{ik} \leftarrow w\, r_{ik}\) for \(i \in U\). Unlabeled rows then contribute \(w\sum_{i\in U} r_{ik}\) to \(n_k\), \(\bar y_k\) and \(W_k\), while labeled rows count fully. \(w = 0\) ignores the unlabeled data (a fit on the labeled rows alone); \(w = 1\) treats all rows equally. Small \(w\) protects against a mis-specified component density letting the (typically much more numerous) unlabeled rows swamp the labels.

label_confidence \(=c\) (default 1.0). For labels you don't fully trust, a labeled row's responsibility is the blend

\[ r_{i\cdot} = c\; r^{\text{in-block}}_{i\cdot} + (1 - c)\; r^{\text{out-of-block}}_{i\cdot}, \qquad r^{\text{out-of-block}}_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k f_k(x_i)\,\mathbb{1}[k \notin B_{c_i}]}{\sum_{j \notin B_{c_i}} \pi_j f_j(x_i)}, \]

i.e. mass \(c\) stays on the stated class (renormalized inside the block, as above) and mass \(1-c\) goes to the other classes' components in proportion to their posterior -- a soft correction for occasional mislabeling. It is a heuristic for noisy labels, not part of the likelihood: lower_bound_ still evaluates \(\ell_{\text{SS}}\) with the labels taken at face value.

CEM. With algorithm='cem', unlabeled rows are hard-assigned to their highest-responsibility component each iteration; labeled rows keep their clamped (soft or one-hot) responsibilities.

Scope note: semi-supervised fitting (partial labels) currently supports algorithm='em'/'cem' only; 'sem'/'saem'/online EM (step_size set) raise NotImplementedError. Gibbs-sampling mode (n_components=None) is not supported with labels, and tied covariance types combined with components_per_class > 1 aren't supported either.

docs.title: More than one component per class
docs.text:
Real classes aren't always unimodal. components_per_class (an int, or a dict keyed by label value) gives a class more than one component:

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, components_per_class={0: 2, 1: 1})
gmm.fit(X, labels=labels)  # class 0 gets 2 components, class 1 gets 1

predict(X) returns raw component indices; predict_class(X) sums each row's responsibility over every class block and returns the class with the largest total, mapped back through classes_:

\[ \hat c(x) = \arg\max_c \sum_{k \in B_c} r_k(x). \]

When components_per_class is a dict, its keys define the full set of classes (a key needn't appear in labels); every labeled value must be one of those keys.

docs.title: Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning
docs.text:
Positive-unlabeled learning is the more extreme case: you know some rows are positive (e.g. confirmed cancer cells), and everything else is unlabeled -- it could be positive or negative, you just don't know. PositiveUnlabeledMixture models the unlabeled density as

\[ p_U(x) = \pi\, f_P(x) + (1-\pi)\, f_N(x), \]

with \(f_P\) and \(f_N\) themselves mixtures (a positive block of n_components_positive components and a negative block of n_components_negative), and estimates both densities and \(\pi\) jointly:

from tgmm import PositiveUnlabeledMixture

pu = PositiveUnlabeledMixture(n_components_positive=1, n_components_negative=5)
pu.fit(X, positive_mask)  # bool mask, True = confirmed positive

pu.class_prior_                  # estimated fraction of *unlabeled* rows that are positive
pu.predict_proba_positive(X)     # P(positive) for arbitrary X
pu.predict_positive(X, threshold=0.5)

docs.title: How it is fit
docs.text:
PositiveUnlabeledMixture is a thin wrapper over the semi-supervised fit above: it builds the chosen family's mixture with components_per_class={1: n_components_positive, 0: n_components_negative} (so the negative block comes first in component order, the positive block last), labels 1 on positive_mask and -1 everywhere else, and fits it. The labeled positives are clamped to the positive block; each unlabeled row keeps the full posterior over both blocks. The estimates are

\[ P(\text{positive} \mid x) = \sum_{k \in P} r_k(x) \quad(\texttt{predict\_proba\_positive}), \qquad \hat\pi = \frac{1}{|U|} \sum_{i \in U} \sum_{k \in P} r_{ik} \quad(\texttt{class\_prior\_}), \]

i.e. class_prior_ is the average total positive-block responsibility over the unlabeled rows only. (Do not read it off weights_: the mixture weights are estimated over all rows, labeled positives included, so the positive block's total weight is \(\approx (n_L + \hat\pi\,|U|)/n\), larger than \(\hat\pi\).)

This assumes SCAR (Selected Completely At Random; Elkan & Noto, 2008): the labeled positives are a uniform random sample of all true positives, not a biased subset (e.g. "the easiest-to-confirm cases"). Under SCAR the labeled positives are draws from \(f_P\) itself, which is what lets them be clamped to the positive block. If your labeled positives were selected some other way, class_prior_ and the fitted densities can be biased -- SCAR is a real assumption, not a formality.

This is also sometimes called mixture proportion estimation: the whole point is estimating \(\pi\), the mixing proportion of the (fully-unobserved) positive class within the unlabeled pool. A related, distinct problem is semi-supervised novelty detection (Blanchard, Lee & Scott, 2010): given a labeled "normal" sample and an unlabeled mix of normal and novel points, decide which unlabeled points are novel -- closer to anchor='fixed' below (treating the labeled class as a known, unmoving reference density) than to PU's 'prior' default.

docs.title: Picking anchor
docs.text:
The mixture proportion \(\pi\) is only identifiable if the negative block can't simply absorb the positive one (a sufficiently flexible negative block can always explain every unlabeled point, driving \(\hat\pi \to 0\)). anchor controls how tightly the positive block stays tied to the labeled positives. All three start from a first fit of the positive block on the labeled positives alone, \((\mu_P^{0}, \Sigma_P^{0})\):

anchor Positive block behavior Corresponds to 'fixed' Frozen at the labeled-only fit after every M-step; only the negative block (and the weights) keep moving. Classical mixture-proportion estimation / semi-supervised novelty detection (the "normal" class is a fixed reference). 'prior' (default) Used as an NIW prior of strength \(n_L\) (below), so unlabeled positives can still refine it without drifting toward the negatives. Gaussian-only. A softer version of the same -- lets genuinely-positive-but-different-looking unlabeled points still pull the estimate, within reason. 'free' Initialized from the labeled-only fit, then plain semi-supervised EM, no further anchoring. Plain PU learning with no identifiability safeguard -- can drift toward the negatives on strongly overlapping data.

For 'prior', after each M-step the positive block's parameters are replaced by an NIW posterior (the same conjugate update as in the Gaussian guide) with prior mean \(\mu_P^0\), prior scale \(\Psi_0 = n_L\,\Sigma_P^0\) and prior strength \(\lambda_0 = \nu_0 = n_L\) (the number of labeled positives), using the positive block's current responsibilities:

\[ \mu_P = \frac{\lambda_0 \mu_P^0 + n_P \bar y_P}{\lambda_0 + n_P}, \qquad \Sigma_P = \frac{\Psi_0 + W_P + \frac{\lambda_0 n_P}{\lambda_0 + n_P}(\bar y_P - \mu_P^0)(\bar y_P - \mu_P^0)^\top}{\nu_0 + n_P}, \]

where \(n_P\), \(\bar y_P\), \(W_P\) are that block's effective count, weighted mean and scatter. The labeled positives therefore enter twice -- once through the prior, once as data with responsibility \(1\) -- which anchors the block strongly; the prior is worth about \(n_L\) pseudo-observations.

family='gaussian' (default), 'student_t', or 'vmf' picks which mixture family models both blocks; 'student_t' is a reasonable choice when either class has outliers, 'vmf' when X is L2-normalized directional data. anchor='prior' is Gaussian-only (NIW conjugate priors aren't a concept for the other two families) -- use 'fixed' or 'free' with family='student_t'/'vmf'.

Any keyword not listed above (covariance_type, random_state, max_iter, ...) is forwarded to the underlying mixture's constructor; anything not defined on PositiveUnlabeledMixture itself (bic, score, sample, ...) is transparently forwarded to the fitted mixture (pu.model_) too. n_components_negative=None (an unbounded Gibbs sampler for the negative block) is not implemented and raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• class_prior_ quality depends on the negative block being able to model the negative class without wandering into the positive region; more negative components make that easier and make identifiability harder -- use anchor='fixed'/'prior' and check class_prior_ is stable across n_components_negative.
  • Labeled positives are clamped to the positive block, so (with the default label_confidence=1) a mislabeled "positive" is never corrected. To allow that, pass label_confidence=c with c < 1 through **family_kwargs; the unlabeled rows are handled as usual.
  • predict_proba_positive uses the fitted mixture weights, which include the labeled positives (see above); class_prior_ is the right estimate of the positive fraction in a fresh unlabeled sample.

See notebook 18_semi_supervised_pu.ipynb for a worked example of both features.
